In addition, while attuned to the map, you can't be lost by any means, know exactly where you are, and can't roll below 15 on Wisdom ({@skill Perception}) checks.

If the place you choose is some sort of settlement, it teleports you to an unoccupied space close to its entrances (not inside of it). If you choose a non-settlement area (such as a forest), the map teleports you to an unoccupied space as well. Just like the {@spell teleport} spell, you can choose eight people with you. The item can be used 2 times before you finish a long rest.

item.name: Potion of Coordination
entries: This magic potion resembles a white wine with magical shimmers in it. The drinker gets advantage on the next {@dice 1d4} attack rolls it makes in the next minute.

item.name: Titian's Brush
entries: This magical brush absorbed the essence of Titian's magic, one of the greatest talents in the era of the Renaissance. It has the marks and traces of being used for many years and resembles almost a worthless object, rotten by the touch of time. While attuned to the item, the user can cast the {@spell beaux-arts|EchoesOfRenaissance} and {@spell alter scent|EchoesOfRenaissance} cantrips at will. Charisma is the spellcasting ability for the spells mentioned in this item's description.

The user can cast each of the {@spell fabricate} and {@spell creation} spells three times a day. They regain the ability to cast them this way when they finish a long rest. When they cast the {@spell fabricate} spell this way, they can cast it as an action. When they cast the {@spell creation} spell this way, an object's duration is extended until they cast the spell again.

item.name: Artisan's Hat
entries: While wearing this hat, you can cast the {@spell inspect substance|EchoesOfRenaissance} cantrip at will. Each casting of the spell consumes 1 cp in your pocket.

item.name: Book of Countless Pages
entries: This magic book was the result of a dying scholar's waning willpower, who wished for the spread of knowledge and was sentenced to death for it. The blank pages appear as mundane paper bound in a leather binding with no apparent book or author name.

By speaking aloud the name of a nonmagical book you have read before, the Book of Countless pages becomes an exact replica of the book you named and stays like that until it is read fully by a creature or the holder names another one. You cannot name another book until you finish a long rest.

The term magical books mean magic items like {@item tome of understanding} or {@item manual of golems}, not books, guides or notes about magic. At the discretion of the GM, it could be used on spellbooks of wizards.

item.name: Cunning Merchant's Hat
entries: This hat has been carried by many famous merchants, travelers, and the like throughout many adventures at sea and has become enchanted with their will. While attuned to it, you can expend a charge before a Charisma ({@skill Persuasion}) roll or a Wisdom ({@skill Insight}) roll and treat the d20 as 15. The hat has three charges which are restored at dawn.

item.name: Faithful Priest's Cape
entries: This cape is adorned with white and gold and carries symbols of protection and safety. While attuned to this cape, you have advantage on saving throws against spells and take half damage from spells.

item.name: Good-luck Helmet
entries: This magic helm carries a child's drawing etched on it with these words: "Good luck, papa!" While attuned to it, the wearer is under the effects of the {@spell death ward} spell. Once {@spell death ward}'s effect happens, the wearer is instantly healed {@dice 4d8}. The {@spell death ward} spell is cast on the helm at dawn, and the healing effect can't be used again until the {@spell death ward} spell is restored.

item.name: Infinite Pen
entries: This quill is made by a priest with an ambition to finish copying a Bible in very little time. This quill can be used without need of any ink, and the ink appears in any color of the user's desire.

item.name: Enchanted Cape
entries: This enchanted cape is adorned with fine fabric of many colors and grants proficiency in {@skill Performance} checks to the one who wears it.

item.name: Enchanted Puppet
entries: While holding this puppet and attuned to it, you can face toward a creature of your choice that you can see and cast one of these spells: {@spell hold person}, {@spell hold monster}, {@spell dominate beast}, or {@spell dominate person}; it must be fitting for the spell's description, such as creature type and range.

item.name: Marvelous Picture
entries: This glorious painting depicts a group of actors performing a play on stage. By touching it and saying the command word "Virtù!" the painting transforms into a stage according to your desires in 10 minutes. For example, it could have all the necessary devices, props, objects, stage decorations to play the famous Greek Tragedy, Prometheus Bound. The stage stays like this for 8 hours. It gives +10 bonus to {@skill Performance} skill checks to creatures that perform on the stage, unless they are hostile towards you. To mundane eyes, the stage is wonderfully crafted.

item.name: Mask of the Mist
entries: While attuned, this mask is {@condition invisible} on your face. In its normal form, it carries different strands of hair or tiny body parts of different creature types etched into its surface. You can speak its command word, "Abu Ahmar," and change how other spells or effects discern your creature type: for example, if you are humanoid, you can change it to appear as a celestial.

item.name: Mirror of Moonlight
entries: This mirror can be used to cast both the {@spell moongaze|EchoesOfRenaissance} and {@spell moonflare|EchoesOfRenaissance} spells once each before shattering. The spell save DC is 13, and the spell attack roll is +5.

item.name: Mirror of the Crescent
entries: This mirror can be used to cast each of the {@spell moongaze|EchoesOfRenaissance} and {@spell moonflare|EchoesOfRenaissance} spells. The mirror has five charges. Each spell expends one charge. The charges are restored at dawn.

item.name: Nightingale Root
entries: This consumable root, when cooked properly while singing a song worthy of nightingales, grants the consumer the following ability: you do not need to sleep for the next two days.

item.name: Nobleman's Signet
entries: This magic ring carries a magical sigil created by a cunning con-artist to resemble a noble house's sigil. It actually has a magic stone on it rather than an actual noble sigil. Anyone who tries to remember the sigil must succeed on a {@dc 20} Intelligence ({@skill History}) check. On a failed save, they will think it is legitimate but won't be able to remember which noble family had it.

item.name: One-Eyed Doll
entries: This doll is imbued with magic and powers of augury. You point it toward a creature within 15 ft. of you and force it to make a Wisdom saving throw. On a failed save, it believes any statement about its future for the next minute. Once you do so, you can't use this item again until the next dawn.

item.name: Oar of the Sturdy
entries: This magic oar carries the essence of the willpower that is lost at sea. While commanding a waterborne vehicle with it, you are considered proficient with it, and the vehicle takes less damage each time it is hit. The damage reduction is equal to your proficiency bonus.

item.name: Potion of Wanderer's Vitality
entries: This potion appears to be clean white clouds and makes one want to sleep while looking at them. When consumed, it reduces one's {@condition exhaustion} level by 1.

item.name: Root of the Deep
entries: These moonlight-touched roots were collected by men of the coast and put into enchanted water. The potion resembles a wavy day at the beach under the crescent moon's radiance. When consumed, they grant the ability to have a swimming speed equal to one's walking speed for 1 hour.

item.name: Scholar's Ring
entries: The ring carries a magic shard with the essence of an ancient scholar's breath. While attuned to it, a creature is counted as proficient in all Intelligence checks, thus adding its proficiency bonus to all of them. In addition, it can cast {@spell Da Vinci's mind lantern|EchoesOfRenaissance} cantrip at will.

item.name: Surgeon's Arcane Kit
entries: While holding this kit, which includes needles, sharp objects, and other items needed for a surgery, you can cast the {@spell doctor's sense|EchoesOfRenaissance} cantrip at will and the {@spell cure wounds} spell once a day.

item.name: Trident of the Mediterranean
entries: This incredible trident belonged to seafarers with great ferocity and bravery who have roamed one of the greatest seas in the world as pirates. This magic weapon gives +2 bonus to attack rolls and damage rolls made with it. While attuned to it, you gain the following benefits:

items: Your attacks with the weapon deal an additional {@damage 1d8} cold damage.
You are immune to cold damage.
You have a swimming speed of 40 ft.
When you throw the weapon, you can make it appear on your free hand (no action required).

item.name: Wanderer's Necklace
entries: The necklace is adorned with colorful gemstones from all over the world. While attuned to this item, you are under the effects of the {@spell tongues} spell, and you have +2 bonus to your {@skill Persuasion} skill.

item.name: Wristband of Protection
entries: This magical wristband has five charges. By expending a charge, you can cast one of the following spells: {@spell shield}, {@spell mage armor}, {@spell lesser restoration}, {@spell protection from evil and good}, and {@spell dreamcatcher|EchoesOfRenaissance}. The expended charges are restored at dawn.

item.name: The Lance of the Last Knight
entries: The Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian the First was an avid jouster. His lance still hungers for the thrill of the tilt, though it knows its days are numbered.

You have a +1 bonus to attack and damage rolls made with this weapon. If mounted, when a hit is scored on a mounted opponent, they must pass a {@dc 13} Dexterity saving throw or be knocked from their mount and {@condition prone}. They take {@damage 1d6} bludgeoning damage from the fall.

item.name: The Sword of Grutte Pier
entries: This black zweihänder once belonged to the Frisian hero Pier Gerolfs Donia, or "Grutte Pier" (Great Pier). Pier was reportedly so strong that he could decapitate several attackers in one swing of this mighty blade. On the hilt is inscribed the famous shibboleth that Pier would make captives recite, to be able to tell if they were Frisian or an enemy: Bûter, brea en griene tsiis: wa't dat net sizze kin, is gjin oprjochte Fries. (Butter, bread, and green cheese: if you can't say that, you're not a real Frisian.)

This sword is a +2 magical greatsword which negates any resistances to slashing and bludgeoning damage. Additionally, you can target two creatures of the same size who are within 5 ft. of each other with the same sweeping attack. On a hit, you deal identical damage to both targets.

item.name: The Yatağan of Kemal Reis
entries: The gilded tughra on this sword bears the name Ahmed Kemaleddin, feared Ottoman pirate admiral. Sunk along with the rest of his fleet, the sword was thought lost until recovered by the Duke of Naxos and taken to Venice. It is said that once engaged in combat, nobody escaped this heavy duty cutting blade.

The yatağan is a +2 magical longsword, and while attuned to the sword, Attacks of Opportunity made with the blade are made with advantage. Additionally, the wielder's movement speed is increased by 10 ft.

item.name: Arrow of Distraction
entries: When you hit a creature using this magic ammunition, the creature must succeed on a {@dc 15} Constitution saving throw. On a failed save, it subtracts {@dice 1d10} from all of its attack rolls, ability checks and saving throws for the next minute. It can repeat the saving throw each time it takes damage to be freed from the effect.

item.name: Arrow of Soul Reaping
entries: When you hit a creature with this magic ammunition, a curdling wave of necrotic energy forces all creatures within 20 ft. of it to make a {@dc 17} Constitution saving throw. On a failed save, their maximum hit points is reduced by {@dice 6d8}. On a successful save, they take {@damage 6d8} necrotic damage. If the maximum hit point reduction kills the target, you control the targets as suitable undead (GM's decision) for 1 hour. The maximum hit point reduction lasts until the end of their next long rest, if they survive.

item.name: Amulet of Adam and Eve
entries: While attuned to and wearing this amulet, a humanoid belonging to a non-human race will appear outwardly human without altering their general appearance features. For instance, a tiefling will seem to lack a tail and horns, and will have skin resembling a shade of brown of their choosing. However, these changes, such as the disappearance of a tail, can be detected through physical touch.

item.name: Goblet of Perspicacity
entries: This wine glass is made from fine Murano glass but is as durable as stone. Once per day, a creature can drink a glass of wine from this goblet and regain 1 hit point. In addition, they have advantage on Wisdom ({@skill Insight}) checks for 1 hour. They can use the goblet as a regular wine glass before or after they choose to activate its ability.

item.name: Decanter of Endless Wine
entries: This item works exactly like a {@item decanter of endless water}, except that it produces a chilled white wine instead of water. This stoppered flask sloshes when shaken, as if it contains liquid. The decanter weighs 2 pounds. You can use an action to remove the stopper and speak one of three command words, whereupon an amount of chilled white wine pours out of the flask. The wine stops pouring out at the start of your next turn. Choose from the following options:

items: "Geyser" produces 30 gallons of wine that gushes forth in a geyser 30 feet long and 1 foot wide. As a bonus action while holding the decanter, you can aim the geyser at a creature you can see within 30 feet of you. The target must succeed on a {@dc 13} Strength saving throw or take {@damage 1d4} bludgeoning damage and fall {@condition prone}. Instead of a creature, you can target an object that isn't being worn or carried and that weighs no more than 200 pounds. The object is either knocked over or pushed up to 15 feet away from you.

item.name: Coral Candlestick
entries: This candlestick carved from red Aegean coral imbues whatever candle is placed in it to have the abilities of a {@item lantern of revealing}.
Additionally, the one attuned to the candlestick learns the {@spell guidance} cantrip even if they do not have the ability to cast spells normally. They can cast {@spell guidance} 3 times per day.

item.name: Lazarus Flail
entries: You gain a +1 bonus to attack and damage rolls made with this magic weapon. In addition, when you hit with this weapon, the target takes an extra {@damage 1d6} radiant damage.

item.name: La Teriaca, Venetian Treacle
entries: This potion originated in the experiments on prisoners conducted by King Mithridates VI of Pontus to create his mithridatium remedy. Later, Roman medical minds and the great Greek physician Galen perfected a theriac of 64 ingredients, including such wildly diverse items as ground viper flesh, castoreum (excretion from a beaver), cinnamon, myrrh, turpentine, and Dead Sea bitumen. Since then numerous variations have emerged, and Venice, being at the center of the spice trade, has perfected its own state-sanctioned version. Efficacy is debatable, and most of the stuff touted as teriaca on the streets is an overpriced and spurious palliative. However, genuine teriaca will relieve pain and work against certain poisons.
Ingesting genuine teriaca will cure one poison afflicting the one who drinks it. It will also remove one level of {@condition exhaustion}.

This magic dagger has +1 bonus to attack and damage rolls and has three charges. On a hit, you can expend a charge to force the creature you hit to make a Constitution saving throw. On a failed save, it can't cast magic for 1 minute. However, you must concentrate on this ability as if you are concentrating on a spell. Expended charges return when you finish a long rest.

These kinds of swords were forged by a faithful blacksmith on a rueful night in order to protect their realm. This magic weapon gives a +2 bonus to attack rolls and damage rolls made with it. While attuned to it, the sword gives you the following features:

items: When you miss an attack roll, you can use your reaction to hit instead.

feat.name: Artisan Apprentice
entries: You trained in the ways of artisans and you aspire to be one of the greatest. You gain the following benefits:

items: You gain proficiency in the {@skill Insight} skill and in an artisan tool of your choice. If you are already proficient in {@skill Insight}, you can choose another skill tied to Wisdom.
When you encounter an object using your artisan tool proficiency, you know its worth immediately.

feat.name: Elegant Dancer
entries: The way you move and perform on stages or streets enthralls crowds and grants you these features:

items: You gain proficiency with the {@skill Performance} skill, and you have advantage on it when you are dancing.
You can cast each of the {@spell expeditious retreat} and {@spell longstrider} spells once, without expending a spell slot, and you regain the ability to do so when you finish a long rest.

feat.name: Enchanting Singer
entries: You trained your voice over the years, and it contains amazing power.

items: You gain proficiency with the {@skill Performance} skill and have advantage on it when you are singing.

You can cast the {@spell charm person} spell once without expending a spell slot and regain the ability to do so once you finish a long rest. If you cast it this way, it must be in the form of a song, and you can't force the {@condition charmed} people to do anything harmful towards others. However, if they are {@condition charmed}, they will not know it was you who charmed them, unless someone casts the {@spell identify} spell on them or has a way to tell if there is magic involved.

feat.name: Esteemed Painter
entries: You excel at artistic pursues, especially giving life to white canvases.

items: You gain proficiency in {@item painter's supplies} and double your proficiency bonus with it if you don't already double it from another source, such as Expertise.

You learn a bard cantrip of your choice and can cast it at will. You also learn a 1st-level bard spell and can cast it without expending a spell slot twice a day and regain the ability to do so when you finish a long rest. Charisma is your spellcasting ability modifier for both of them.

feat.name: Artisan Master
entries: You have mastered the way of the artisans, and your experience helps to improve your work greatly.

You can cast the {@spell inspect substance|EchoesOfRenaissance} cantrip at will. You can also cast {@spell identify} and {@spell adept ears|EchoesOfRenaissance} spells once without expending a spell slot. Intelligence, Wisdom or Charisma is your spellcasting ability for these spells, you choose which one you gain this feat.

feat.name: Hearth-Tender
entries: You always keep a flame to light the night, and you know the abilities of fire to bring life and warmth.

items: You can use your action to cause flames to flicker, change color or make shapes to appear in them for 1 minute. You also can light or put out a torch or a campfire by touching it, without hurting yourself.
You learn the {@spell produce flame} cantrip and can cast it at will. Wisdom is your spellcasting ability for it.
You gain resistance to fire damage.

feat.name: Lightbringer
entries: You always have your way with light and pushing away the darkness at dire times.

items: You know the {@spell light} and {@spell dancing lights} cantrips and can cast them at will.

You learn the {@spell guiding bolt} and {@spell daylight} spells. You can cast each of them once without expending a spell slot. You regain the ability to do so after you finish a long rest. Charisma is your spellcasting ability modifier for the spells.

feat.name: Adept Interrogator
entries: You are adept at interrogations and extracting information from those who are unwilling. You can cast the {@spell detect thoughts} spell twice, without expending a spell slot. You can increase the duration by 1 minute or more, but you risk increasing amounts of {@condition exhaustion}: you must make a DC 14 Constitution saving throw for each extra minute added (including the first additional minute); on a failure, you gain one point of {@condition exhaustion} and take {@damage 1d4} psychic damage for each minute that you push this ability further. Charisma is your spellcasting ability for the spell.

feat.name: Marvelous Mender
entries: You learn the {@spell mending} cantrip and can use it in ways unimaginable to others. You can cast {@spell mending} to restore consumable magic items after they are consumed. The magic items must be common or uncommon, and once you restore a consumable item, the same item can't be restored by you or another creature with the same feat. For spell scrolls, it can't be higher than a 2nd-level spell scroll. You also can't restore charges to an item, even if the item ceases to function after the charges are used. Wisdom is your spellcasting ability for the cantrip.

When you reach certain levels, your abilities grow more powerful, and you can restore magic to rarer items than uncommon and more powerful spell scrolls than 2nd-level spells. You can restore magic to rare items and 3rd-level spell scrolls at 8th level; very rare magic items and 4th level spell scrolls at 12th level; and 5th level spell scrolls at 16th level.

feat.name: Physician's Eye
entries: You have spent time learning and honing your skills in medicine and dealing with diseases.

items: You double your proficiency bonus with the {@skill Medicine} skill unless you double it from another source, such as Expertise. You can use the {@skill Medicine} skill with Wisdom or Intelligence.
You have advantage on saving throws against diseases.
You have resistance to poison damage and have advantage on saving throws against being {@condition poisoned}.

You can use your bonus action to diagnose your companions' conditions with only a look. You learn if they are under the effects of any condition, spell, curse or similar, and you also learn their current hit points. You can use this against an enemy as well if you succeed on a {@skill Medicine} check against their Charisma ({@skill Deception}) check that the GM rolls in secret. On a success, you also learn their resistances and immunities.

feat.name: Spellbreaker
entries: Your study of the arcane arts has led you to find a way to break the weave while it is formed. You can cast {@spell counterspell} twice without expending a spell slot. You regain the ability to do so when you finish a long rest.

feat.name: Spell Disruptor
entries: You spend enough time working to disrupt the already knit strings of the weave. You can cast {@spell dispel magic} twice without expending a spell slot. You regain the ability to do so when you finish a long rest.

feat.name: Swimmer
entries: Your time spent in canals, rivers, lakes, and seas has improved your abilities in water.

items: Your swimming speed increases to 40 ft. if it is not greater already.
You don't provoke opportunity attacks in underwater combat or while swimming.
Your time to hold your breath is doubled.
If a watery surface is considered difficult terrain, you are not affected by it.

feat.name: Undead Hunter
entries: You have devoted your life to fight the plague that is the enemy of life, and you gain these abilities:

items: You gain resistance to necrotic damage.
You sense any undead within 30 ft. of you.
When you deal damage to an undead creature, you deal an additional {@damage 1d4} radiant damage.

feat.name: Witch Hunter
entries: You are trained and have shown incredible skill in hunting dark creatures at night.

items: You learn the {@spell hunter's mark} spell and one of the following spells: {@spell moonflare|EchoesOfRenaissance} or {@spell moongaze|EchoesOfRenaissance} (you choose when you gain this feat). You can cast each of them once without expending a spell slot, and you regain the ability to do so when you finish a long rest. Wisdom is your spellcasting ability for these spells.

feat.name: Watcher in the Night
entries: You are aware of non-human dangers and the threats they pose. You are ready for such danger.

You learn these spells and can cast each of them once without expending a spell slot: {@spell detect evil and good}, {@spell darkvision}, and {@spell see invisibility}. You regain the ability to do so when you finish a long rest.

feat.name: Vigilant
entries: You have survived many traps and ambushes, and you are ready for such attempts.

items: You can cast these spells once without expending a spell slot: {@spell alarm} and {@spell shield}. Wisdom is your spellcasting ability modifier for these spells.
You add +2 to your initiative rolls.

feat.name: Valiant Warrior
entries: You are known for your courage and bold actions in battles. You have access to these features:

items: You can cast the {@spell heroism} spell twice without expending a spell slot. You regain the ability to do so when you finish a long rest. Charisma is your spellcasting ability for this spell.

When you fail a saving throw against being {@condition frightened}, you can use your reaction to cast the {@spell heroism} spell if you have uses left. The spell's target can also be a creature within range, when it fails the saving throw.

When you score a critical hit, you can force the creature to make a Wisdom saving throw against your spell save DC (from Charisma) or be {@condition frightened} of you until the end of your next turn.

variantrule.name: Spell Rebound Effects

entries: This section is the revised version of the Spell Rebound Table section in {@i Historica Arcanum: The City of Crescent}.
Magic comes at a price.

This is the first lesson every disciple of the arcane arts learns—the easy way, or the hard way—whether they are in the esteemed arcane chambers of mighty libraries, twilight forests with the deepest roots, the coldest zeniths of the highest mountains, or amongst scorching deserts where the dunes forgive nothing.
A GM may want to include these rules in a game set in the world of Historica Arcanum to show why magic is considered dangerous universally and to add some consequence to spell casting.

entries.name: Core Mechanic
entries: In the table below, a trigger for a Spell Rebound is shown depending on the caster's proficiency bonus. However, a GM may deem a situation to be appropriate for a Spell Rebound.

entries.caption: Spell Rebound Triggers
rows: Expending all spell slots.
Expending a highest level spell slot.**
Casting two spells in successive rounds or in the same round***. Cantrips do not count.
Casting a spell that includes a damage roll, such as {@spell fireball}, {@spell magic missile}, {@spell blight}, and {@spell scorching ray}. Cantrips do not count.
Casting a spell of 6th level or higher.
+7 or higher*

Dropping a creature to 0 hit points with a spell, magical ability, a supernatural feature or the like or restoring life to a creature while it is on 0 hit points with a spell or a similar magical effect.
footnotes: *The usual maximum proficiency bonus for a player character is +6. Some creatures may have higher proficiency bonuses than that, such as a lich or an ancient red dragon, but those kinds of immensely powerful creatures are very rare or nonexistent in the Historica Arcanum universe.

**For warlocks, this trigger is considered as such: "Casting a spell that is provided with Eldritch Invocations and requires one to expend a spell slot or use in a somehow limited way, such as casting {@spell compulsion} through bewitching whispers."
***Such as casting the {@spell magic missile} spell on its own initiative count and casting the {@spell shield} spell at another creature's turn but during the same round.

entries: Triggers are cumulative. If a creature has +4 proficiency bonus, the triggers for lower proficiency bonuses apply as well.

entries.name: Trigger
entries: The character makes a saving throw using the same ability used for spellcasting. For example, a wizard makes an Intelligence saving throw because the wizard's spellcasting ability is Intelligence. The DC equals the character's own spell save DC. On a failed save, consult the Effects table below.

On a successful save, nothing happens, and the character cannot trigger the same Spell Rebound until it finishes a long rest (a creature that fails can trigger the effects again). If it can trigger it by another means, the trigger will happen again. For example, a 5th level wizard casting a {@spell fireball} triggers the spell rebound. When the wizard expends their last spell slot, the spell rebound is triggered again.

If a creature has two separate spellcasting ability scores due to multiclassing, taking a feat or other reasons, the source of the spell determines the ability score. If a spell somehow comes from separate sources at once, use the highest DC possible.
Some situations can cause more than one trigger, so each one requires its own saving throw.

entries.name: Effects
entries: There are three types of effects: Cosmetic, Destructive, and Internal. Cosmetic effects usually do not harm creatures or affect nearby objects or constructs by means of dealing damage, but it may bring many social or similar consequences with them. Destructive effects usually damage nearby people and/or objects, possibly including the caster. Internal effects usually only affect the caster.
There are alternative ways to determine which category of effect occurs:
A GM may roll a {@dice d6} and choose which categorical effect occurs:
It may depend on the school of magic of the spell that triggers the effect. A GM may choose a different category from the ones listed below:

items: The GM may decide which category to use depending on the triggering spell's theme, effect, or type. For example, a {@spell healing word} spell may cause internal damage, while a damaging spell could cause destructive damage. A necromancy spell may cause internal damage regardless.
It may depend on the situation. If the caster tries to harm someone, the effect could be internal. If the caster is deceiving someone, the effect could be cosmetic.

Some spells are ignored when its casting coincides with a trigger: {@spell detect magic}, {@spell identify}, {@spell lesser restoration}, {@spell dispel magic}, {@spell counterspell}, {@spell greater restoration} and {@spell antimagic field} (except when cast using 9th level spell slots).
Casting a spell that is 4th level or higher from a spell scroll always causes a trigger.

Using a class feature or a similar effect that enables a creature to cast a spell of 3rd level or higher, or expending a spell slot of 3rd level or higher directly causes a trigger: for example, a warlock's Mystic Arcanum, or a paladin's Divine Smite (3rd level or higher).

Some vague but apparently magical features require the caster to succeed on a Constitution saving throw. The DC is equal to the caster level's + its proficiency bonus. On a failed save, it causes a trigger. These magical features include Channel Divinity, and some Eldritch Invocations.
Casting a 9th level spell or expending a 9th level spell slot is counted as another destructive trigger, no matter what the spell is.

entries.name: Optional Rule: Disease & Curse Tie-in
entries: As an optional rule, you can check out the Plague & Disease Module in Empires of the Silk Road for Rituals or Magical Symptoms to replace an Effect or a Special Condition. For example, Power Drain could be an effect, and its special condition can be "removed by a Clover Ritual."

entries.name: Cosmetic Effects
entries: These effects usually cause visual changes on the caster or their surroundings. Applying advantage or disadvantage on a check besides the stated effects is up to the GM. For example, the first and fourth effects could cause disadvantage on Charisma checks as well.
The GM rolls on the table or determines which effect occurs (The options below only provide ideas and guides; the GM may come up with their own effects):

entries.caption: Cosmetic Effects
rows: {@b Stutter:} The caster stutters for the next {@dice 3d6} hours. Disadvantage on spell attack rolls for the duration (Spells with verbal component).
The {@spell greater restoration} spell ends this effect early.

{@b Bodily Dysfunction:} The caster suffers a malevolent effect that badly affects the body. For example, if the leg is affected, the caster may suffer a limp and thus have their walking speed reduced by half. It lasts for 3d4 days.
{@b Rot:} Vegetables and plants within 120 ft. of the caster wither and die. It lasts {@dice 2d6} days.
Bathing under the moonlight reduces the area to 30 ft for the next 24 hours.
{@b Pale Skin:} The caster appears sickly and extremely pale. The effect lasts {@dice 2d6} days.
The {@spell greater restoration} spell ends this effect early.
{@b Glow in the Dark:} The caster's eyes or other limbs (for example, their hands) glow in total darkness. The effect lasts for 3d4 days.
Drinking water from a river during sunset negates this effect until midnight.
{@b Scar:} The caster receives a scar determined by the GM.
The scar can only be removed with a {@spell greater restoration} spell that is cast from an 8th-level or higher spell slot.
{@b Wild Despise:} The wild seems to despise the caster. Wild beasts are aggressive towards them, and urban animals are terrified of them. Dogs and cats alike usually hiss and growl at the caster.
Chewing a three-leaf clover at the start of the day reduces the aggressiveness of the beasts.

{@b Shaking Hands:} The caster's hands start to shake, and it constantly gets worse. The caster has disadvantage on Dexterity or Strength checks that are related to the hands. It lasts for {@dice 2d4} days.
{@b Constant Cold:} The caster constantly feels cold and appears to be shivering.
While in extreme heat, this effect is not seen.

{@b Reflection Mishap:} The caster's reflection in proper surfaces looks wrong, such as facing in the wrong direction, doing something else entirely: crying, appearing angry, or appearing extremely happy. These oddities usually happen briefly, for mere seconds, and disappear. These effects can be seen for 2d8 days.

entries.name: Destructive Effects
entries: Many effects trigger a saving throw. While dealing with those effects, the DC is equal to the caster's spell save DC. If not specified, the caster also gets impacted by the effect.
The GM rolls on the table or determines which effect occurs:

entries.caption: Destructive Effects
rows: {@b Hellfire:} Flames erupt from you as if you were bringing the fire from the depths of Tartarus itself. Any object that is flammable catches fire within 120 ft. of the caster. Each creature within 120 ft. must succeed on a Constitution saving throw or take {@dice 5d6} fire damage. Each proficiency bonus after +2 adds another {@dice 2d6} fire damage.
A {@spell counterspell} stops this effect if the triggering spell is 3rd level or lower. If it is higher, the DC is equal to 10 + spell slot's level.

{@b Quake:} The ground shakes. Each creature within 300 ft. must succeed on a Dexterity saving throw or fall {@condition prone}. For the next minute the shake continues, and standing up requires another Dexterity saving throw. Each fail results in {@dice 1d6} bludgeoning damage. Each proficiency bonus after +2 deals another {@dice 2d6} damage.

{@b Blinding Light:} A bright light erupts from the caster. Each creature within 120 ft. of the caster must succeed on a Constitution saving throw or be {@condition blinded}. At the end of each day, the affected creatures can make another saving throw to be free from the effect.
A {@spell greater restoration} spell reverses this effect.

{@b Deafening Sound:} A horrible scream, a crash of thunder, or another loud noise is heard within 300 ft. of the caster. Each creature within the area must succeed on a Constitution saving throw or be {@condition deafened}. At the end of each day, the affected creatures can make another saving throw to be free from the effect.
A {@spell greater restoration} spell reverses this effect.

{@b Poison Aura:} A foul stench overwhelms you. Each creature within 60 ft. of the caster must succeed on a Constitution saving throw or be {@condition poisoned} for the next {@dice 4d6} hours, and they take {@dice 3d6} poison damage (damage occurs only once). Each proficiency bonus after +2 deals another {@dice 2d6} damage. The stench stays in the area for the next {@dice 2d4} hours. Each creature that enters the area or starts its turn there must make the saving throw.
A {@spell lesser restoration} or a {@spell greater restoration} spell reverses this effect.

{@b Smell of Mortem:} A feeling of dread and the impending doom of time pervades the area. Each creature within 120 ft. of the caster must succeed on a Wisdom saving throw or age {@dice 1d6*5|1d6 x 5} years. The magical aura stays there for 24 hours. Each creature that enters the area or starts its turn there must make the saving throw.
A {@spell greater restoration} spell reverses this effect.

{@b March of the Dead:} A loud heartbeat fills the caster's mind and creates an aura within 300 ft. of it. Dead creatures within the aura become undead creatures proper to their state and body. The creatures in the aura take {@dice 1d6} necrotic damage at the start of each of their turns or when they enter for the first time; undead creatures are immune to this. The undead created by this aura are relentless and attack everyone on sight. If no creature has become undead, a blast within the area deals each creature {@dice 2d6} necrotic damage.
A touch of a believer immediately destroys the undead if it is CR 1/4 or lower.

{@b Thunderous Hands:} A flash of lightning erupts from the caster. Each creature within 120 ft. of the caster must succeed on a {@dc 15} Constitution saving throw or take {@dice 3d6} lightning damage. The creatures who failed the save take extra {@dice 1d6} lightning damage whenever they touch a metal object. This effect lasts for {@dice 2d4} days.
Spending a long rest on soil that at least one believer prayed on will end the effect early.

{@b Enduring Cold:} The reign of foretold winter in the ancient myths comes to life within 120 ft. of the caster. Each creature within range must succeed on a {@dc 15} Constitution saving throw or take {@dice 3d6} cold damage, or half of it on a successful save. Each proficiency bonus after +2 adds another {@dice 2d6} cold damage. The cold aura persists after the first blast. If a creature enters the aura for the first time or starts its turn there, it takes {@dice 1d6} cold damage.
A {@spell counterspell} stops this effect if the triggering spell is 3rd level or lower. If it is higher, the DC equals to 10 + spell slot's level.

{@b Aura of Nightmare:} An apocalyptic voice screeches out from the depths with a vision of terror. Each creature within 120 ft. of the caster must succeed on a {@dc 15} Wisdom saving throw. On a failed save, they see random visions and hallucinations. In addition, whenever they attempt a long rest, they must succeed on a {@dc 10} Wisdom saving throw. On a failed save, they can't benefit from a long rest, as their sleep is haunted by terrible nightmares.
Starting the long rest while having the good will and/or the blessing of an innocent creature gives the caster advantage on the saving throw.

entries.name: Internal Effects
entries: The GM rolls on the table or determines which effect occurs:

entries.caption: Internal Effects
rows: The caster has disadvantage on saving throws for the next {@dice 1d6} hours.
The caster gains two levels of {@condition exhaustion}.
A {@spell greater restoration} spell reduces all exhaustion related to spell rebound.
The caster can't cast a spell for the next {@dice 3d6} hours. This includes cantrips and features like Divine Smite.
If the caster receives an inspiration, it can spend it to cast a spell. A spell cast this way must be 3rd level or lower.
The caster can't gain any benefit from a short or long rest for the next {@dice 1d6} days.
A {@spell greater restoration} spell negates this effect.
The caster's spell save DC is reduced by {@dice 1d4} for the next 24 hours.
A {@spell greater restoration} spell reverses this effect.
The caster has a short term memory loss. It lasts for {@dice 4d6} hours.
If the caster receives a hug or a kiss from a loved one, the effect ends early (minimum of 1 hour).
The caster loses the ability to move one of their limbs.
A {@spell greater restoration} spell reverses this effect.
The caster loses the ability to see or to hear for the next 24 hours.
The caster's maximum HP is reduced by {@dice 1d6}. Each proficiency bonus after +2 reduces it for another {@dice 3d6}. For example, a creature with +4 proficiency loses {@dice 7d6} maximum HP.
A {@spell greater restoration} spell reverses this effect.
The caster is driven mad in a way determined by the GM.

entries: Spell Rebound Effects can be applied as a curse or a similar effect in other settings. For example, a wizard can be cursed by a fey lover to deal with the spell rebound until he completes a daring task. A paladin must take this burden until she atones for her sins. A warlock may anger his patron, and until the patron is appeased, the warlock may be cursed with something unpleasant, and probably painful.
There may be cursed objects, such as staffs or wands that could give one of these effects, or a witch coven could curse a heroic adventuring party.

entries.name: Permanent Effects
entries: Apart from any instant effects which are triggered, many characters may develop permanent effects due to using magic for a long period of time, having badly failed the trigger, or using dangerous spells frequently. A GM may choose some of the effects below for players characters and NPCs in our Renaissance adventure {@i A Serenade for the Damned}, some NPCs that are encountered in this book (City of Venice: Locations section), or the ones that they create when playing.

Permanent Effects must be extremely hard to remove if not entirely impossible (there are a few useful effects, if the caster is lucky). Gaining divine favors, completing daring quests, seeking out holy fountains, or similar solutions must be pursued.

entries.caption: Permanent Effects
rows: {@b Troubled Mind:} Supernatural toxins begin to leach into the mind of the caster, slowly pushing them towards amnesia, paranoia, or psychopathy. It starts with small things in their life and slowly gets more serious. Triggering spell rebound effects accelerates the process.
{@b Speechless:} The caster loses the ability to speak.
{@b Staring at the Sun:} The caster is {@condition blinded}, and their corneas are scorched.
{@b Deep in the Sea:} The caster is {@condition deafened}. Each dawn their ears bleed.
{@b Useless Limb:} One of the caster's limbs becomes numb and useless.

{@b Rotting Body:} The rot starts as just a dot on the caster's body. It slowly grows (timing determined by the GM). If it covers a whole limb, it will render the limb useless. If the rot manages to cover the whole head or chest, the caster dies and cannot be resurrected. The only exception may be the {@spell wish} spell.
{@b Eye for an Eye:} The caster loses one eye. It slowly rots away.
{@b Plagued:} Each morning the caster must succeed on a {@dc 15} Constitution saving throw or be {@condition poisoned} for the rest of the day.
{@b Poisonous Water:} Whenever the caster drinks water, they take 2d8 acid damage. It can't benefit from drinking water.

{@b Arcane Drain:} The caster slowly loses its spellcasting ability, starting from highest level spell slots. If the caster has access to multiple sources of magic (such as multiclass), all wither slowly without exception.

{@b Aura:} The caster has an aura determined by the GM. The aura may be visible, such as the caster may seem darker among the shadows, the light sources may grow weaker within 20 ft. of it, or similar. The aura may be an invisible one and affect creatures in a mental way, such as making people angrier, sadder, or the like.

{@b Eyes among the Shadow:} The caster's eyes become overly sensitive to sunlight. While in sunlight, the caster has disadvantage on attack rolls, as well as on Wisdom ({@skill Perception}) checks that rely on sight.
{@b No Reflection:} The caster casts no reflection in mirrors and other reflective surfaces.
{@b Forbiddence:} The caster can't enter a residence without an invitation from one of its occupants.
{@b Wither and Bloom:} The caster, by touch, can accelerate or reverse an object's rot/decay. For example a sword rusts away, a piece of bread sprouts mold and so on.
{@b Crimson Touch:} When the caster touches an object, it can be ignited if it is flammable. In addition, the object may illuminate light (10 ft. bright, 10 ft. dim) until dispelled.

{@b Wild Presence:} The caster slowly resembles an entity from the wilds and the heart of the world. Their looks may resemble a wild beast, a tremendous monstrosity, or a vicious predator. Their hair may become green, it could smell of petrichor, or their speech raises listeners' hackles as surely as a wolf's howl. Their nails could grow out to claws, or their teeth may curve into fangs.

{@b Abyssal Being:} The caster slowly resembles an abyssal being, a fiendish creature. Their eyes may glow a sinister red or orange, they may give out a sulfuric stench, their skin may resemble a reddish color, or a similar effect.

{@b Divine Presence:} The caster slowly resembles an angelic being, a celestial creature. Their body may shine dimly in the darkness, their eyes may shine like an angel, their limbs may resemble beams of light, or a similar effect.
{@b Arcane Ark:} The caster has advantage on saving throws against spells and magical effects.

variantrule.name: Waterborne Combat Expanded
entries: Some of the iconic locations in Historica Arcanum could host many adventures or quests that can resolve in watery areas, such as the Bosphorus in Istanbul, the River Nile in Cairo and of course the canals in Venice. In this section, some guides and suggestions are presented for underwater combat and many rules surrounding it. The rules presented here are optional.
The rules appearing in the official sources are preserved:
If a creature does not have a swimming speed (which could be a natural one or it could be granted by magic), its melee weapon attacks are made with disadvantage unless the weapon is:

items: A {@item dagger|PHB}, {@item javelin|PHB}, {@item shortsword|PHB}, {@item spear|PHB}, or {@item trident|PHB}.

entries: Ranged weapons are also affected. The ammunition does not reach beyond the normal range; thus, any attack against a creature outside of range automatically misses. Moreover, attack rolls are made with disadvantage unless the weapon is:

items: A {@item light crossbow|PHB|crossbow}, a {@item net|PHB}, or a thrown weapon ({@item javelin|PHB}, {@item spear|PHB}, {@item trident|PHB}, or {@item dart|PHB}).
Creatures and objects that are fully in water have resistance to fire damage.

entries: The rules on weapons and other items are expanded in this section.

entries.name: Swimming Speed
entries: Since Venice is a water-based setting due its unique topography, most creatures in the Bestiary have a swimming speed to enhance their efficiency in on-water or underwater combat scenarios. The swimming speed enables creatures to effectively fight combat in and on water as well as contribute to interesting combat scenarios.
Below, there are different approaches for player characters to acquire swimming speed.

entries.name: Optional Rule: Swimming Proficiency
entries: When you gain a skill through your class, feat, feature or background, consult your GM about replacing one of them with Swimming Proficiency. This proficiency enables you to have swimming speed equal to your walking speed.

entries.name: Optional Rule: Swimming Training
entries: When you spend downtime for the acquisition of a skill or a tool proficiency, you can instead train in underwater combat and how to effectively use your weapons, thus granting you swimming speed equal to your walking speed.

entries.name: Optional Rule: Obscure Vision
entries: When a creature is fully submerged in water, it is counted as lightly obscured due to water breaking the light.

entries.name: Optional Rule: Water in Lungs
entries: Many occasions while swimming, especially hazards, combat, strong waves or currents, may trigger a {@dc 10} Constitution saving throw (or higher depending on the hazard). Swimming in Armor section below provides such an example and running out of breath or some similar situations may be called by the GM to determine the possibility of swallowing water into the lungs. On failed saves, water enters the lungs of the creature and causes some problems for them, especially humanoid creatures. If the creature is amphibious or can breathe water, water in lungs does not affect them.

While there is water in your lungs, check out the table for possible effects and the Wisdom ({@skill Medicine}) check made to get rid of it. Unless no check is applied, the effects linger until you finish a short rest, except for Level 4.

entries.caption: Water in Lungs
rows: You can't speak.
You can't regain hit points.
Your hit point maximum decreases by {@dice 1d6} at the start of each of your turns. It is restored after you finish a short or long rest.
You start to suffocate.*
footnotes: *Check out the Suffocation section below.

entries: Events that may trigger the saving throw:

items: Running out of air while underwater.
Having a swimming speed of 0 ft.
Being hit by a powerful wave or wind.
Any other hazard determined by the GM.
Any condition that is hazardous enough, such as becoming {@condition stunned}, {@condition paralyzed} or {@condition incapacitated}.

entries.name: Optional Rule: Breathing Under Water & Suffocation
entries: Holding breath while underwater is also another matter of careful consideration. Regular rules state that creatures can hold their breath underwater for a number of minutes. Unless magic is involved, these optional rules are made to implement a more challenging way for combat.

items: Creatures can hold their breath for a number of rounds equal to their Constitution score. For example, a creature with a Constitution score of 14, can hold their breath for 14 rounds.
Each time a creature is hit with a damage greater than their Constitution score, it loses one round of breath. This also applies at critical hits no matter the damage type or amount.
After it loses all air, you start to suffocate.
When it starts to suffocate, it can't regain hit points or can't be stabilized, it drops to 0 hit points and is dying.

entries.name: Swimming in Armor
entries: One of the most heated debates on tables usually revolves around whether or not characters are able to swim with their armor on, especially there are stories about emperors and kings drowning in their armor while crossing a river (one of the most vivid example would be Emperor Frederick Barbarossa's case during the Third Crusade: He drowned while crossing Saleph River). There are no official rules covering that area and we introduce some options for GMs to decide.

entries.name: Carrying Capacity
entries: Carrying capacity is usually overlooked in some campaigns to leave out the more crunchy stuff. If your game already takes optional carrying capacity/encumbrance into consideration, use these rules:

items: If you are encumbered, you can't use your swimming speed.

While encumbered, you must make a {@dc 10} Strength saving throw each time you try to move. On a failed save, you descend 5 ft. and water enters your lungs. If water enters your lungs enough (check out the table above) times in the next minute, you start to suffocate. If you have water breathing through spells or magical effects or some other way, water being in your lungs does not affect you.

entries.name: Armor Proficiency
entries: If you do not exceed your carrying capacity, the only thing left to do consider is armor proficiency.
If you wear armor that you are not proficient with, you are counted as encumbered and the rules above about Carrying Capacity apply to you.
If you are proficient with your armor, different rules apply when you are underwater:

entries.caption: Armor in Water
rows: Light Armor
Your speed is reduced by 5 ft.
Ranged attacks have disadvantage against you.
Medium Armor
Your speed is reduced by 10 ft.
Melee attacks have disadvantage against you.
Heavy Armor
Your speed is reduced by 15 ft.
You take {@dice 1d10} less damage from weapon attacks.

entries.name: Damage Effects & Optional Situations
entries: While fully submerged in water or while swimming in water, damage types may have different effects as well as some of the optional moves and actions introduced in official rules.

entries.name: Lightning
entries: Creatures take double damage from lightning.

entries.name: Thunder
entries: Creatures take half damage from thunder.

entries.name: Cold
entries: If the cold damage exceeds 15, the receiver's movement speed becomes 0 until the end of its next turn. This damage does not trigger the "water in lungs" optional rule.

entries.name: Strength & Dexterity Checks
entries: Strength and Dexterity checks underwater are made with disadvantage, unless the creature has a swimming speed.

entries.name: Gunpowder
entries: Weapons that are considered firearms and rely on gunpowder do not work underwater or if they are exposed to water enough.

entries.name: Illusions
entries: Characters have disadvantage on ability checks detecting and discerning illusions that are underwater or somewhat submerged in water due to light's breaking in water.

entries.name: Fall Damage
entries: Fall damage is an important part of some dungeons and encounters, as some enemies may push characters into great heights or vice versa. Here are some optional rules about fall damage based on the creature's size and what happens if a creature attempts to land on another creature.
As a rule of thumb a character descends 500 ft. in a round.

entries.name: Size Matters
entries: Fall damage depends on height and size.

entries.caption: Fall Damage by Size
rows: Tiny
{@damage 1d4}
Small
{@damage 1d6}
Medium
{@damage 1d8}
Large
{@damage 1d10}
Huge
{@damage 2d12}
Gargantuan
{@damage 2d20}

entries: X stands for a creature's minimum amount needed to fall before taking a damage. Y stands for when the damage is increased by doubling the dice.

For example, if a medium creature falls 30 feet, it takes {@damage 3d8} damage but if it falls 50 feet, it takes more damage than regular: it increases by {@damage 1d8} for each 10 feet that exceeds 40. In this case, it takes a normal amount of damage {@damage 5d8} for falling 50 feet and the damage increases by {@damage 1d8} because it fell 10 feet more after the designated number of 40 for a total of {@damage 6d8}.

entries.name: Falling on Another Creature
entries: If a creature willingly jumps from a certain height that would damage itself to inflict damage on other creatures or gain the upper hand in combat, it gets no damage reduction, rather, the target creature could be damaged by the falling creature. Check out the table below for the optional rules.

The first column is in comparison to the attacker and the target and the attacker can cover more area due to its size and there may be more than one target because of it. For example, a mammoth could leap and target about seven medium or smaller creatures that happen to be very close to each other.
The DC is for Dexterity saving throws. In cases of failures and success check out the relevant columns.

entries.name: Golden Rule:
entries: If a creature wants to target another creature this way, they must use their action. If they don't, simply follow this rule before consulting the table below: The character that is about to be hit by a falling character must succeed on a {@dc 15} Dexterity saving throw.

entries.caption: Falling on Another Creature
rows: Smaller Size
The attacker is small and the target is large.
Same amount of the falling damage minus {@damage 1d8} bludgeoning damage.
Half amount of the falling damage minus {@damage 1d6} bludgeoning damage.
Same Size
Both the attacker and the target are medium.
Same amount of the falling damage.
Half amount of the falling damage.
One Size Larger
The attacker is large and the target is medium.
Same amount of the falling damage + {@damage 2d8} bludgeoning damage more.
Half amount of the falling damage + {@damage 1d8} bludgeoning damage.
Two Sizes Larger
The attacker is huge and the target is medium.
Same amount of the falling damage + {@damage 4d8} bludgeoning damage more.
Half amount of the falling damage + {@damage 1d8} bludgeoning damage.
Three Sizes Larger
The attacker is large and the target is tiny.
Double amount of the falling damage.
Same amount of falling damage.
Four Sizes Larger
The attacker is gargantuan and the target is small.
Double amount of the falling damage + {@damage 2d10} bludgeoning damage.
Same amount of the falling damage + {@damage 1d10} bludgeoning damage.
Five or More Sizes Larger
The attacker is gargantuan and the target is tiny.
Triple amount of the falling damage.
Double amount of the falling damage.

entries.name: Perfect Landing
entries: The falling creatures may attempt, as a reaction, to fix their posture and position and align themselves to neglect fall damage to an extent. When a creature is about to hit the surface and falls no more than 30 ft, it can make a {@dc 15} Dexterity saving throw to reduce the damage by {@dice 1d8} + its Dexterity modifier.

{@b Slow Fall:} The Monk Class gains the Slow Fall ability at Level 4. Until Level 4, if a monk spends 1 Ki Point on their attempt at a perfect landing, they also roll their Martial Arts die and reduce the total from their damage as well.

entries.name: Falling on Water
entries: The creatures that fall on water must make a {@dc 10} Strength ({@skill Athletics}) check or {@dc 10} Dexterity ({@skill Acrobatics}) check to make a good landing on water, heads or feet first. On a successful save, their fall is considered one category lower while taking damage. For example, a medium creature falling from 30 feet is considered to have fallen from 20 feet high.

variantrule.name: Hosting a Carnival
entries: There are bountiful times of the year, famous for their festivities and awash with beautiful colors that make the sunrise envious. They bring music, trade, competition, and many people together. In Venice, there are several grand festivals throughout the year, though the most famous is undoubtedly the Carneval de Venèsia, the Carnival. In tabletop games, festivals offer a great opportunity to kick off an adventure, introduce interesting NPCs or factions, offer some quests, and bring unique experiences not typically on offer in the day-to-day lives of PCs.

In this section, you can find guidelines, tables, and optional rules for your tabletop festivals and how to make them come alive, including interesting rewards, captivating quests, and NPC suggestions.

entries.name: Festival Grounds
entries: Where does the festival take place? Is it an encampment erected in a glade surrounded by trees? In a cozy Venetian campo? In a bustling city square? The festival's place can speak for itself before anything else does.

entries.caption: Festival Grounds
rows: A flat surface in a rural area
Plenty of villagers, seasonal crops and trade goods, including local religious rituals, probably a local event bringing people together mostly in close cultural ties.
A flat surface with access to water in drylands or desert
Many people with nomadic lifestyles, a good selection of different types of mounts, an important trade event, possible visitors from far-flung regions.
A town's square
Most civilians with urban lifestyles and locals from nearby towns and villages. Possibly organized by a local noble or wealthy tradesman.
An area in a woods or forest
Local guides, tribesmen and similar people who are used to living in lands covered with forests and woods. Possibly many travelers, tradesmen, pastries and similar goods.
The side of a river or a lake
Plenty of natural resources and possibly has a local character rather than a giant festival.
A large fortress

Possibly organized by a noble with military leanings, such as a general or a pasha. Tight security and strict law enforcement. An opportunity to establish ties with the higher society. Many locals and subjects of the nobles attend from nearby settlements.
A city's square

Possibly organized by administrators or people in similar power over economy or politics. It probably has a variety of visitors from relatively far lands; including goods and trade items nonexistent in the area, and interesting people from different cultures. It's a strong possibility that the tournaments are highly competitive and offer great rewards.
A giant building like the Colosseum

Possibly organized by nobles who are powerful enough to rule a country. Uniting people of different cultures and tongues together. Could be an annual and long-expected event. Rewards may be greater than any commoner could dream of. Professional athletes, musicians, competitors, and the finest of their fields can be found at the event.
An island, or a dedicated place only used in such an event

It is possibly a world-famous event with its unique characteristics, such as the masks in a Venetian Carnival. Nobles, tradesmen, adventurers, scientists, musicians, dancers, storytellers, warriors, heroes, thieves, ambassadors and all kinds of people can be found here. It is an annual event that sets expectations.
Several squares connected with big streets in a huge city

Probably a once in a lifetime or at least very rare event, such as a monarch's ascension to the throne, the election in a republic, a victory celebration after a dire battle, the birth of an heir or a similar singular event. It has the possibility to be the most remarkable event of its own and be remembered throughout centuries to come.

entries.name: Who Funds the Festival?
entries: The festivals are funded by coins, possibly a large amount of coins. It is important to determine who covers such expanses.

entries.caption: Festival Patrons
rows: Locals cover their own expenses.
25 to 100 gp
Enough to buy a horse.
A wealthy merchant.
100 to 250 gp
Enough to buy many clothes of silk and other quality ingredients.
A guild, such as a merchant guild or an artisan guild.
100 to 400 gp
Enough to buy exotic items or trade goods that are rare.
A high ranking noble, such as a duke or a pasha.
200 to 500 gp
Enough to buy an uncommon magic item, such as a blade with good magical properties.
A governor in an area.
Enough to buy valuable gems.
A monarch, head of a government.
Enough to buy a rare magic item.
A king, who is a renowned ruler in the world.
Enough to build a manor.
An imperial ruler, such as the Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire, Sultan of the Ottoman Empire, or a similar ruler with similar characteristics and power.
5,000 to infinity
Enough to buy a warship, a castle or a very rare magic item.
footnotes: *Many settings use different types of currencies and economy; this is purely to give out ideas rather than exact numbers.

entries: Depending on the patron, the tournaments and all kinds of competitions may reward players greatly, or it could be just a simple place where many people gather to trade and have fun.

entries.name: Characteristics
entries: Different types of festivals may have different causes that shape their characteristics. This can create many ideas for certain participants or events in a festival.

entries.caption: Festival Characteristics
rows: Religious

The festival is organized for a religious holiday, such as Christmas, Eid, Holi, or a similar event. There are many religious or ritualistic happenings around the festival, such as creating a giant bonfire and the youth jump over it, a collective chant in the city square, decorating the area, wearing costumes, gifts of charity, and other traditions.
Entertainment
The festival is organized to entertain the people, blow off steam, and to make the locals happy. Events in the festivals usually consist of plays, dance, music, theatrical performances, and the like.
Celebration

There is an event to celebrate a special moment: the birth of an heir, victory in a battle, a peace agreement, the restoration of a symbolic building, or the ascension of a new ruler to the throne. The festival is set up to announce and celebrate the event, usually involving donating money to the locals. It might involve heavy drinking and dining.
Show of Power

The festival is set to demonstrate the abilities of a certain person in power, and it could have a giant tournament to show the greatest swordsmen are in the person's service or to show that the economic power of a certain town or city is in place and going strong. It usually involves military marches, martial tournaments, and the like.
Distraction

There may be worrying events around: war, famine, economic crisis, decline in culture or things that may have a huge impact on society and the lives of locals. The festival is organized to create a distraction and pull people's minds away from the problems. It usually involves many entertaining events. A gladiator fight is a good example.
Traditional/Annual

It has been like this for some time, at least years. The festival is organized because it was the way of their ancestors. It does not need to have a religious aspect. Some causes for some festivals may be lost in time. Or it may be such an event that many people wait for it to happen and attract many visitors, so it is hosted traditionally or annually. The Venetian Carnival or Festa della Sensa are good examples for annual festivals.
Economic

The festival is organized to stir the economy in a good way, revive the market, and help out the merchants and villagers to sell and buy needed products. Usually there are many opportunities for merchants to display their goods, some tax discounts or other incentives.
Cultural
It is a part of local cultural activities, such as a nomadic people's celebration of summer, or an esteemed warrior throwing a feast to celebrate the birth of his newborn son.

entries.name: Competitions
entries: Some festivals include interesting competitions where individuals can shine and show their talents, from call and response duets in Turkish cultures to one-on-one fights against experienced warriors or archery competitions.

entries.name: Archery
entries: Great marksmen and hunters of the land gather to show their talent as they aim at targets from 50 yards or a similar range. If players join such competitions, you can follow the rules below to determine if they won or not. They make three attack rolls and check if they meet the criteria in the table below. If more players compete, the one who passed the most tests wins; if there is a tie, just add up the numbers they rolled and determine the winner.

entries.caption: Archery Contests
rows: Very Easy
{@dice 2d4+2}
{@dice 1d10 * 5|1d10 x 5} gp
Easy
{@dice 2d8+2}
{@dice 2d10 * 5|2d10 x 5} gp
Moderate
Hard
Very Hard
Extremely Hard**
footnotes: *Although highly dependent on the patrons and the characteristics of the tournament, the difficulty of a test could give ideas about the reward.
**This implies the players are up against professionals or other NPCs who are some of the greatest marksmen in the area or potential former tournament winners.

entries: If the player succeeds with all 3 shots, they are the winner. The DC may change for each shot; such as a contributor underestimating the player, focusing better or other circumstances. The higher DC determines the reward or a preestablished characteristics could alter the result, you can check out the table above in the Who Funds the Festival section.

entries.name: Jousting - Lance Game
entries: It is a thrilling sight to see armed combatants march towards each other while mounted. Jousting is a classic engagement in festivals that attract many crowds and possibly high rewards.

In jousting, both participants make an attack roll with their lances and make a {@dc 10} Wisdom ({@skill Animal Handling}) check. If a participant fails their Animal Handling check, their attack roll result is decreased by {@dice 1d4}.

The attack roll results are compared with the opponent's Armor Class as usual. If it's a hit, roll for the lance's damage roll as usual, adding Strength modifier to it. There is an option if you want to approach this as a safe sport: Creatures do not take damage, instead some optional situations may arise:

items: If the damage roll is maximum, the target falls {@condition prone}.
If the damage total is above 12, the target must make a Strength saving throw (DC = 10 + the damage taken). On a failure, it falls {@condition prone}.
If the attack roll is a critical hit, the target falls {@condition prone}.
If the damage total is below 7, nothing happens to the target.
If the damage total is between 8-12, the target reduces {@dice 1d4} from its next attack roll in this event.
If the attack roll is a natural 1, the attacker has disadvantage on its next roll in this event.

entries: The joust progresses until at least one of the participants falls {@condition prone}. The one that stands is the winner. If both participants fail, the test is continued until only one of them is still standing while the other is on the ground.

If you want this event to progress as normal, like applying damage to characters to create more realistic scenes, apply the damage of the used weapon directly and whoever falls to 0 hit points is the loser. However, the creature that falls to 0 hit points is not dead and starts death saving throws or it is instantly stabilized as you see fit.

entries.name: Gladiator Fight
entries: The gladiator era may have been over, but you can include similar contests where warriors engage in a sword fight in arenas and prove their worth as a courageous blood. Playing out a whole combat with regular rules, with rolling initiative and all, could prove to be longer than desired. Here's a streamlined and shortened version:

entries.name: Duel
entries: If it's a one versus one, follow these rules:

items: Both participants roll an attack roll.
Compare them with corresponding Armor Classes.
If both hit or miss, repeat this until one of them fails to hit the other.
If a participant scores a critical hit, and the other does not, it's a win for them.
If only one of the participants hit, they are the winner.
To make it longer, you could make the best of three or other versions of this, until one participant reaches the target number of wins.

entries.name: Arena
entries: If there are more than one participant or one humanoid against several other beasts or monsters, regular combat rules could be applied. For a more straightforward version for the player characters, follow these rules:

items: The player character makes an attack roll, a Constitution saving throw against {@dc 10} and a percentile die roll. The percentile die represents the chaotic nature of the conflict. It is recommended to set the target number to 50. Rolling 50 or higher counts as a win. The GM can adjust the number depending on several factors. They may also increase the DC if the fight is considered hard ({@dc 15}), dangerous ({@dc 20}), or deadly ({@dc 25}).
If two out of three results are successful, the player character is the winner.
If all three results are failures, check out the Hazards for Players table below, under Supplementary Tables.

entries.name: Musical Standoff
entries: In many festivals, talented bards or musicians take the stage and challenge each other by using their wits, performative abilities and quick comebacks. It may grow organically in a tavern where everyone enjoys, or it could be arranged on a stage where all sorts of audience attend.

You can basically let participants roll for Charisma ({@skill Performance}) as a general rule as it's a performative art or Intelligence ({@skill Performance}) if it's a witty comeback or a clever answer. It is advised to make the rolls best of five and award the one with three wins.
If the player characters actually perform what they are saying, you may consider awarding them with inspiration or advantage on the roll.

entries.name: Random Events
entries: What stirs a festival towards even more fun for adventurers? Random events. These events could be fleshed out into small quests, combat encounters, or social struggles to actively include the adventurers into the festival, rather than being just bystanders.

entries.caption: Random Festival Events
rows: Three merchants have been killed. Their throats were slit, but nothing was taken.
A great heist was committed; a lot of merchants were robbed of a great deal of money. Curiously, the most interesting stolen items were empty parchment pages.
A man was found drowned (or a manner of death suited to the environment for places far from water sources). No one knows him.
A child was found while crying near a tent, searching for their mother and father. No one in the festival claims the child as their own.
A brawl breaks out between rival performers accusing each other of sabotage. The dispute threatens to ruin the evening's main attraction.
A mysterious fortune-teller predicts doom for the festival unless a dangerous task is undertaken. Many dismiss them, but they disappear soon after.
A prized festival contest trophy goes missing, and participants are refusing to compete without it.
A series of brightly colored fireworks misfire, setting part of the festival grounds ablaze. Suspiciously, a figure is seen fleeing the scene.
A celebrity bard loses their voice under strange circumstances. Rumors of foul play circulate, and their loyal fans demand answers.
A rare animal escapes from an exotic pet merchant's cage and causes chaos among the festivalgoers. Catching it seems impossible.
A shadowy figure offers a strange game with enticing prizes, but losing comes at a personal cost. Those participating in the game begin disappearing.
A local noble's heir gets into a heated argument with a commoner, which escalates toward violence. Mediation could win favor—or make enemies.
Someone accuses a well-loved merchant of being a fraud or a thief, but their evidence seems questionable. Who is lying?
A performer collapses mid-act, muttering about "poison in the air." Panic spreads, and attendees demand answers.
A mysterious fog rolls in, obscuring the festival grounds. Strange shapes appear in the mist, frightening attendees.
An eerie melody drifts through the air, entrancing some festivalgoers to wander into the nearby woods. They are unresponsive to attempts to stop them.
A local legend about a ghost haunting the festival site seems true when a spectral figure is spotted at dusk.
A rich merchant offers a substantial reward for anyone who can beat their bodyguard in a friendly duel. The bodyguard appears unbeatable.
A popular food stall is accused of serving cursed or spoiled food after several patrons fall ill. The vendor pleads their innocence.
A winged creature swoops down and steals a magical trinket from a festivalgoer. Witnesses claim it looked like a mischievous fae creature.

entries.name: Trade Goods
entries: To determine a random trade good or an object sold in the festival, you can use the table below.

entries.caption: Festival Trade Goods
rows: Papyrus or vellum – Specialty writing materials still used for manuscripts.
Medicinal ingredients – Imported from the East, such as myrrh or opium.
Paint pigments – Rare colors like ultramarine or vermilion for artists.
Ornamental pearls – Natural ones harvested from the Persian Gulf.
Dried fruits – Dates, figs, or raisins, both for eating and baking.
Perfumes – Fragrant oils and powders from Arabia or Persia.
Books – All kinds of books from all kinds of languages.
Amber beads – Prized for jewelry or as exotic curios.
Gold leaf – Used for religious art or decorative gilding.
Salt – Essential for preservation and trade, often referred to as "white gold."
Ceramics – Fine plates and bowls, especially maiolica pottery.
Exotic feathers – Used for hats or quills, from African or Indian birds.
Ivory carvings – Intricate figurines or religious artifacts.
Wool – High-quality textiles imported from England or Flanders.
Wine – Aged vintages from the Veneto region or imported.
Silver ingots – Used for crafting jewelry and currency.
Velvet cloth – Highly sought after for clothing among the wealthy.
Glassware – Murano glass is a trademark of Venice and may be sold in other settings or cities as well.
Spice – Cinnamon, saffron, or cloves brought from the East.
Silk Fabric – One of the most precious items for elegant clothing and decor.

entries.name: Hazards for Players
entries: Player characters may suffer accidents, be the target of misfortune, or have other bad circumstances happen to them. Check out the table below for ideas for such hazards.

entries.caption: Hazards for Players
rows: Losing an important item, such as a weapon, spell focus, shield, a letter, a potion or the like.
Suffering an injury. Hit point maximum is reduced by double their proficiency bonus.
Accused of a crime they didn't commit.
They have a number of enemies who are obsessed with them equal to their Charisma modifier (minimum of one enemy).
Losing a magic item. It's been stolen or vanished in a well/river or a similar unreachable place.
Eye Injury. They are {@condition blinded} for {@dice 1d4} days. This reduction can be cured with the {@spell lesser restoration} spell.
Leg Injury. Movement speed of the player character is halved for {@dice 1d4} days. This reduction can be cured with the {@spell lesser restoration} spell.
Head Injury. They gain one level of {@condition exhaustion}.

entries.name: General Hazards
entries: Sometimes misfortune can strike the festival and its attendants as a whole. Check out the table below for ideas for such hazards.

entries.caption: General Hazards
rows: A fire strikes, and it spreads too quickly. Lives are in danger.
An earthquake shakes the land. Many tents collapse. Roll a {@dice d20}: if it's lower than 5, there may be casualties.
A section in the soil collapsed due to erosion, and many tents were damaged.
It rains so heavily that a flood occurs quickly. / A wind strikes and quickly takes the shape of a sandstorm. Roll a {@dice d20}: if it's lower than 5, there may be casualties.
A strong storm is threatening the festival, and some people swore they saw some tents in the air.
A nasty sickness spreads among the crowd.
A water well was poisoned. The poison is hardly traceable.
The news of a raiding party was heard. Everyone is on alert. (Reroll if the festival is heavily protected by an armed force or in a city well guarded).
