entries.name: Welcome to Venice
entries: It is the second decade of the sixteenth century, and the Golden Age of the Renaissance has begun to show signs of receding into the twilight, like a blood red sunset meeting the horizon. Our setting is Venice, La Serenissima Republica, a place of wealth, strict governance, and stability, but also one of constant existential threats from beyond–their neighboring city states, the great kingdoms of Western Europe, and of course, the Ottoman Empire.
Before diving into the setting in more detail, it is important to examine the political environment and the main actors of this High Renaissance era.

entries.name: Flourishing Culture, Flourishing Conflict
entries: With the deft strokes of painters' brushes and soldiers' blades, the peninsula of Italy is vibrant and seething. While the arts are flourishing under the patronage of the wealthy elite of Florence, Milan, Venice, Naples, and the Papal States, the ground beneath everyone's feet quakes with the thundering, incessant march of war. The Holy Roman Emperor and the King of France have both invaded and laid claim to huge swaths of Italian territory, and in these seemingly never-ending "Italian Wars," the various Italian city-states and kingdoms take sides, protect their interests, and often change allies with the shift of the wind. They fight these battles with condottieri, professional soldiers for hire who have a vested interest in the battles being prolonged so that they get paid well. Sieges are common, stalemates and doublecrosses commonplace. In the most recent hue of these wars, the War of the League of Cambrai, practically all of Europe united against Venice, and though Venice suffered humiliating early losses, by the end of the war La Serenissima had regained its lost territory, and the map returned, for the most part, to its pre-war uneasy position.

As Western Europe squabbles amongst itself, the Ottoman Empire prepares itself for Mediterranean domination. After Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453, many Greeks fled to Venice, which helped spur the Renaissance humanists' rejuvenated interest in the Classics. Mehmed's forces soon landed in Italy and prepared for a grand conquest of old Rome; however, Mehmed's sudden death put a halt to Ottoman interest in Italy. The most recent sultan, Selim I, has spent considerable effort on conquering Muslim lands to the south, giving Venice and the other citystates of Italy a bit of a reprieve. Yet it would not last. In late 1520, Selim I dies and a new sultan ascends: Suleiman I, otherwise known as Suleiman the Magnificent. Suleiman quickly gets to work invading Europe by land and by sea. His corsairs harry Genoese and Venetian shipping lanes while his armies besiege Belgrade. The island of Rhodes is next on the sultan's list.

Amidst this bloody backdrop, Michelangelo, Raphael, and Da Vinci create masterpieces for whomever will pay, Titian flourishes as the brightest artistic star of Venice, and Machiavelli observes and opines what is required to be a clever leader in these precarious times. Meanwhile, Venice's monopoly on trade with Asia has not only been challenged by the Ottoman might, but also the Atlantic voyages of the Portuguese and Spanish. From the outside, Venice looks like the wealthiest and most stable of the Italian city-states, and the city has an incredible streak of being able to weather the storms of its rivals–but this floating city is perched precariously on ground that is sinking around it. The world is changing, and Venice's serene stability may not be enough to secure its existence.

entries.name: The Echoes of Renaissance
entries: The Republic of Venice eyes its neighbors and the encroaching Ottomans warily, but after shrewdly navigating shifting alliances with former enemies and regaining everything it lost in the War of the League of Cambrai, it has also, in its eyes, proven its superiority over its neighbors. The future is uneasy, but as Venice prepares for the Carnevale, it exudes a veneer of permanence.

entries.name: Political and Religious Figures
entries: {@b Leonardo Loredan, the Doge of Venice}, has reigned as the head of state since 1501. Loredan was born into an influential family and given an excellent education. Growing up, he was perfectly positioned for work in the political labyrinth of Venice. He married Morosina Giustiniani from another prestigious Venetian house and further solidified his trajectory to greatness. After working his way up through legal and political postings, he became Doge in 1501. In his 20-year reign he presided over one of the most turbulent periods in Venetian history, but he led his Republic through the bloody and muddy waters with shrewd and Machiavellian leadership. Leonardo Loredan makes an appearance in our adventure module, A Serenade for the Damned.

{@b The House of Medici} rose to become the most powerful family in Florence, the owners of the largest bank in Europe, and a major driving force of the Renaissance spirit in the 1400s. From 1494 until 1512, however, they were expelled from Florence for giving in to invading French demands. There were three Medici Popes in this era: Leo X (1513-1521), Clement VII (1523-1534), and Pius IV (1559-1565); Catherine de Medici reigned as Queen of France from 1547-1559 and was also a major power during her three sons' reigns. Pope Leo X makes an appearance in our adventure module, A Serenade for the Damned.

{@b The House of Borgia} was a family originally from Spain who became extremely influential in Italian politics, particularly in Rome and the Papal States. Rodrigo Lanzol Borgia became Pope Alexander VI and ruled from 1492 to 1503. His children Cesare Borgia and Lucrezia Borgia were infamous and powerful nobles in their own right: Cesare was a cardinalturned- condottiero, and Lucrezia, through arranged marriages and a talent for politics and administration, became a powerful duchess. Lucrezia Borgia, now the Duchess of Ferrara, makes an appearance in our adventure module, A Serenade for the Damned.

{@b The House of Sforza} was in control of the Duchy of Milan in the last half of the 15th century and part of the early 16th century. Lodovico il Moro was the Duke of Milan until 1499, when Louis XII of France took control. Lodovico had, among other things, patronized Leonardo da Vinci. Sforzas then were placed back in power twice when the French were driven out by the Holy Roman Empire - first in 1512 and then in 1521 Francisco II Sforza was installed as Duke. Though the Sforzas used to rule Milan with an iron fist, their position in 16th century Italy is atop a house of cards.

{@b Alfonso I d'Este}, the Duke of Ferrara from 1504-1534 was a major player in the War of the League of Cambrai, siding against the Republic of Venice. He and his dukedom became famous for their fortifications, artillery, and their patronage of the arts. Alfonso I d'Este married Lucrezia Borgia in 1501. Duke Alfonso makes an appearance in our adventure module, A Serenade for the Damned.

entries.name: Cultural Figures
entries: {@b Leonardo da Vinci} was an accomplished polymath. An itinerant genius, he spent a lot of his formative creative years in the court of Lodovico Sforza, but he also worked in Florence, Rome, and finally France. Da Vinci makes an appearance in our adventure module, A Serenade for the Damned.

{@b Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni} was a famed sculptor and painter, known as the "Divine One" or "The Terrorinducing One" (if you ask Pope Julius II) and the only one of the famous Renaissance painters to have a biography written about him while still alive. His sculptures Pieta and David were completed before he was even 30 years old; he was also known for his sculpture's terribiltà, a special quality that strikes the viewer with terror, awe, or a supreme sense of the sublime.

{@b Niccolo Machiavelli} was a senior official in the Florentine government, working in the fields of law, diplomacy. At the time of Echoes of Renaissance, he has not yet become famous for the seminal work The Prince, which would be published after his death.

{@b Tiziano Vecellio}, better known as Titian, is the greatest of the Venetian painters during the Renaissance. He is known as "the Sun amidst small stars" by his contemporaries. Titian makes an appearance in our adventure module, A Serenade for the Damned.

Another famous polymath, {@b Nicolaus Copernicus} is a recent graduate of studies in Bologna and Padua, studying astronomy and humanities. He has yet to publish the work which will unleash the Copernican Revolution, but he has already been developing those famous ideas, and in 1514 he wrote the Commentariolus, the outline of his heliocentric theory.

{@b Aldus Manutius} is an Italian printer and humanist whose Aldine Press publications helped disseminate Greek philosophy and language. He also popularized a proto-paperback called an Enchiridion, which was also the name of a dagger–the meaning here being that books were the weapons of the learned. Manutius's Aldine Press makes an appearance in our Locations chapter and in the Sidequests.

{@b Martin Luther} was a German priest who shot to fame and notoriety when he published his 95 Theses in 1517. The Theses criticized the Catholic Church's practice of indulgences and papal authority, among other things. He was subsequently excommunicated, thus igniting the Protestant Reformation.

entries.name: The Origin of Magic
entries: "Magick took her name and original form from Persia," wrote John Baptista Porta in his Natural Magick (originally Magia Naturalis, 1558 CE. The English translation is dated 1658 CE). "A magician is nothing else but one that expounds and studies divine things."

In the world of Historica Arcanum, humankind discovered the power of magic in ancient times, through many different methods of channeling: chanting, dancing, rituals, prayers, battle cries, potions, and more. The unnatural power they possessed was rare, wild, and dangerous, as it broke the laws of reality.

No human knows the true origin of these abilities that can break apart reality, but it is known that, through practice, some words, movements, and materials trigger the power. The raw talent of the practitioners from ancient civilizations slowly turned and diversified into the enlightened magicians, able priests, and powerful sorcerers who developed methods of their own.

Yet one thing has remained constant: reality does not take kindly to those who break its rules. Time and space will expunge the effects of arcane powers either through "coincidences," or, in more severe instances, collapsing the spells back on the arcanists, and even onto innocent bystanders in the proximity of the spellslingers. Beyond superstition, this is the reason why magic is forbidden in many cultures, and why species and races that carry the taint of magic are distrusted. Once you are involved in magic, reality will take its vengeance, one way or another.

entries.name: A Vengeful Reality and Magic Untamed:
Running a Story in Renaissance Italy

entries: "Well might it seem that such a city had owed its existence rather to the rod of the enchanter, than the fear of the fugitive; that the waters which encircled her had been chosen for the mirror of her state, rather than the shelter of her nakedness; and that all which in nature was wild or merciless—Time and Decay, as well as the waves and the tempests—had been won to adorn her instead of to destroy."

The following section provides a detailed overview of Renaissance Venice and the immediate world around it in 1520-1521 so that intrepid GMs will feel more comfortable running a game in the tumultuous world of the High-to-Late Renaissance. Though our setting guide and adventure module are based in Venice, we hope that the following tools and information will help you if you choose to have your adventures roam to other parts of the Italian peninsula, or further afield.

entries.name: Arcane & Divine Matters
entries: The world of Historica Arcanum is where arcane powers, occult secrets, and eldritch creatures lurk in the shadows– hiding, hunting, or pulling the strings.

Most of the common folk of Renaissance-era Italy may believe in the existence of magic due to bedtime stories, urban legends, religious revelations, and folktales; however, most of them don't know about the actual spellcasters and arcane matters that truly exist in this world.

entries.caption: Italian and Venetian
rows: Magic is rare but focused.

In Renaissance Italy, magic is very rare. Spellcasters can only be found if one knows where to look; eldritch creatures and non-humans are an even rarer sight; and objects with arcane properties are extremely hard to come by. However, in the cases of Venice and the other city-states, many secrets, both arcane and divine, may be hidden in their dark alleys and underground places.
Magic is usually hidden.

Spellcasters, magical monsters, and arcane humanoid species exist throughout Italy, but they keep a very low profile–especially if they are sentient. In discreet districts of large cities and remote villages within the wilderness, non-human species can be found–if you know what to look for. In Venice, they often conceal their identities by wearing cloaks or headgear, and if it is Carnevale season, it is easier to blend in.
Magic is punishing.

Magic means breaking reality. It is a dangerous life, where vengeful Reality pushes back against arcanists by setting up traps disguised as coincidences, and most importantly, by rebounding spells. All magic users and arcane researchers are aware that spell rebound is real, and the cost of spellcasting can be harsh, even deadly.
Magic hunts Magic.

For the few that already exist behind the arcane veil, Reality ensures their doom by entangling them in the lives of others like them–curious coincidences, unfortunate accidents, or paranoid encounters. Once one is marked for death, they will keep stumbling upon eldritch creatures, spellcasters, or abhumans–and in such a dangerous world, these encounters often carry deadly consequences. Only the very cautious or talented can hope to survive, for Lady Luck seems to never be on the side of the marked.
Divine matters are unknown.

Everyone is entitled to their own beliefs. One's ability to harness divine power doesn't have to prove or refute a religion or belief. Spellcasting may be achieved through faith, but magical prowess is primarily a result of one's studies, mindset, and the power that lies within them. Believers from various faiths and religions can demonstrate remarkable feats in spellcasting, and many indeed believe that this is a reward for their faith.
Monsters are hidden or dwell among the common folk.

Monsters hide in the wilderness or disguise themselves in dark corners using their shape-changing abilities, spellcasting, or other talents. Some lurk under your beds, dwell within your stories, or scheme for a bloody hunt or political power through sinister means.

entries.name: Non-Human Races
entries: As magic plays a vital role in the world of Historica Arcanum, non-human races hold a significant place. Even when their kinds are exceptionally rare, dangerous are the survivors from backgrounds where life expectancy is nothing but a few short years.

Sentient non-humans are mostly half bloods, such as halfelves, and half-orcs. Although even rarer, pure blood nonhumans also exist. In both cases, the end phenotype is not the look of a truly new species, but that of a mutated human. While most non-humans are the offspring of non-human parents, or at least an ancestry that contains significant enough non-human blood, there are some who are the offspring of regular humans, with arcane irregularities stemming from their birth.

Players can select a non-human race for their characters, and they may also encounter NPCs from these races. The purpose of this table is to provide guidance for blending in within a city, town, or while traveling, and to assist the GM in creating non-human NPCs, societies, and interconnected ideas that encompass the realm of nonhuman races.

entries.caption: How to Disguise{@sup *}
rows: Elf / Half-elf
Usually, concealing their ears is sufficient, but some of them resort to using makeup and similar substances to avoid drawing the attention of humans.
Dwarf

Dwarves are generally perceived as shorter, sturdier individuals by humans, making it easy for them to blend in. They are encountered more frequently than other non-human races, and most of the time, there's no need for them to disguise themselves.
Halfling

Halflings typically present themselves as children among the common folk, or by behaving like exceptionally short humans who were born that way. They don't raise suspicion or fear, unlike a tiefling or an orc might. One thing they excel at is going unnoticed by taller individuals.
Orc / Half-orc

Orcs who don't make an effort to move stealthily through a bustling city may encounter difficulties due to their distinctive features, such as tusks. They often conceal these attributes by wearing heavy cloaks and garments that obscure their appearance. It's not uncommon for orcs to hide their faces, as it helps them blend in with the human-dominated populace. Half-orcs, on the other hand, might find it easier to go unnoticed than their full-blooded counterparts, as their tusks are typically less prominent.
Gnome

Like halflings, gnomes excel at sneaking around. While their facial features are more obviously 'nonhuman' than halflings, they rely on their talents and arts as means of distraction. Their access to innate spells like illusions makes this easier for them. Additionally, if their illusions fail, they might pretend to be afflicted by a disease to divert suspicion. However, a failed disguise can arouse suspicion and subject them to the humans' fears of the supernatural.
Dragonborn{@sup **}

Dragonborns are born with parts of their skin covered with dragon-like scales, serpentine eyes and slightly forked tongues. As their condition is far more visible, they require more extensive means of concealment than any other race. They heavily rely on masks, cloaks, and magical items to disguise themselves, often posing as individuals suffering from a skin disease to avoid drawing attention. Additionally, the GM may allow a dragonborn character to begin with the Amulet of Adam and Eve (see below), a powerful magical item that offers a range of beneficial effects to hide among plain sight. If a disguise fails, humans may perceive a dragonborn as a monster or a threat.
Tiefling

The tails, irregular color of their skin, and horns of a tiefling can arouse suspicion and supernatural fear among the humans of Renaissance Italy. Consequently, tieflings often take great care to disguise themselves effectively. Additionally, the GM may permit a tiefling character to begin with the Amulet of Adam and Eve. If a disguise fails, tieflings may encounter hostility from humans due to their resemblance to devils in folktales and urban legends.
footnotes: {@sup *}During the Carnival season in Venice, or any other event in a game in which costumes or masks feature heavily, a GM could allow non-human characters to pass more easily.
{@sup **}A GM could allow a character to play a dragonborn with a more human appearance, featuring scales on their body but a human-like face.

entries.caption: Where Do They Live
rows: Secluded Streets and Districts in Cities
They typically reside in destitute and rudimentary areas adjacent to major cities, carving out their own distinct districts where a majority of the non-human population dwells.

It usually requires a successful {@dc 13} Intelligence ({@skill Investigation}) or Wisdom ({@skill Insight} or {@skill Perception}) check to determine a district that houses non-humans. Most districts have signs here and there in Thieves' Cant to explain the situation.
Secluded Settlements in Wilderness

Certain forests, deserts, valleys, and coastal areas provide secluded and hidden locations where many non-humans seek refuge to lead peaceful lives away from the cities. To deceive tax collectors and other officials, humans may reside among them and dabble in the arcane arts. Furthermore, outposts and watchtowers serve as warnings for incoming strangers.
The tracks of such a settlement can be perceived with a successful {@dc 15} Wisdom ({@skill Survival}) check.
Among Humans
Some of them choose to live, work, and marry among the humans by disguises or other methods. It is easier for dwarves, halflings, and elves to live like this.
Detecting these individuals varies depending on the quality of disguise and usage of arcane methods. Usually the DC is not lower than 10.
Nomadic Lifestyle
Some don't stay in one place for too long and are always on the move. They work as sellswords, caravan guides, foresters, explorers, hunters, and many different professions.
It usually depends on the individual's ability to disguise themselves to determine whether they are non-human or not. Again, the DC is not lower than 10.

entries.name: Notes on Religions & Divine Powers
entries: Within the Historica Arcanum universe, real-world religions manifest in every corner of the late Medieval and early Modern Mediterranean world. Churches, mosques, synagogues, pagan shrines, ancient temples, and sacred sites are strewn across this realm. Faith constitutes an indelible aspect of most individuals' lives, occupying a significant position within their culture and psyche. Some individuals profess that their extraordinary abilities stem from their convictions, pledges, deities, gods, beings, and benefactors: the landscape is dotted with individuals assuming titles like clerics, druids, rangers, and paladins. Additionally, there exist warlocks who assert that their power flows through a pact with entities beyond this world.

All of these are true. They genuinely believe that their power comes from a higher or deeper place, and they have strong proof through their achievement of amazing and unbelievable feats before your eyes. This raises the question: are religions real?

Answers pertaining to the existence or nature of higher powers in the Historica Arcanum universe are inherently unknowable. Such beliefs are personal matters, influenced by one's individual faith, values, and spirituality. Magical and divine powers are not conclusive evidence of the existence or superiority of any particular deity or higher power.

For instance, a Muslim cleric might assert that their God, Allah, is the only true deity, yet they could witness another cleric from Kyoto harnessing similar powers in the name of Izanami. In the Historica Arcanum universe, divine powers are believed to be a consequence of an individual's devotion, hard work, prayer, and willpower.

When it comes to warlocks and their patrons, the matter is quite different. While the existence of divine beings like God, Zeus, Leviathan, Ishtar, or Osiris may be a matter of belief, demons, fey creatures, aberrations, celestials, djinns, and elementals are more commonly accepted as existing in the world. Warlocks typically form pacts with these beings, which are often of a lesser power than the divine beings mentioned previously. For example, they may make a pact with a specific succubus, a greater djinn, or a hag, depending on the nature of their powers and the terms of their agreement.

entries.name: Pantheons
entries: Most TTRPGs, and especially 5th Edition, include pantheons for clerics, paladins, rangers or druids. These pantheons also exist in the world of Historica Arcanum. For example, all of the gods from Greek Mythology are sources of godly beliefs and magical power of their own respective domains.

entries.name: Notes on Languages
entries: In most TTPRGs, humanoids have languages based on their cultures, and other races largely speak the same language, such as elves speak Elvish. However, in Historica Arcanum, humans speak a variety of different languages, and fantasy tongues, such as Elvish, Dwarvish, or Orc do not exist, or at least are exceedingly rare (GM discretion).

entries.caption: Table of Languages
rows: Common

entries: If a player's chosen character allows them to speak Common, there are three alternatives for a player:

items: Choosing from languages/dialects that are spoken in the Italian City-States: Latin, Tuscan, Venetian, or another dialect/language of the player's choice.
Choosing from languages that are spoken in other areas of the Mediterranean: Spanish, Catalan, Portuguese, Arabic, and Ottoman Turkish.

If they are from another civilization, they can choose the civilizations' native tongues (e.g. German, Danish, English, Mandarin Chinese, Mongolian, Spanish) and one extra language that is spoken in the Mediterranean region.

rows: Normal Languages

If a player's chosen character allows them to speak regular languages in the 5th edition (Elvish, Gnomish, Dwarf, and the like), they can choose other living languages throughout the world and take the other option in the Common section. Examples of living languages include: German, Greek, Aramaic, Hebrew, Kurdish, Armenian, Mandarin Chinese, Tibetan, and more.
Exotic Languages

If you allow your players to choose exotic languages, they can learn dead and/or worldly exotic tongues, such as Ancient Greek, Ancient Latin, Sumerian, Sogdian, Old Norse, and even hieroglyphs in Egypt. Alternatively, you could allow for the existence of languages like Infernal, Abyssal, or Draconic.
footnotes: Note: To avoid confusion in the matters of communication, as there are many languages in the area, players may be allowed to choose the first two options of the Common bracket, as they will encounter those languages most frequently.
Note on script: Most of the Western languages use the Latin alphabet.

entries.name: The People of Renaissance Venice
entries: Due to its status as one of the most important entrepôts in the Mediterranean, Venice was one of the most diverse cities in Europe at the start of the 1500s. In addition, it was also one of the most populous, as the wealth of the city and its famed (albeit exaggerated) stability in a sea of war brought waves of immigrants. In theory, the city was welcoming to those incoming peoples, provided that they offer the Floating City something it could capitalize on. The local population can be divided into four rough categories: Italian Venetians, foreign merchants such as Germans and Muslims, permanent non-Italian residents, and slaves/servants.

entries.caption: Overall demographic make-up:
rows: People from the Italian peninsula

These people trace their ancestry to the original people of the peninsula who fled the Fall of Rome and sought refuge in the marshy islands of the lagoon; there is perhaps some truth to this, but Venetian foundational myth has played up the connection to Rome and overlooked possible connections to northern Italian and Carolingian areas that may have also provided the lagoon with some of its first peoples. It is known that these early settlers worked hard to make the islands habitable, and that the lagoon offered safety from marauding groups. They grew prosperous from salt, fish, and the Carolingian slave trade Alternatively, they are immigrants from other parts of Italy who arrived in the uncertain centuries between the Fall of Rome and the 16th century. For example, the illustrious Loredan family, the family of the current doge Leonardo Loredan in our story, is among these latter immigrants, coming to the city in the 11th century.
Foreign Visitors

These are peoples who have come to the city from locations outside the Venetian colonies for mercantile or diplomatic purposes and generally do not intend to live in Venice indefinitely. Typically these foreigners reside and work near each other, whether it is for communal solidarity or Venetian prerogative. They often congregated in fondaco, which were a combination of warehouse, market and living quarters. A prime example of this would be Fondaco dei Tedeschi, the headquarters of Venice's Germanic merchants.
Foreign Immigrants

These are peoples who have come to the city to live, having fled economic hardship or war in other regions, or just seeking opportunities in the Floating City. Many of these peoples hail from Venetian colonies, such as the Dalmatian coast. The process of naturalization and becoming "Venetian" is a bit complex, and it is hard to pinpoint how many of these inhabitants were able to become naturalized citizens, but what is clear is that they are an essential part of the fabric of Venetian life. It was Greek immigrants from Constantinople, fleeing the fall of the city in 1453, that helped bolster the flourishing appreciation of Greek and Latin classics as well as the art styles prevalent in Byzantium. These groups often form scuole piccole, confraternities devoted to specific religious works, like the altars of particular saints or charity work. One example of this is the The Dalmatian immigrants and infantry, called schiavoni, formed a confraternity called Scuola di San Giorgio degli Schiavoni in 1451.
Slaves{@sup *}

Despite their high-mindedness about the serenity of their republic, the Venetians were not above stooping to the vilest of trades. From the marketplaces near the Rialto, the slavers of Venice supplied not only the local houses with domestic servants and workers but also far-flung areas like the Mamluk Sultanate in Egypt. Many of the gondoliers in the city were freed African slaves, for instance. The trade gradually died down due to Ottoman conquests in the Balkans and Black Sea region, in which the Ottomans took over as the masters of the trade. It is possible that the Venetian slave merchants tried to carry on in the 1500s with their connections across the Mediterranean to Saharan Africa, but with the burgeoning Atlantic Slave Trade, they were soon eclipsed.
footnotes: {@sup *}Slavery is a tragic, damning fact of human history, one which we feel is important to shed light on and not ignore. By mentioning Venice's history in the slave trade, however, we are in no way advocating that GMs incorporate master/ slave dynamics in their games. We recommend GMs make sure their tables are comfortable with whatever subject matter they choose to include in their games (See our section entitled Safety Tools at the end of this chapter).

entries.caption: Social Structure of Venice:
rows: Nobility (Patriziato)

These are the aristocracy of Venice whose families' house names are recorded in the Golden Book (Libro d'Oro). In the early days of the Republic, the differences between nobility and the common folk were perhaps less pronounced due to the geographical realities of life in the Venetian Lagoon. However, as the city grew, so did the stratification. At the end of the 13th century, entry into the nobility solidly became based on hereditary rights, and in 1315 the names of the noble houses were written in the Libro d'Oro, which is closely guarded in the Doge's Palace. The Noble Houses are the only ones who can sit on the Great Council and have a voice in city affairs. They are referred to as "nobil uomo" or "nobil donna," or with the initials N.H. or N.D. before their name.
Citizens (citadinni)

entries: There are different types of cittadini, or Venetian citizen:

items: {@b Original citizens (cittadini originari):} In order to be a cittadino originario, one has to be born in Venice as legitimate offspring, not engaged in menial labor (arte meccanica as opposed to arte liberale), and your family being in the census and not having a criminal record for at least three generations. The cittadini originari are inscribed the Libro d'Argento — the Silver Book — since 1315, just like the patrizio had been in the Libro d'Oro, and they could also aspire to high-ranking government posts outside of the Grand Council.

{@b Citizens "within and beyond" (cittadini de intus et de extra)} are afforded the rights of citizens in Venice and afforded the privileges original citizens have while doing business abroad; however, they are not able to access higher level positions.

{@b Common people (cittadini de intus tantum)} have the rights of citizens within Venice but not abroad, and they cannot hold important positions. They are, however, able to participate in the scuole that dotted the city– these are charitable organizations that were an important part of the fabric of Venetian society.

rows: Foreigners

Those merchants, immigrants, and servants from the previous table who do not have citizenship rights in the city. This category also includes commoners from the dominions of Terraferma and Stato da Màr–at best, traditional aristocracy from those places can achieve the ranking of original citizens, but that is rare.

entries.name: Scuole Grandi
entries: Venice has many charitable organizations called scuola, five of which are the Scuole Grandi ('Great Schools'). These are confraternities, brotherhoods, and charitable organizations. Citizenship is required to be a member of a scuola, but they are not as restricted in their membership as guilds are. Typically, they are dedicated to a particular saint and are often connected to a church, but sometimes they form around a particular community and its interests. The scuole generally donate to the needy, organize events and festivals, patronize the arts, and act as a social club, amongst other pursuits. The scuole grandi, since they are religious organizations, are overseen by the Procurators of St. Mark.

entries.name: Names in Italy
entries: Some common names from Venice and the other Italian city-states in the 15th and 16th centuries are:

rows: Masculine Names

Alessandro, Leonardo, Dante, Giulio, Jacopo, Guiseppe, Matteo, Niccolo, Lodovico, Andrea, Cosimo, Paolo, Giovanni, Gasparo, Francesco, Stefano, Tommaso, Vittorio, Marco, Giambattista, Lorenzo, Banetto, Claudio, Luca, Vincenzo, Carlo, Bortolo, Aurelio, Bastiano, Antonio, Alvise, Salvador, Petro, Ottavio, Federigo, Rodrigo, Giacomo
Feminine Names

Chiara, Ursula, Lucia, Lucrezia, Christina, Caterina, Agnese, Cecilia, Ippolita, Filippa, Lizabeta, Veronica, Stella, Vittoria, Joanna, Isabetta, Lorenza, Magdalena, Leonarda, Maria, Giuliana, Flora, Grana, Antonia, Francesca, Antonia, Olimpia, Loretta, Simonetta, Lavinia, Camilla, Paola
footnotes: Optional Footer

entries: Italian city-states have a plethora of surnames, all with regional particularities. Surnames are usually familial, such as patronyms; nicknames; or based on birthplace, occupation, or other convention.
{@b Place Name examples:} da Vinci, da Padova, da Bologna, di Bari, Umbro, Veneziani, Romana, Spagnolo
{@b Patronym or Family examples:} di Giovanni, Andreini, de Medici, di Giacomo, de Bernardo
{@b Nickname examples:} il Moro ("the dark"), Rossi ("red"), Ricci ("curly"), Sforza ("force")
{@b Vocation examples:} Pane (baker), Ferrari (blacksmith), Massaro (farmer)

entries.name: The Jewish Community in Renaissance Italy**
entries: The Jewish community has lived on the Italian peninsula at least since the time of the Roman Empire, yet with the fall of the Western Roman Empire and the dominance of Europe by Christianity, the Jewish people have faced near constant discrimination that often boils over into anti-Semitic violence. In the late Middle Ages, Jews were expelled from many European kingdoms, resettling somewhere else only to find themselves persecuted once more and forced to leave. Many of these Jewish communities eventually found their way to the Ottoman Empire.

Many of the Jews expelled from Spain and Portugal in the 1490s also arrived in Italy, where they were surprisingly welcomed by the Papal States and the Kingdom of Naples. However, despite official welcoming, day-to-day discrimination occurred, and wherever Catholic orthodoxy gained sway, the Jews found their livelihoods threatened once more. In Venice, the city decided not to expel their Jewish population, but instead established the first ghetto in 1516 under Doge Leonardo Loredan. This decree limited where Jews could live and also their mobility: the bridges leading to and from the ghetto were closed at night, and any Jew caught breaking curfew was severely punished.

items: They are devoted to their religion and even practice it in hard times. If necessary, they practice their religion while hiding from the governing factions.

They have suffered harshly from the anti-Semitic policies of European kingdoms, and this has made the communities deeply resentful of the ruling Catholic Christians. On the other hand, the relationship between the Jewish population and Muslim visitors to Venice might be considerably stronger due to shared discrimination.

entries: {@sup **}Anti-Jewish sentiment and laws are a stain on European and Mediterranean history. We include the ghetto in our Venetian setting in order to try to be as accurate to the era as possible, but this is neither an endorsement of anti-Jewish attitudes, nor is it a fiat that GMs must follow. We recommend GMs make sure their tables are comfortable with whatever subject matter they choose to include in their games (See the Safety Tools section).
Marco Polo describes a bridge, stone by stone.
"But which is the stone that supports the bridge?"
Kublai Khan asks.
"The bridge is not supported by one stone or another,"
Marco answers, "but by the line of the arch that they form."
Kublai Khan remains silent, reflecting. Then he adds:
"Why do you speak to me of the stones? It is only the arch that matters to me."
Polo answers: "Without the stones there is no arch."

entries.name: The Political Structure of Venice
entries: She calls herself La Serenissima, The Most Serene. The Republic of Venice put forth the image of a bastion of peace, security, and prosperity amidst the carnage, corruption, and chaos of the rest of the Mediterranean and European world. When a traveler first catches sight of Venice, floating on the lagoon like a mirage in the desert, it is understandable that one would start to believe the stories, as the city shimmers like a mirage in the desert and almost lulls one into believing its reality. The truth is, of course, much more complicated; it is buried beneath layers of myth, arrogance, and competition with other city-states. One thing for certain is that the power is not in the hands of "the people" but instead a select few (which should surprise none of our readers). It would be more appropriate to call Venice an oligarchy, which would make it less unique in comparison to its Italian neighbors. The leader, the doge, is elected, but only by a number of voters entirely pulled from the aristocracy.

rows: Doge

The doge (a Venetian variant of "dux" or "duke,") is the head of state and all state institutions. The doge is elected by 41 members of the Maggiore Consiglio and generally serves for life. Their power is limited, and their old age at election is a natural limit to their time in power.
Minor Consiglio del Doge / Signoria

entries: The Signoria of Venice consists of:

items: the Doge, head of the Republic
the Minor Council (Minor Consiglio), created in 1175, which was composed of the Doge's six advisors.
the three leaders of the Quarantia, the supreme tribunal, created in 1179.

rows: Consiglio dei Pregadi (Senate)

The Venetian Senate was initially an informal group of patricians which the doge called to ask for advice in state matters. From 1229, however, the Great Council took control of this advisory council, and elected sixty members annually, later expanded several times to 120. The Senate gradually inherited more and more responsibilities from the Great Council, especially in matters of commerce, foreign relations and war, while always formally acting on behalf of the Great Council.
Consiglio Maggiore (The Great Council)

The Great Council is, since its inception in 1172, the highest authority of the Republic of Venice. Despite the name, the Great Council is not an elected body, but the assembly of the entire electorate. The members are men aged twenty-five or more, and are the legitimate offspring of parents from recognised aristocratic families. However, some younger members are added through the annual Barbarela (the drawing of lots from an urn from the names of thirty patricians aged between the ages of twenty and twenty-five in order to be admitted to the Great Council).
Procuratore di San Marco (Procurators of St. Mark)

These are honorary positions, second only to the doge in prestige. It is granted to patricians of notable families in terms of wealth and position, who distinguish themselves with the services provided in embassies, in the command of armies, in the long exercise of the main offices of the State. There are nine procurators: the first three (de supra) are responsible for the administration of the Basilica of St. Mark; the next three (de citra) look after the guardianships, commissioners, and wills of the sestieri of San Marco, Castello, and Cannaregio; the last three (de ultra), to the guardianships, commissioners, and wills of the sestieri of Dorsoduro, San Polo and Santa Croce.
Consiglio di Dieci (The Council of Ten)

The Council of Ten - This council oversees state security and sat a court for the prosecution of crimes against the state and in cases against patricians. It was created in 1310 following the failed Baiamonte Tiepolo conspiracy. It consisted of ten patricians elected by the Consiglio Maggiore for a one-year term. When it sat as a court, there were seventeen judges, as the Doge and his six counselors also participated. In many ways, The Council of Ten is the most powerful and most feared organization in Venice, and it has spies everywhere.
Avogadori de Comùn (Public Prosecutors/State Attorneys)
The Avogadori serve as public prosecutors, as guarantors of the legality of the political and administrative procedures of the Republic of Venice.
Quarantia (Council of Forty)

The Council of Forty is a judicial branch of Venetian government. In the 1400s the Quarantia was split into three branches: Criminal, Old Civil (Venice and the Dogado) and New Civil (the Dominions). The Quarantia adjudicates only cases between cittadini (citizens), while patricians are tried in front of the Council of Ten.
Inquisitori di Stato (State Inquisitors)

State Inquisitors are always on the lookout for threats against the safety of the state. They have broad and largely unchecked powers. The three inquisitors are appointed by the Senate and the Council of Ten.
Magistrato alla Sanità (Magistracy of Public Health)

The Magistracy of Public Health has administrative powers over everything health related, which, besides the lazzaretti (quarantine islands), also includes inns, prostitutes, pharmacies, doctors, garbage collection, and the water supply.
Signori di Notte (Lords of the Night)
6 magistrates chosen from the patrician class. One for each sestieri, the "Lords of the Night" would watch over their designated district and keep their eyes out for various crimes.
Protomaestri

Not technically part of the government but an integral part of its operations, the protomaestro, or proto, is the head architect and technical specialist in charge of major construction projects in the city. Proti are, for instance, responsible for the design and construction of buildings like the Arsenale, the Campanile, churches and confraternities, and many more. The people chosen to be protomaestri are well-paid and often keep their positions for long periods of time so that they can oversee a building's construction from conception to completion.

entries.name: What is going on around Venice
entries: The Italian peninsula in 1520-1521 is a tangled web of power politics and rivalries, but the overall social structure of each city-state is relatively consistent to earlier generations: a Medici is in charge of Florence, a Sforza is in charge of Milan (though Milan is controlled by the Holy Roman Empire), and southern Italy is a prize larger kingdoms are fighting over. This section is meant as a brief overview with broad brushstrokes of Europe in 1520-1521, as a deep dive into every aspect of late Medieval to early Modern Europe is beyond the scope of this setting guide.

entries.name: Florence
entries: Although the golden era is over for Florence, the last rays of its excellence extend into the 16th century. The city as we know it in 1521 was shaped by the Medici family, who were a prominent family of bankers and transformed the city through their largesse and political acumen. Cosimo de' Medici and Lorenzo de' Medici were the de facto rulers of "La Bella," but at the end of the 1400s, the family was exiled from the city after having made a deal with Charles VIII of France, acceding to the monarch's demands on his way to invading Naples. However, the Medicis returned to Florence in 1512, and now in 1520-1521 the city is jointly ruled with the Papal States by Pope Leo X (Giovanni de Medici). Leo X placed his Medici family back in charge of Florence–first Giuliano and then Lorenzo II–and made sure to guide their hands. In 1519, Lorenzo II de' Medici, the father of the future queen of France Catherine de Medici, died, and Cardinal Giulio de' Medici took over running Florence. Giuliano, in 1523, will become the new pope and take the name Pope Clement VII.
The pope, and therefore the Medici family, is at best wary of Venice and at worst openly hostile, as in the League of the War of Cambrai.

entries.name: Milan
entries: The Duchy of Milan's early Renaissance history is dominated by the Visconti family and then the Sforza family. In 1521, Milan has been at the center of much of the turmoil of the Italian Wars. In 1521, Milan is under the control of the Holy Roman Empire.

entries.name: Rome and The Papal States
entries: The first two decades of the 1500s saw the reign of Pope Alexander XI, also known as Rodrigo Borgia, and later Medici Popes. In late 1521 a new Italian War, the "Four Year War," will break out, with the Papal States allied with Holy Roman Emperor Charles V and King Henry VIII of England against Francis I of France and the Republic of Venice.

entries.name: Kingdom of Naples
entries: It can be argued that the Kingdom of Naples is the spark which lit the powder keg of the Italian Wars, as the question of rights over the Kingdom is what led France to invade the Italian Peninsula. By 1504, the Kingdom was a kingdom under Spain, which then became ruled by the Holy Roman Empire under Charles V. France, however, will continue to contest the right to rule Naples until 1559.

entries.name: Europe Surrounding Italy
entries: The rest of Western Europe is dominated by large kingdoms or empires and leaders based on hereditary rights.

items: Charles V, grandson of Ferdinand II and Isabella I of Spain, is the Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain, having taken the mantle in 1519.
Francis I is the king of France. Originally from Orleans, Francis continues the Italian Wars and patronizes the arts.

Henry VIII is the King of England. While the Holy Roman Empire and France have duked it out over the fate of the Italian peninsula, Henry has sat back and waited for his chance to retake the north of France. He aligned himself with Charles V, the Holy Roman Emperor, but he is relatively unconcerned with affairs in Italy, instead focusing more on trying to secure a male heir to his throne.

entries: For those GMs interested in making plagues and diseases a bigger part of their game, please see the {@b Plague and Disease} module in one of our previous releases, {@b Historica Arcanum: Empires of the Silk Road}.

entries.name: The Ottoman Empire
entries: In 1520 Sultan Selim I died, but instead of a lull in action in the Mediterranean that would calm the nerves of their neighbors, a loud crack of thunder sounded and heralded a new storm rising. Suleiman I, more famously known as Suleiman the Magnificent or Suleiman the Lawgiver, became sultan, beginning the longest reign in Ottoman history. In 1521, Suleiman's attention is on taking central Europe, and he will begin a long siege of Nándorfehervár (Belgrade) in May, which will end victoriously for him in August. Suleiman then will turn his attention to control of the Mediterranean, starting with Rhodes in 1522, then later turning his attention back to the Balkans and Central Europe.

entries.name: Religious Strife
entries: As with the previous installment in our Historica Arcanum series, Era of the Crusades, it is necessary to address the strife between Christianity and Islam–in this case, the conflict between the Christian kingdoms of Western Europe and the Muslim Ottoman Empire. Though the days of the Crusades were long over, the kings, queens, lords, and ladies looked towards the fall of Constantinople in 1453 and the growth of Ottoman power and territory as an existential threat. As the years progressed, the Ottoman march was eventually stalled in Europe, and the wars between Christian kingdoms did not abate; in this murky new era of gunpowder-flecked Europe, the Sultans were often watching the Christians ruin themselves with a wry and curious smile on their faces, and offering alliances and ultimatums to stir the pot.

entries.name: Another Great Schism in Christianity
entries: In 1054 CE, the Roman Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox Church had split over a variety of ecclesiastical and theological issues. In 1517, a new schism was growing: Martin Luther wrote a letter to his bishop criticizing the practice of selling indulgences in the Church; this letter became known as the 95 Theses, and led to Pope Leo X issuing a papal bull calling for Luther to recant his writings. Luther refused, and in the Diet of Worms in 1521, overseen by the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, Luther was branded a heretic. However, because of rising public support, Luther was not arrested or killed. Thus began the Protestant Reformation. As the decades go by, the Catholic Church mounts a Counter-Reformation, and internecine war breaks out across the continent.

entries.name: Plagues
entries: Much time has passed since the dreaded Black Death pandemic of 1346 to 1353, yet plague epidemics are still a palpable threat to Venice and the rest of Renaissance Italy. Between the Black Death and the end of the 15th century, Venice–due to its maritime location and vocation–put in place effective quarantine regulations which would in turn be adopted in other parts of Europe. The island of Lazzaretto Vecchio contained a hospital and leper colony, and the island Lazzaretto Nuovo served as an anchor point for ships suspected of carrying plague. Visitors were required to stay confined for forty days, the number of days Jesus Christ was said to have spent fasting in the Judean desert. After another epidemic in 1478–possibly the first instance of typhus in Europe–the previously temporary Provveditori alla sanità (Superintendents of Health) became a permanent office.

entries.name: Accommodation
entries: The main source of accommodation in Venice is the many inns, or osterie, where one is sure to find, at the very least, wine and bread, and a humble place to lay one's head. These are mainly located near the two centers of socio-economic and political life in Venice: the Piazza San Marco and the Rialto market district. The osterie are monitored by the government in order to keep an eye on who passes through them; additionally, there are a number of spaces the government has allowed to be open for particular foreign groups, such as the Fondaco dei Tedeschi near Rialto, where merchants from the Holy Roman Empire are required to stay. Additionally, after the establishment of the Jewish Ghetto in 1516, an inn opened there specifically to receive Jewish travelers.

However, these official spaces are not sufficient to accommodate the influx of travelers, officials, and merchants who make their way to the city; concomitantly, not every foreign traveler wants to stay where the government tells them to. Therefore, unofficial private lodgings–camere locande and albergarie–have begun appearing in the city. As these have grown in popularity, the authorities have sought to make these types of lodging houses identifiable (and taxable) and bring them into the fold of spaces they controlled. Therefore, reforms have been introduced to limit the number of tenants these private establishments could lodge, and if they want to accommodate foreigners, they have to obtain a license first (for a fee, of course). Naturally, many individuals do not want to do this, so there are still a number of unofficial lodging houses and private rooms where visitors who want a quiet place to sleep can stay away from the government's record-keeping.

entries.name: Muslim Travelers
entries: In 1621, a palazzo on the Grand Canal will be transformed into the Fondaco dei Turchi, where Muslim merchants from Albania, Bosnia, the Ottoman Empire, and other places will be required to stay. However, during the time period of Echoes of Renaissance and A Serenade for the Damned, in 1520-1521, Muslim merchants are mainly left to find private lodging, either with a friendly patrician or in the many privately run lodging areas that have begun to spring up. Most merchants from the Ottoman lands looking to do honest work in Venice find accommodation in inns and private lodgings in sestiere Cannaregio and near San Giovanni e Paolo in sestiere Castello. It is an open secret that the Venetian government spies on those places, but they do not interfere provided the merchants are registered, stay a limited time, and do not bring families. Apart from those places, there are many unofficial lodgings willing to take in travelers of all sorts with no prejudice, provided they have coin.

entries.name: Money
entries: The history of coinage in the Republic of Venice and in the Mediterranean is complex, with the major city-states not only minting their own coins, but also changing the weight and names of their coins in circulation. Though Venice's coins are often found all over the place due to their prominent trading position, they are by no means the only type of coin in use. We know that the characters your players choose to bring to life may be from far-flung places and may have different coins with different names. At the same time, we know running a game with 20 different names for gold coins of various sizes is a logistical nightmare for GMs.

With all this being said, though we have taken some liberties (soldi were another silver coin, for instance–though it was later minted in copper), have have tried to come up with a system of coinage that matches what is expected in a fantasy TTRPG while also being true to the historical setting. We suggest using the following coin names and denominations in Echoes of Renaissance and A Serenade for the Damned for your games in and around Venice. If your Renaissance adventures take you to other locales which are out of the purview of this book, feel free to substitute the Venetian names with more local ones (such as florin in Florence, piastra in Naples, and so forth).

entries.name: Safety Tools
entries: The universe of Historica Arcanum is one of real world history combined with undercurrents of arcane mysteries, occult secrets, and monstrous revelations. With that said, moments of horror, violence, and danger and other mature themes do occur as a by-product of the genre of storytelling we occupy.

We cannot honestly write a story about the Crusades, for example, without including what they were–a series of violent ideological conflicts, to put it very mildly. We do not shy away from the grim realities of historical moments and eras, but we do strive to approach these time periods with care, diligent research, and an unbiased perspective.

Human history is, in many ways, a history of annihilation, involving countless tragic events, from the decimation of natural areas to the exterminations of peoples through warfare, disease, and prejudice. Due to this, telling stories from history–fictional and magical they may be–is fraught with the dangers of approaching topics some players at your tables may not be comfortable with.
Therefore, we highly recommend–we stress, in fact–that you incorporate safety tools into your gameplay so that everyone at your table can engage with the material in a safe and entertaining manner.

items: Run a session 0 so that the tone and content of your game is clear, and players can opt out if they wish. This works to talk about character ideas and story so that you find out what kind of game people enjoy most; however, it also works well to learn what people would like to avoid. For instance, when you talk about likes and dislikes in gameplay, maybe you'll discover that one of your players is arachnophobic, so you shouldn't incorporate giant spiders into your game.

entries: Use safety tools during the game to ensure that everyone is comfortable:

items: 'Lines and Veils' is a popular Safety Tool, first formulated by Ron Edwards in the 2004 Sex and Sorcery supplement for the game Sorcerer. Lines are areas that definitely should not appear in the game at all, and Veils are areas which a player wishes to be handled off screen, delicately, or abstractly. For instance, a player might say in session 0 that torture is a Line and sexual content is a Veil, meaning that torture should not come up in the game at all, and sexual scenes should not get detailed or graphic (like how the camera pans away in video games, TV series, and films). For another player, torture may be a Veiled subject (meaning it can be implied but not shown in game), but harm to animals is a Line that should not be crossed. In session 0, the GM and the players should create a list so that everyone is on the same page about what content is acceptable.

Using an 'X Card': the X card was developed by John Stavropoulos and allows an easy way to let everyone at the table know that the current scene is uncomfortable. A card with an X on it is placed on the table, and whenever anyone doesn't like where the scene is heading, they simply tap the card, and the scene is skipped or those enacting the current scene stop and move on. Read more about the X card here: {@link http://tinyurl.com/x-card-rpg}.

'Script Change', created by Beau Sheldon, is an alternative to X card that works off verbal statements rather than a card on the table, so it might work better for certain groups. With Script Change, one can change the nature of the scene with words like 'pause' 'fast forward' 'rewind,' etc. to make sure everyone is okay. For instance, a player could say: "Pause for a second: can we fast forward past this execution? We don't need the gruesome details" or "Pause for a second: can we fast forward through this scene? I'm glad my character is hooking up with this elf warrior, but I'm not comfortable playing that out in detail." You can find Script Change here: {@link https://thoughty.itch.io/script-change}

entries.name: Who Are You in the Renaissance?
Your Journey

entries: This section is optional. These are not rules meant to be followed by the letter but are instead inspirational hooks that we hope will spark some great ideas for player characters. It is worth noting that we purposefully did not put gameplayheavy choices into these tables, including races and classes.

Roll, read, or ignore these tables as you wish when you are making a new character to start your adventure in the world of Historica Arcanum. We recommend that you give luck and fate a chance; after all, we don't get to decide where we will start our journey in the real world.
{@b Origins:} These tables will give you information about your birth, childhood, and family. Also, there is one special table about the beliefs of your childhood community.
{@b Personal Decisions:} These tables will give information about your adventurer background, your class, your past education, and your profession if you have any.
{@b Life Experiences:} In this section you will learn about your character's past deeds and experiences. Results may spark new ideas about ideology, life goals, phobias, or even deep personal traits.
{@b Supplementary Tables:} These tables are here to support the main tables.

How Did Your Arcane Abilities First Manifest

entries.name: Magic Items
entries: In the world of Historica Arcanum, and especially Yatamon, magic items are abundant, diverse, and highly sought after—each possessing unique powers and abilities. This section lists the new magic items that can be found in Yatamon. The magic items are listed alphabetically.

entries.name: Common
entries: Common items are usually mundane-looking items that can be found among the world, even within most obvious places, to those who know where to look. Most of the common magic items, although named common, are not that frequently encountered among the common markets or are mostly ignored by the common folk due to not knowing they are magic items at all. Most of them became magical over time due to the natural magic surrounding the world and thanks to the will of others rather than sentiently crafted by magicians and inventors.

entries.name: Uncommon
entries: Uncommon magic items are harder to come by in regular markets and remote corners of the world. Unlike common magic items, they are usually crafted by magicians or inventors, most notably potions, weapons, shields, and ammunition. For regular people, these items might seem to have inestimable value, while those with knowledge of the arcane can accurately appraise these items.

entries.name: Rare
entries: Rare magic items might not catch one's eye in a market; they will be in the hands of the most prominent figures or be lying within the dust and rust in forgotten corners. Due to Historica Arcanum's magical rules, rare items are hardly encountered, and thus are very hard to find. Their value reaches the sky if the eyes that touch them know their prominence. They can change the tides of fate in wars, conflicts, and other difficult times.

entries.name: Very Rare
entries: Only a handful of very rare items are in the world of Historica Arcanum and possibly the items have witnessed the rises and falls of civilizations, great magical encounters, events that broke the world or once belonged to very powerful individuals; possibly adventurers lost in time, viziers in great palaces, veteran soldiers and valiant warriors that are encountered in legendary tales. It would be odd to stumble upon a very rare item in a marketplace or in the hands of a seller. Very few could put a price on them and even fewer could afford it.

entries.name: Legendary
entries: God-kings, empresses, king-makers, shapers of destiny, those names that are never forgotten by history leave behind certain items whose magical prowess exceeds any expectations and breaks regular rules of destiny. Legendary items are indeed filled with legends and myths - only with the right touch can their power be observed, and the world will never feel the same when they are seen by mere mortals. It is almost impossible to put a price on a legendary item; probably it would cost kingdoms, upending the tides of fate, or the breaking of the world.
The legendary items are listed under "Artifacts in the Renaissance" below.

entries.name: Feats
entries: When you gain an Ability Score Improvement and your GM allows feats, these options can be added to the Feats list.

entries.name: Art of War
entries: The Art of War Combat is a brand new Weapon Loadout and Battle Stance system that allows you to bring more variety to your combat turns. In this section, you will find a number of unique styles and stances, which provide the characters with dynamic combat options instead of simply taking the Attack action. In order to have access to one of the following stances, the character needs to be a Martial class, and they need to fulfill the specific Prerequisites. However, all of these are subject to GM discretion; be sure to check with them beforehand. Note: only one stance can be active with a particular weapon in combat at a time.

entries.name: Legendary Inspirations Deck
entries: In this section, the Legendary Inspirations Deck is provided as a series of tables that let you or your players roll when they gain a point of Inspiration, instead of drawing a card from the deck. They can keep that ability just like an Inspiration and use it whenever they like with a free action, provided that it is their turn. They can also trade the ability in for a regular Inspiration, which gives Advantage on a d20 roll.

entries.name: Venice - The Most Serene Republic

entries: "Cities, like dreams, are made of desires and fears, even if the thread of their discourse is secret, their rules are absurd, their perspectives deceitful, and everything conceals something else."
"Great men built Rome, but Venice was built by gods."
entries.by: Jacopo Sannazaro, from the Opera Latina

entries: It is night. The lights of fires on the nearby bridge reflect off the canal water and create phantasmagoric shapes on the building opposite mine. As I sit here in this drawing room, window open to the city, I hear two women speaking, and I know not if their voices come from just around the corner or several alleys away. The canals and buildings have an eerie manner about them, as if they were following the rules of a universe tangential to ours but altogether different.

It is an absurd dream, this city on the water. It is a whimsical chimera which should not exist. Yet it does, and not only does it exist, it thrives. Those who had arrived in this brackish water sought refuge from the sword and fire of invasion after invasion. They hid in the silt and tall grass, they waited, and when the way back home became untenable, they began to make a new life. They blended with the customs of local fishermen and began building settlements on the shifting muck. They harvested salt and maintained their connections to Eastern Rome while watching warily to see if Rome would survive the Germanic onslaught.

They grew and, miraculously, began flourishing. They hammered Dalmatian tree trunks into the anaerobic mire of the islands; they built grand palazzi, churches, and shipyards of graceful Istrian limestone and Veronese marble. It is often said that salt was Venice's first bringer of wealth, but I would say the lagoon itself, and the murky protection it provided, was the first indicator of future success. The lagoon sheltered them, and would continue to do so even as the world burned around them. After the riches of salt came the lucrative spice trade, and ship building, and the theft of St. Mark's body from Alexandria, which lent some religious legitimacy to the nascent republic. Along the way came the sacking of Constantinople in 1204, which brought untold Byzantine riches and a final, violent parting with their former Eastern parent. The people of the city grew richer, vainer, more arrogant, but also more circumspect. They deploy shrewd skill in intelligence, navigating medieval alliances, open arms to those with coin to spend, and a government system capable of the very best in draconian tactics and shadowy arts should the need arise.

All the while, they build and build, more edifices to glorify their god, their saints, and themselves. When night falls, they look up at the sky and see the sugary stars; they see their floating city reflected in the cosmos...

entries.name: The Domains of Land and Sea
entries: In 1521 CE, Venice is not only a city of islands floating in a lagoon, but is also an empire. Overall, there are three domains, politically and geographically, of Venice:

items: {@b The Duchy of Venice (Dogado)} — This is the city proper of Venice, which includes the six sestieri (districts) and immediate surrounding islands like Murano, Burano, and Torcello. Echoes of Renaissance focuses on this central part of Venice.

{@b Domain of the Sea (Stato da Màr or Domina da Màr)} — This domain is the Republic of Venice's overseas territories along the Adriatic coast and across the Mediterranean. Some key territories in this domain at the time of our setting include: Istria, Zadar (Zara), Corfu, Crete (Candia), and Cyprus.

{@b Mainland Domains (Domini di Terraferma)} — These are Venice's expansive territories in Northeast Italy, including much of the Po River Valley, neighboring the Duchy of Milan to the west and the domains of the Holy Roman Empire to the north and northeast. Some key places in Terraferma include Bergamo, Verona, Padua, and the Friuli region.

entries.name: The City of Venice - The Sestieri and Surrounding Islands
entries: The Duchy of Venice is separated into six major districts, or sestieri, as well as islands in close proximity in the lagoon, such as Giudecca and Murano. This chapter will detail each sestiere, as well as factions, NPCs, and points of interest in each area.

entries.name: Introduction
entries: Named after Venice's adopted patron St. Mark, sestiere San Marco is the crowded, beating heart of Venice, and the center of its political power. Here is where the Palazzo Ducale (Doge's Palace) and most of the government offices are located, as well as the most important religious symbol of the city: Basilica San Marco (St. Mark's Basilica). Spreading out from the basilica and the palazzo are the grand public squares (the connected piazza and piazzetta), where processions, festivities, markets, and executions all take place to the rhythm of the Campanile tower's bells.

San Marco also includes one half of the bustling Rialto area, where merchants, visitors, and locals—both citizen and non-citizen alike—gravitate for fresh food, and fresh news. Between Rialto and Piazza San Marco are the finest shops in the city, imposing churches, and several important palazzi where nobles look after their family fortunes and look down on the warren-like canals and alleys that spill out around them. In these busy alleys are many taverns, lodging rooms, merchant shops, and dens of ill-repute. One could easily get lost or make a name for themselves in this beautiful chaos.

entries.name: Doge's Palace (Palazzo Ducale)

entries: The alabaster and rose palace appears to float elegantly on two floors of arcing Istrian columns. Much like the city itself, it appears to be pulling off a gravity-defying feat, thumbing its nose at the cosmos and its laws. A crowd gathers in the Piazzetta di San Marco, and there are even onlookers on boats moored at the nearby docks. All eyes are on the upper loggia and the 2 red marble columns which stand out in the forest of white limestone. There the doge stands in his corno ducale and illustrious robes of crimson and gold damask. He is flanked by members of the Council of Ten, the power behind the throne. The doge's voice is tempered but carries far, and his words are grave: the execution of a disgraced noble for theft of state assets. The noble is brought forth in white robes, stripped of all position and wealth; his right hand, already cut off, hangs on a chain around his neck. The executioner swiftly takes his head, which falls to the piazzetta below, and the crowd cheers for the doge, "His Serenity."

The Palazzo Ducale is the official residence of the ruler of Venice as well as the location of the meeting chambers for the various government councils. The doge is elected in a complicated process by the Councils of the government, and once he is elected, he serves for life. However, he is almost always voted in at an advanced age so that his time in power is limited. Once he dies, his family has a limited amount of time to leave the palace, and the government elects a new doge. Although some doges have been able to assert their authority and put forth agendas of their design, the position is mainly that of a figurehead, and the councils of state hold the real decision making power. In fact, the doge cannot leave the palace unless it is for an important event, like the Marriage to the Sea Ceremony, or if the journey has been sanctioned by the high councils.

The current version of the palace took form in 1423 after the wing facing the Piazzetta San Marco was added. The building astounds upon first viewing it, as it seems it should topple over, with its grand upper floors of Veronese marble sitting on two floors of elegant arched loggie. However, like much of Venice, it seems to defy gravity and float. The ground floor exterior loggia is often choked with Venetians beseeching patricians entering the palace for meetings, as well as thieves, beggars, and notaries. The first loggia overlooking the Piazza and Piazzetta is where pronouncements are often read out to the public, and where the occasional important execution takes place (most public executions are conducted between the pillars in the Piazzetta). The 9th and 10th columns from the left are darker colored, as if stained in the blood of the traitorous patricians whose fates are sealed here.

Next to the Basilica San Marco, there is the ceremonial entrance to the palace courtyard within: the Porta della Carta (Paper Door), crafted by father and son master architects, Giovanni and Bartolomeo Bon in the fifteenth century, and given that name due to its proximity to the administrative offices of the palace. Above the doorway, a bas relief shows Francesco Foscari, a former doge, kneeling in front of the Winged Lion of St. Mark. Normally, there are {@dice 1d4} {@creature oltremarino|EchoesOfRenaissance|oltremarini} stationed at the Porta della Carta, as well as another {@dice 1d6} {@creature oltremarino|EchoesOfRenaissance|oltremarini} doing rounds around the exterior ground floor loggia.
The Palazzo Ducale is featured in detail in Acts III and IV of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.

entries.name: Faction: Oltremarini
entries: The Reggimenti oltremarini, also known as schiavoni, are the elite infantry corps that serve as the Doge's personal bodyguards. The group was originally made up of people from the Dalmatian holdings, like Zadar, hence the name schiavoni ('Slavs' in Venetian). The oltremarini are mainly attached to the navy as infantry units, and have been instrumental in fighting the Ottomans in Venice's territories in the Eastern Mediterranean. However, they have occasionally been deployed to deal with issues in the Terraferma. Each unit has a local commander, and the commander of the troops guarding the Doge's Palace is Marco Marolizio (LG, human male, early 50s, {@creature oltremarino|EchoesOfRenaissance}), a veteran of several skirmishes with the Ottomans who has since settled into a cosier posting.
{@b Faction centers:}
The main headquarters of the oltremarini is in Zara (Zadar) in Venetian Dalmatia, but in Venice the oltremarini can be found at their recruitment center on the Riva degli Schiavoni.

The Scuola di San Giorgio degli Schiavoni, established by the oltremarini as well as Dalmatian merchants and sailors, is a great meeting place for any characters from the Dalmatian area who is looking to strengthen their social connections in the city.

entries.name: Basilica di San Marco (Basilica of St. Mark)

entries: The golden mosaics of the basilica's grand façade radiate with the blaze of the sun's dying light. The gleam washes over you as you approach the central portal flanked by columns of marble and porphyry. Above your head, four copper horses—stolen from the Hippodrome in Constantinople—rear and prance, and even higher still, the lion of St. Mark proudly stands sentinel between gilded scenes of Jesus's life. This is Venice at its most turgid yet pulchritudinous, its best attempt to capture Venus rising from her sea shell.

The Basilica of St. Mark is technically the private chapel of the doge, hence its location next to the palace. However, it is undoubtedly also the most important religious focal point in the city, partly because of its splendor, partly its central location, and partly its legendary status as the resting place of the relics of St. Mark (or at least some of the relics). Venice had been searching for a more important patron saint that would increase its legitimacy in the eyes of Rome and Constantinople, as well as overshadow the nearby Patriarchate of Aquileia. In 828 CE, Venetian merchants in Alexandria reportedly smuggled the remains of St. Mark out of the city—hidden in pork fat to get past the Muslim custom officers in the port, if legends are to be believed—and brought the remains not to the Patriarchate of Venice in San Pietro di Castello but to Doge Giustiniano Participazio. In his will, the doge called for a special church to be built for the saint; therefore, curiously, the protector of the patron saint's remains has first and foremost been the City of Venice itself, not the church.

The church has been rebuilt several times, with different doges putting their stamp on the building, but the current version was mainly completed in 1094 CE, with extensive exterior modifications in the 13th century. Every bit of the church is an amalgamated vision of Venice's history and its self-perception: its origins are evident in its domes, mosaics, and design, which were inspired by the great Byzantine churches of Constantinople, such as the Church of Holy Apostles. At the same time, the building's decorations reveal a city inventing and enriching itself: as a republic-turned-empire which turned its back on its Byzantine former parent (and, indeed, stabbed it in the back). Brilliant marble stolen from the Levant and Egypt adorns the walls, and the building (and its treasury) is lined with booty taken from the sack of Constantinople during the 4th Crusade, such as the horses and 'Pillars of Acre' outside.

At any given time during the day, the area directly in front of the main entrance to the basilica is teeming with vendors selling their goods, as well as beggars, frauds, and doomsayers. The south entrance, closest to the palace's Porta della Carta (Paper Door), was sealed two decades earlier to make room for the tomb of a cardinal who donated generously to the church. The northern entrance (the Portal of Flowers), and the central portal facing Piazza San Marco are closed unless there is a special occasion. It is not permitted to enter the basilica unless one has express permission from the Doge or the Procurators of St. Mark (government officials who aid the doge in administering to the basilica's finances and expenses, such as decorations and repairs). Alternatively, during important state occasions, such as a doge's funeral or the coronation of a new doge, there is a higher chance of getting into the church but would require posing as a patrician or being on very good terms with one.

The entrances are magically bolstered by Primicerius Jacopo de'Barbari (LN human male, early 60s, {@creature clergyman|EchoesOfRenaissance|priest of Venice, clergyman}), who is responsible for all the religious functions of the basilica. De'Barbari has the {@spell alarm} spell cast on each door, and he or one of his attendants re-casts the spells every eight hours; if an interloper triggers the spell, they are quickly apprehended by {@creature oltremarino|EchoesOfRenaissance|oltremarini} patrolling outside the basilica and the Doge's Palace. The captured people are then brought to the prisons on the ground floor of the Doge's Palace, where they will later be interrogated. De'Barbari has {@dice 1d4} {@creature acolyte|EchoesOfRenaissance|priest of Venice, acolyte} assistants in his employ, helping him oversee the chapel and guard its treasures. At night, the interior of the basilica is guarded by {@creature Ales Leo|EchoesOfRenaissance|Ales Leo, the Winged Lion} (GM discretion).

entries.name: Interior:
entries: The church interior is laid out in a Greek cross, with one central dome and two domes above each arm of the cross.
