The cupolas are covered in gold and mosaics depicting saints, prophets, the Last Judgement, Ascension, and Pentecost. The altar in the eastern arm is raised and art around it shows scenes from St. Mark's life. The stone sarcophagus holding his remains is in the crypt below.

entries.name: Pala d'Oro (Golden Panel)
entries: This ornate golden panel behind the main altar is bedecked with 2,000 emeralds, amethysts, sapphires, rubies, pearls, and other gemstones. In addition to the gold and gems, there are colorful cloisonne scenes of saints, Mary, and Jesus. There are also more recent and decidedly Venetian scenes added, such as the spiriting of St. Mark's body out of Alexandria.

entries.name: The Treasury
entries: The treasury is filled with untold riches stolen from Constantinople during the Fourth Crusade, as well as other items brought from the Levant, Alexandria, Greece, Dalmatia, and beyond. Feel free to consult the table below or add magic items to the treasury that suit your party and your story. However, it should be noted that it is extremely difficult to get into the vault. Not only would an adventurer have to get past the alarmed doors and the priests keeping an eye on things, but they would also have to get past the watchful eyes of the Ales Leo at night. Moreover, the doors to the vault are sealed with an {@spell arcane lock} spell as well as an {@spell alarm} spell.

entries.caption: Items in the Basilica Treasury
rows: Pair of agate lamps in shapes of fish
Sardonyx chalice
Ewer of the Fatimid caliph al-Azĩz-billãh, 10th century
Chalice made with serpentine
Fragment of the True Cross and ampulla of Christ's blood
Icon of St. Michael from late 10- early 11th century
Turquoise glass bowl mounted in gilded silver
Reliquary of the column of the Flagellation
Ceremonial bowl covered in gold and precious stones
Alabaster throne-reliquary of St. Mark

entries.name: Pilastri Acritani ('Pillars of Acre')
entries: Located at the southern side of the basilica, near the Porta della Carta leading into the Doge's Palace, are two elegant marble pillars decorated in floral patterns. Dubbed the 'Pillars of Acre,' it is believed by many that these pillars stand as a monument to Venice's victory over Genoa at Acre in 1258. However, they were actually pilfered from Constantinople during the 4th Crusade in 1204. These were part of the Church of St. Polyeuctus, the grandest church in Byzantium before Hagia Sophia, commissioned by princess Anicia Juliana to celebrate her lineage and cast aspersions on the pedigree of Emperor Justin I.

On rainy evenings, or on nights of a new moon, a successful {@dc 14} Wisdom ({@skill Perception}) check or 14 passive Perception can reveal the faint sound of singing, emanating from the pillars. For one that has noticed it and concentrates on it, the song grows louder; for those who didn't notice, it remains imperceptible. The song is oddly both a paean and a lament, a song of triumph sung in a mournful tone:

What choir is sufficient to sing the work of Juliana, who, after Constantine — embellisher of his Rome, after the holy golden light of Theodosius, and after the royal descent of so many forebears, accomplished in few years a work worthy of her family, and more than worthy? She alone has conquered time and surpassed the wisdom of renowned Solomon, raising a temple to receive God, the richly wrought and graceful splendour of which the ages cannot celebrate. How it rises from deep-rooted foundations, springing up from below and pursuing the stars of heaven, and how too it is extended from east to west, glittering beyond description with the brightness of the sun on both sides!

If an adventurer listens to the whole song, they gain Advantage on Wisdom and Charisma checks and saving throws and {Disadvantage on Strength and Dexterity checks and saving throws for the rest of the day.

entries.name: Piazza and Piazzetta San Marco

entries: The piazza and piazzetta form an L-shaped area of bustling juxtapositions. The piazzetta near the harbor is filled on most days with people selling herbs, and nearby, cheese vendors set up shop between the lagoon and the Zecca, the city's Mint. Under loggia on either side of the little square, patricians gossip and discuss upcoming elections. Pedestrians wander by, sure to avoid walking between the pillars of St. Theodore and St. Mark, where executions take place. From the side of the Campanile, the bell tower, hangs a metal cage (cheba), which holds a former priest condemned to end his life with only bread and water. Unfazed by the fading light of the prisoner, money-changers operate at the base of the Campanile, and even though it is mid-morning, there is already a vendor selling wine in the shadow of the tower. Along the southern edge of the piazza, vendors in dilapidated wooden huts sell vegetables along the south side of the piazza. Peasants meander around with long poles topped with hair, which they hope to sell to patrician women for use in their wigs. In front of the basilica, beggars loiter and hope for aid, and amidst all of this confusion, black-and red-robed patricians shuffle in and out of the Doge's Palace, in hushed conversations with each other.

Despite the grandeur of the surrounding buildings and the orderly image Venice would like to present to the world, the piazza is as much a chaotic, commercial space as it is a locus of political might. It is common to see patricians gathering to gossip, solicit votes, and discuss elections in the piazzetta before entering the Doge's Palace for council meetings. The loggia opposite the Doge's palace and the promenade alongside the palace are the favored spots to congregate, especially the latter, which is known as the piazza del broglio. Aside from the Great Council room itself, this area is the nexus of political exchanges and conversations in the city. Younger patricians in black Venetian togas bow—as low as they dare to go without debasing themselves—and touch the sleeves of an elder senator's purple robes.

Gasparo (CG, human male, {@creature vendor|EchoesOfRenaissance}) sells wine by the glass, called ombra (shadow) because he sells it under the shadow of the Campanile. Gasparo is in his sixties, has wild white hair, and his face is a tapestry of wrinkles. He always carries a smile which fluctuates between contentment and mischief. For 1 sl, he will not only share a glass of wine but a bit of gossip as well. The stories he chooses to share are almost always of the lighthearted kind—tales of romance and heartache, mostly. However, unlike other gossipmongers, his stories are unerringly accurate.

entries.name: Campanile (St. Mark's Bell Tower)
entries: The bell tower of St. Mark, standing at 323 feet tall, is the tallest edifice in the city. At the top is the Marangona, the massive bronze bell that signals the start and end of the working day for workers, named after the craftsmen (marangoni) at the Arsenale. It also rings out for special sessions of government councils, and other bells signify the times of senate meetings, prayer and Mass. A smaller bell, maleficio, signals when an execution is to take place, though oftentimes the execution will occur early in the morning before the bell can announce it.
The Campanile is featured in Act III of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.

entries.name: Torre Dell'Orologio (The Clock Tower)
entries: Venice's gold-leafed, 15th-century timepiece tracks lunar phases. Wooden statues of the three kings and angels emerge from panels annually on Epiphany and the Feast of the Ascension. Steep, vertiginous stairs lead from the ground floor up into the clockworks.

The clock requires constant upkeep by a live-in clockwatcher named Giancarlo Ranieri (LG temperatore, master clockkeeper), a 50-year old human male. His family and his employees help keep the clock running—his wife Portia (LG human female, {@creature merchant of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}), his two sons, and his two gnome employees, Ghiro and Sebastiana (CG, male and female gnomes, respectively, {@creature artisan of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance|artisans of Venice}). To protect Ghiro and Sebastiana, Bastiano says that he has four children.

entries.name: Chiesa di Santo Stefano (Church of St. Stephen)
entries: This large brick church in the Gothic style dates from the 13th century. The entry portal is made of marble and was designed by the famous architect and protomaestri Bartolomeo Bon (d. 1464). The interior ceiling is wooden and resembles an overturned ship's keel (carena di nave); in fact, it was designed by shipwrights. Two stately arcades help support the ceiling, while the aisles are lined with evocative shrines. Adjoining the church is a large cloister monastery built by the Order of St. Augustine. They dedicated the monastery and church to St. Stephen, believed to be the first Christian martyr. Buried inside the monastery is Doge Andrea Contarini, famous for being doge during the War of Chioggia with Genoa. Also nearby is the church's bell tower, freestanding but leaning heavily. It is a popular pastime amongst locals who frequent the streets and campi near the tower to predict when it will fall.

Also adjoining the church is one of the largest campi in the city, campo San Stefano. Palazzi belonging to noble families like Morosini and Mocenigo overlook the campo on the western and eastern sides, while the churches of St. Stephen and St. Vitale watch over its northern and southern ends, respectively. The area of the campo is mostly grass and is used for bull hunts on occasion; when the latter occurs, grandstands are erected so people can watch from relative safety. When it is not being used for horrid sport, it is a place for markets.

A small canal, Rio del Santissimo, runs under the church, connecting the Grand Canal near its southern entrance to Campo Sant'Angelo. The passage under the church is only navigable with a boat during low tide. It is a perfect location for a late night meeting, or an ambush.

entries.caption: Passage Encounters
rows: A gondola carrying thieves ({@creature bandit} stat block) waiting to spring out and rob passersby on the adjoining canal (Rio de San Anzolo) or Campo Sant'Angelo.
A young and very hungry {@creature canali plaguebeast|EchoesOfRenaissance} has made the passage its new home.

Luca Tron, the signore della notte of San Marco, meets with an informant in the cramped passage, each on their own gondola. Tron has three armed guards with him ({@creature veteran of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance} stat block). If Tron notices the party has seen the meeting, he will try to apprehend them and question them about their reasons for being out at night, and whether they are thieves targeting noble homes (see the Chiesa di San Vidal below).

A young woman is hiding from her family, which is planning on sending her to a nunnery for her rumored indiscretions. However, the young woman claims that the stories are slander, and her family won't listen to reason.

entries.name: Chiesa di San Vidal (Abandoned Church of St. Vitale)

entries: The church lurches forward and to one side, a grand and beautiful ship slowly sinking below the surface. Its brick exterior cracks and crumbles, while its sculpted marble façade has grown grey and melancholy. Darkness seems to bubble in the sediment, but music and laughter can be heard from inside. Outside the sad structure is a lovely little campo with several trees and which opens up to the Grand Canal to the south. To the north is the larger campo San Stefano, a grassy field which occasionally hosts bull hunts.

The church of St. Vitale is originally from the 11th century, but a fire which swept through the city destroyed it in 1105 CE. The church has recently been reconstructed, but almost immediately it began leaking and sinking. The proto responsible for the construction blamed the poor foundations and his workers not being given enough time; nevertheless, he has been fined and jailed. The procurators responsible for finding funds to fix the church are at odds as to what they should do: tear it down and start again, or find a way to shore up the fundament? The main argument against tearing down the church is that the city would lose some valuable works of art, principally the altarpiece painting done by Vittore Carpaccio in 1514 entitled {@i St. Vitale on Horseback and Saints}.

The church has been closed to parishioners to limit any more damage to the building. However, a troupe of musicians led by a vivacious, sharp-eyed woman named Nicoletta (half-elf {@creature bandit captain}) is squatting in the church. They are called I Randagi di Nicoletta (Nicoletta's Strays), or I Randagi for short. They use the church for their rehearsals, and also as a base of operations for their nighttime thieving escapades. Since the church has been deconsecrated until it is ready to be used again, the Lord of the Night (human {@creature signore della notte|EchoesOfRenaissance}) for sestiere San Marco, a noble named Luca Tron, allows the I Randagi to continue using the church as their base of operations provided that they do not make too much noise at night and do not vandalize the interior. Luca is a handsome man in his mid 20s. He is a good decade younger than the other signori della notte, but his family helped grease the right wheels to get him into a reputable position. Despite his youth and inexperience, he is a ruthless investigator and sentry, perhaps overly eager to prove his worth beyond his family name. However, he turns a blind eye towards the I Randagi occupying St. Vitale because he is hopelessly smitten by Nicoletta. He does not know that Nicoletta's group are responsible for a spate of burglaries in noble homes in San Marco and beyond, but he is determined to catch the culprits after one of his family's homes was targeted.

entries.name: Faction: I Randagi
entries: I Randagi di Nicoletta, Nicoletta's Strays, are a group of street performers and thieves ({@creature street actor|EchoesOfRenaissance}, {@creature street dancer|EchoesOfRenaissance}, and {@creature street acrobat|EchoesOfRenaissance} stat blocks). They specialize in stealing from the palazzi of the rich and powerful. If the adventurers befriend the Strays, they will be given a free place to stay in the church—that is, until the rich and powerful in the city decide to rebuild the slowly sinking edifice.
{@b Port of Call:}

If the adventurers are on good terms with Nicoletta, she and her group can be used to create distractions in public places in San Marco. For a bit of coin, they may be willing to travel to other districts as well. Additionally, Nicoletta will let the party stay with her group if they need a place to sleep.

entries.name: Faction: Signori delle Notte
entries: The 'Lords of the Night' are special noble magistrates who are responsible for law enforcement in the city. There are six of them, one for each sestiere. Although their actions are not limited to the evening, they are mainly active at night, patrolling the city for any wrongdoing; anyone caught by the signori della notte are generally brought back to the prison cells on the ground floor of the Doge's Palace. Those caught doing more serious crimes were then interrogated in the chambers of torment in the palace attic.
The lords for the sestieri are as follows, but feel free to put your own NPC in place of one of these:

items: {@b San Marco — Luca Tron:} human male, mid 20s; his family got him the job, but he is dedicated to proving himself. He is also proving to be quite ruthless in his handling of cases.

{@b San Polo — Zuan Vellera:} human male, late 30s. Vellera got the position through connections at the Arsenale. His mother is a sailmaker there and is friends with the Admiral, and his father is a merchant in olive oil. Vellera has a murderous streak, using his position to settle scores and advance his influence. He has recently been killed, however, and in his place is a living mask.

{@b Santa Croce — Olivia Mocenigo:} undead female who appears to be in her 30s. She dresses as the other signori do, but she covers her face and hands, so her undead nature is hidden. She is hunting for someone who wronged her family, but otherwise she does her job well and doesn't make waves.

{@b Dorsoduro — Bortolo Fornera:} human male, early 40s, serious and taciturn, and a very perspicacious investigator. He feels like he has something to prove because most people in his position got there because of family connections and long terms in politics, whereas he earned his position based on his sharp investigative skills.

{@b Cannaregio — Baldissere Morosini:} human male in his early 50s. He is a veteran magistrate and Lord of the Night, unwilling to give the job up even when pressured to. He intimidates council members to not vote for his removal, and if need be will threaten them with violence. At the same time, he is a consummate professional, and Cannaregio's alleys and fondamente have never been safer.

{@b Castello — Hieronimo Venier:} a humorless man in his late 40s. He loathes his job because he finds it to be too taxing. He has a special distaste for non-Venetians, and he makes their lives miserable.

entries: Use the {@creature Signore della Notte|EchoesOfRenaissance} stat block for these officials.

entries.name: Palazzo Contarini Del Bovolo (The Palace and Stairs of the Snail)
entries: This palace, one of many owned by the Contarini family, gets its name from the elegant, exterior spiral staircase. Only the church and the state are allowed to build towers in Venice, but the Contarini family circumvented this restriction by building a staircase that rises above the neighboring buildings and shows off the family's power and wealth. The name "snail" (bovolo) arises from the resemblance of the building to a spiraling snail shell.

Zilia (LN, female human, 60s, patrizia, ducal house), the matriarch of the Contarini family, calls the shots from the palazzo these stairs adorn. Though it is a relatively small palazzo compared to the family's other residences, Zilia prefers its location in the center of sestiere San Marco, where her spies can more easily slip in and out of the arteries of the city. The Contarinis are a large and powerful family in the city, one of the 12 founding families. Zilia is perhaps the most influential of all of them, though she pulls strings from behind the scenes. She orchestrated family members becoming the patriarch of Venice the last two times, with the current patriarch, Antonio Contarini, being one of her sons. She and her scions guide politics and church decisions to places it would be most beneficial for her interests and those of families friendly to her. Zilia is very old and has begun to leave her plots to her first granddaughter, Agnesina (CN, female human, late 20s, occultista).
The Palazzo Contarini Del Bovolo makes an appearance in Act I and Act III of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.

entries.name: Chiesa di San Giuliano (Church of St. Julian)

entries: As you approach this church tucked away in a small square, you are greeted by a brand new marble façade. Above the doorway is a bronze statue of a bearded man in robes, holding a spindly plant and a tome. Oddly, just below the statue, standing near the entrance to the church, is the exact same man immortalized in the statue!

This church, known as San Zulian in the Venetian dialect, has been around since the ninth century. However, the façade has recently been redone by the stellar protomaestro Jacopo Sansovino and funded by physician, philologist, and astronomer Tomasso Rangone (CN, human male, early 50s, astronomer). Rangone used to teach at the university in Padua, one of the most prestigious institutions of scientific thought; however, he left to pursue his personal studies of the sarsaparilla vine (the plant he is holding in the statue above the church portal). Sarsaparilla is a plant brought back from the New World, and Rangone has spent the last few years selling miracle cures based around the vine and getting rich in the process. He sells syphilis cures, and secrets to living past 100, which he has had published in a pamphlet and sells to interested customers for 5 sl. The syphilis cures are 5 gd. Rangone has made a fortune on these supposed cures, especially amongst the soldiers and nobles most likely to encounter syphilis or have deep enough pockets to seek to prolong their lives. Rangone decided to fund the renovation of a church after he had an almost disastrous journey between Padua and Venice. The party he was traveling with was attacked by bandits, only to be saved by a hunter. The day of the attack was St. Julian's feast day, so Rangone swore to donate money to the saint's building in Venice. However, he couldn't help but commission something to glorify himself at the same time. Now, he is so infatuated with how Sansovino's brilliant work came out that he has transformed the church into his own quasi-shop.

The church itself is active, though it does not get a steady stream of parishioners due to locals tiring of Rangone's relentless salesmanship. The ones who do attend are the gullible and desperate. The local priest, a young and conflicted man named Guido (LG, human male, early 30s, {@creature clergyman|EchoesOfRenaissance|priest of Venice, clergyman}) bows to Rangone's will since the church's upkeep has been bankrolled by Rangone. Guido's sermons are often interrupted by Rangone's sales pitches at the entrance.

Rangone sells his cures, potions, and tinctures from the sacristy in the back of the church, something which Guido frowns upon but doesn't have the backbone to stop. Rangone's concoctions will lessen any symptoms of syphilis and, curiously, leprosy, but will not cure the diseases. Out of all his items, he has {@dice 2d4} {@item potion of healing||potions of healing}, though these are ones he made based on the recipes of others.

entries.name: Fondaco dei Tedeschi (Headquarters of German Merchants)
entries: This expansive building, completed in the thirteenth century but recently redone after the devastating 1505 fire, is the officially sanctioned headquarters of 'German' merchants (those hailing from the Holy Roman Empire). It is part warehouse, part palace, and part living quarters for these merchants, whose work is encouraged but heavily restricted: the merchants must do business with Venetians but not other foreigners in the city.

The ground floor has an entrance from the Grand Canal; the first floor is dedicated to offices, dining areas, and other more comfortable rooms, and the upper floors are dedicated to housing, having almost 160 living quarters. The façade facing the Grand Canal is decorated with vivid frescoes done by Giorgione and Titian when the two were younger, in the first decade of the 1500s.

entries.name: Faction: Germanic Merchants and Spies
entries: It is only required for merchants from the Holy Roman Empire to stay in the Fondaco: visiting dignitaries are provided with freer and more lavish accommodations. With that said, there are some amongst the visiting merchants who are not merchants at all: they are spies for the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V. Though his eyes are more narrowly fixed on France and the Ottoman Empire, he still wants to know as much as he can about the Republic of Venice, as they have clashed before over the territories in northern Italy.

If the adventurers have a background that makes it easier for them to connect with the merchants here, they can find places to stay and eat under the cover of being "emissaries of peace." If the adventurers cause trouble while staying in the fondaco, they are quickly thrown out, as the German merchants aren't willing to risk their lucrative position for a few newcomers.

There are a few spies posing as merchants, whose identities are hidden even from their merchant compatriots. If the adventurers are positioned to be helpful to the intelligence-gathering of Charles V, the spies might make themselves known: first through anonymous letters and messages, then through clandestine meetings. Charles V is interested in allying with Pope Leo X and Venice against a potential French attack, and he is also wary of the growing Protestant movement.

entries.name: Osteria di Leon Bianco (The White Lion Tavern)

entries: As soon as you open the door to this modest building cramped between ironsmiths specializing in arrows and crossbow bolts, you are hit by a wave of pleasant aromas and good cheer. A few travelers from Greece, Dalmatia, Albania, and further afield share laughs and stories over stews and fried langoustines. A broad shouldered woman with strong features and an infectious, toothy smile fills their wine glasses and welcomes you in from the cold.

Located to the west of Piazza San Marco on the busy and narrow streets of Frezzaria, The White Lion is the shining star of the many lodging houses offering rooms to travelers in this area. Engineer Massimo de'Massimi and his wife Bartolomea have been offering rooms to travelers for years as a way of making extra coin, but they eventually ran afoul of the government. They were given the chance to turn the place into an officially registered establishment and pay taxes or close down, so they chose the former option. However, the owners are still prone to allowing nonregistered travelers to stay with them.

Massimo is often busy working on construction projects in Terraferma, so his wife Bartolomea (NG human female, late 30s, {@creature merchant of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}) runs the place. The food is hearty, and there are always at least a couple other travelers from outside the city staying at the place, making it a warm and lively atmosphere. Bartolomea is a friendly but no-nonsense woman in her late 30s. She is welcoming to non-humans but asks that they be discreet, as she is, because she has had some run-ins with the government in the past. She will also not tolerate any troublemakers: fighting or carousing in her premises will earn you a swift strike to the head from her calloused palm.

If a lodger gets in good with her and shows interest in making extra coin, she will recommend that they talk to the fishermen at the Riva della Schiavoni, who have been whispering about some creatures haunting their fishing lanes near the mouth of the Adriatic.

entries.name: Mercerie and Calle dei Fabbri

entries: From the portal under the Clock Tower in St. Mark's Square, the street winds north to Rialto, bending and splitting off at each intersection with a church or minor square. You pass through rows of hat makers' shops, then mercers and jewelers, cabinet makers, apothecaries, and as you get closer to Rialto, shops specializing in gold and silver exchange, spices, carpets, and silks from points further east. There is never a dull moment on these jeweled alleys...

...The ships unload metal and coal along the banks of the Grand Canal just south of Rialto Bridge. From here, porters bring supplies down the streets of the "Calle dei Fabbri"—a thoroughfare of several streets that specialize in anchor parts, buckles, cutlery, swords, and all the other metalworks not done behind the walls of the Arsenale. These streets smell of coal and ring with the sound of hammers and anvils.

The Mercerie runs from Piazza San Marco north to the Rialto Bridge, and Calle dei Fabbri runs west to east from the Grand Canal (at the Riva del Carbon and Riva del Ferro, quays to offload coal and metals respectively) towards Piazza San Marco. These two thoroughfares provide the somewhat incongruous elements of Venice's power: luxurious trade and gritty, vigilant preparation for war. Dignitaries brought on tours of the city are shown the streets of the Mercerie, and occasionally the jaw-dropping Arsenale (depending on how luminous the visitor was), but the Calle dei Fabbri—just a stone's throw from the Mercerie—is not often showcased to outsiders, as it shows a less elegant, but necessary, glimpse behind the mask, at what it takes to run an empire.

entries.name: Factions: The Mercer's Guild and the Blacksmith's Guild
entries: Each of these guilds has their headquarters in the area of San Marco just north of the piazza. The Blacksmiths (fabbri) operate on the Calle dei Fabbri, and the Mercer's Guild headquarters is located on campo San Salvador near the Rialto (and next to the Mercerie).

Though the two guilds are rivals, trying to outshine each other in production and donations to charitable confraternities, they often overlap in their pursuits: it is not unusual for a merchant to work with metal to create armor or swords yet at the same time dabble in luxurious bird cages or gilded chests.

entries.name: La Testa d'Oro (The Golden Head Pharmacy)

entries: On the busy streets near the campo San Bartolomeo, where the shops of the Mercerie meet the Rialto Bridge, you see a curious sight: about 15 feet off the ground is a statue of a golden head! The shop it belongs to has graceful mullioned windows and a stately wooden door. Outside the door, a man with fine white clothes and a blue feathered cap is using a large pot and stick like a mortar and pestle to mix a pungent mixture of ingredients. To his right, another man, similarly dressed, stirs a boiling pot of treacle and prepares to pour some into a decorated jar of the finest lattimo glass.

This pharmacy is one of the several pharmacies in the area permitted by the government to make and sell something called a teriaca (theriaca andromachi in Greek). This is a complicated and expensive concoction known as a "divine potion" for being a potential cure-all. It is made publicly on the street outside pharmacies like the Golden Head and another rival pharmacy nearby, the Black Eagle, and it is made in a complicated process that is regulated (and taxed) by the state. Each dose costs 30 gd, far beyond the regular public's price range. However, a {@dc 14} Wisdom ({@skill Medicine}) check will reveal to adventurers that this medicine may relieve pain, as it contains opium poppy, and have other beneficial effects, but it is not a panacea. This does not necessarily mean that all who make and sell the teriaca are charlatans, but those attempting to sell cheaper versions of the potion most likely are.

The owner of the Golden Head is Agustin de Mosto (LG, human male, {@creature dottore|EchoesOfRenaissance}), a tall, slender man in his early sixties, with a reedy voice and thinning hair he keeps hidden under a patrician's cap. Agustin is calm and patient with his words, and he loves hosting physicians and other pharmacists in his shop for debates and discussions on methods. The Golden Head is one of only four pharmacies approved by the government to make and sell teriaca. Because it is genuine, it is expensive, and Agustin will warn any customers away from cheaper alternatives. However, he will push the customer to pay for the antidote if it is not required; he is a consummate professional and does not stoop to some of the manipulative sales tactics of the Black Eagle and other nearby pharmacies. With that said, he does not stop his assistants who make teriaca in front of the shop from loudly professing the wonders of their product and its uniqueness in the city.

entries.name: Introduction
entries: This is the smallest sestiere and one of the oldest, along with San Marco. Part of the neighborhood is the throbbing center of commerce and administrative activity in Venice, near the Rialto Bridge–the palazzo dei Camerlenghi (headquarters for the government fiscal officials as well as several financial magistrates), goldsmiths, wine warehouses, spice shops, and tiny taverns filled with delicacies. As one walks west towards Santa Croce, however, the din bleeds away, and one can find relative tranquility in the winding alleys and more intimate campi.

entries.name: Chiesa di San Giacomo di Rialto (Church of St. James of Rialto)

entries: This somewhat squat church building, with its bell gable instead of a campanile, is less awe-inspiring than some of the other religious edifices in Venice, but its age and position near the Rialto bridge gives it incredible prominence. The square in front of it is surrounded by loggie where patricians gossip in the morning before walking down to the Doge's Palace for council meetings. There is a large clock on the church's façade mocked by merchants for its inaccuracy. As you approach the church, you spy several inscriptions that remind merchants to be honest in their dealings:
{@i HOC ABOUT TEMPLUM SIT JUS MERCANTIBUS AEQUUM, PONDERA NEC VERGANT, NEC SIT CONVENTIO PRAVA.}
"Around this temple the law of the merchant must be fair, the burdens must be fair and the contracts stipulated must be fair."

A fire recently tore through the Rialto area, destroying nearly everything except this church, which was considered a miracle. The edifice is believed to be the oldest church in the city, having been consecrated on March 25th, 421 CE along with the mythical foundation of Venice—when two consuls from Padua laid the first stone in the "Rivo Alto" ('high channel', which became Rialto). In fact, the church most likely dates to the 12th century, but locals do not quibble about the age of the church; it stands as an important marker of the ideals of the city. The square in front of the church is a popular meeting place for merchants on their way to and from work, and for patricians gossiping before going to council meetings (they meet under the loggia around the perimeter of the square).

On the opposite side of the square stands a small pedestal and a statue of a naked hunched figure supporting a podium. This is where official proclamations are often made and where anonymous placards complaining about taxes or slandering certain politicians can be found. The statue is known as Il Gobbo di Rialto (the Hunchback of the Rialto), though the figure is merely stooped due to its burden not due to a physical condition. If an adventurer touches the statue with their bare hand, they can make a {@dc 12} Wisdom ({@skill Insight} or {@skill Perception}) check; on a success, they hear a whisper coming from the statue in Venetian: "tell me a secret. And don't kiss me please; it's embarrassing." If the one touching the statue does, especially one about nobles or church officials, the statue giggles and says, "that is a good one. I'll pass it along." The statue then relays a secret from its friend 'Pasquino' in Rome (see the table below, or make up your own rumor), as well as a rumor they have heard in St. Giacomo Square (GM discretion).

Talking to il Gobbo is an odd but useful way to drop hints about things happening in the city, so feel free to use his Venice secret to give clues to the adventurers—provided it is something he conceivably could have overheard in the square. Below there is a table of suggested rumors he could pass along.
{@i Note: he reports what he hears faithfully, but not everything he hears is true. He doesn't concern himself with the truth.}

entries.caption: Pasquino's Rumors
rows: Cardinal Olivero Carafa uses only the finest silks to clean himself. That's what 12,000 ducats a year will buy!
Pope Leo is selling your places in heaven. He's no lion; he's a snake.
"La Luparella" is not only the finest courtesan in Rome, but she is also a brilliant financial mind. She should open a banking business on top of her night job.

There is a sculpture of Moses in the Basilica of San Pietro in Vincoli. Michelangelo made the sculpture for Pope Julius II's tomb, which is still unfinished, but he gave Moses horns! This must mean that either the statue is a devil in disguise or Michelangelo is. Or maybe he was playing a joke on the pope.

entries.caption: Il Gobbo's Shared Secret
rows: Two of the priests in the San Marco district are selling the confessions of merchants to the highest bidder.
The nuns of Celestia and Zaccaria are not chaste.
A fleet of ships recently sunk near Zadar, and the Vendramin family will be bankrupt soon.
There have been strange disappearances on Burano, lace workers going missing, but nobody seems to care about it.

entries.name: What is going on?
entries: If the party asks Il Gobbo about his friend in Rome, he'll explain that there is a statue of "some dead Greek man holding another dead Greek man" but that the statue, like him, is animated to a certain extent. Pasquino only speaks Latin and Greek, so Il Gobbo delivers the message directly in one of those languages. Characters can make a {@dc 18} Intelligence ({@skill History}) check to determine what the statue in Rome is; if any character is from Rome, you can grant them Advantage. On a success, they recall that there is an eroded statue from the Hellenistic era. The statue doesn't remember who it used to be, but with a successful check, the character might remember hearing that theories are that it depicts Menelaus carrying the body of Patroclus off the battlefield, or Ajax carrying Achilles, or perhaps an earlier Greek hero such as Heracles. The statue, however, only knows itself to be Pasquino, which is a name derived from the Roman dialect term for a type of satirical poem.
Il Gobbo does not know why or how he is animated, only that he is cursed to hold up the podium that proclamations are read from. He also does not know why Pasquino is animated.

entries.name: Ponte di Rialto (Rialto Bridge)
entries: Oldest of the bridges across the Grand Canal, the Ponte di Rialto connects sestieri San Marco and San Polo. Rialto is a wooden drawbridge flanked by busy merchant stalls and a constant flow of boats flowing under it. It has recently been rebuilt after a devastating fire in the area in 1514, but there are already plans to replace it with a more impressive stone structure.

entries.name: Rialto Market

entries: Pescaria fishmongers call out their catches fresh from the lagoon this morning: tantalizing mantis shrimp (canoce), baby octopus (moscardini), and soft shell crabs (moeche). Turning a corner, you find the Erbaria, where vegetable sellers array their colorful produce in eye-catching tapestries: white asparagus, purple Trevisano radicchio, and baby artichokes (Sant'Erasmo castraure). Humbler items from the soil are also on offer and the object of more humble customers: these are onions, carrots, turnips, and pungent garlic. Another turn takes you past cheeses and then galleries of pheasant and chickens. Even further still are the slaughterhouses. Amongst the bounteous and expensive items being haggled over are other tables of items from closer to the soil: carrots, onions, turnips, and pungent garlic.

You take another turn back towards Rialto Bridge and see flower sellers and catch the scent of spice merchants out of sight down a street. You decide to duck down one of these vertiginous alleys and almost become lost before you stumble upon a small tavern, filled with gondoliers and fishermen. They look at you with suspicion, but the smells of the food are too intoxicating to avoid; you plunge into the cramped spot, with space only to stand and eat.. Though the proprietor gave you bristling looks when you entered, they become increasingly friendly once they watch you thoroughly enjoy the food.

The area of the Rialto market is boisterous and busy, with different sections specializing in different products, from fruit and vegetables, to meat and cheese, to streets further still specializing in exotic spices. Just south of the Rialto Bridge is the Riva del Vin, where most of the wine warehouses in the city are located.

The area is not only teeming with the vendors hawking their goods and the fisherman proudly displaying their catches, but also bankers, patricians, and merchants going to and from the fiscal offices in the area. There are also other types of businesses, such as apothecaries and taverns and drinking holes. Poor watersellers, street sweepers, pickpockets, and prostitutes round out the orderly chaos in the Rialto area.

Among the many vendors making a living on these streets, perhaps the most famous is Pelegrina Balbi (CG, female elf, {@creature vendor|EchoesOfRenaissance}). Pelegrina is the master salesperson of the Campo Erberia, the vegetable market, flitting from one area to the next helping the farmers sell their produce. She has long, curly red hair, freckles, and wears a farmer's hat to help hide her ears. No one remembers where she came from; she seems to always have been there to help the people earn a living. The truth of the matter is that she has only been there 100 years, but that seems like forever in most people's eyes. Whenever a magistrate gets too suspicious about the woman who has been selling vegetables and not aging for decades, the Erberia vendors shelter her, or she goes into hiding with one of her gondolier friends.

She and the gondolier Yaqob (Giacobbe) are in love; both of them know it, but they have not acted on it. Yaqob (CG, male elf, gondolier) was originally from Ethiopia and came to Venice originally as a slave but has since earned his freedom. He is a trusted gondolier for the inscrutable information broker, Angós, the Disruptor of Waves.

entries.name: Faction: φόβος (Fóvos, Dread Gondoliers)
entries: The Dread Gondoliers operate in all six sestieri as well as the outer islands. More than mere gondoliers, who are already skilled in keeping their ears open to the world around them, the Dread Gondoliers are the chosen assistants of Angós, the creature who holds the secrets of the canals and hears the wishes of those who pray for help from the water.
Angós and the Dread Gondoliers are featured in Act I and Act III of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.

entries.name: Palazzo dei Camerlenghi (The Palace of Coin)
entries: This palace is situated right next to the Rialto Bridge, on the San Polo side. Located inside its imposing four floors are the city's treasurers as well as other financial magistrates and trader consuls. Due to the important financial position of the offices here, there is also a secure vault and a prison for those who cannot pay their debts.

entries.name: Scuola Grande di San Rocco (Confraternity of St. Roch)
entries: The members of the "Confraternity of St. Roch" are a group of wealthy Venetian citizens who chose to dedicate their organization, established in 1478, to a saint known for protecting against the plague. The building sits next to the church which holds the saint's remains, and it was recently completed, in 1517. Similar to other Scuole in Venice, the San Rocco building consists of a main ground floor hall, and then another large hall on the first floor (piano nobile) above. These two halls are connected by a grand staircase, which has replaced the earlier side staircases.

entries.name: Faction: The Hounds of St. Roch
entries: This is a smaller group within the members of the confraternity. They believe one must go beyond charity projects to combat the plague and its evils. Thus, they have dedicated themselves to remaining vigilant against future epidemics. They are willing to pay handsomely for any rumor of plague and anyone willing to investigate (and risk themselves) on the Chapter's behalf. The Chapter works closely with some in the government (and some chapter members indeed sit on the various councils), but they are willing to keep the government out of it if it means an expedient control of the outbreak and credit going to their Scuola. At times, the Hounds will personally track down rumors of plague, or visit the lazzaretti. They are called the Hounds due to the fact that images of St. Roch usually include a dog with a loaf of bread in its mouth. The dog, legend has it, brought the bread to the saint and licked his wounds. Thus, the members of this secret society see themselves as the faithful servants of the saint and his mission.

The leader of the Hounds is a grim man named Ambrogio Bragadin (LN, human male, late 60s, patrizio, old house), who has seen much death in his family and is dedicated to stopping the plague by any means necessary.

entries.name: Basilica di Santa Maria Gloriosa dei Frari ("I Frari")

entries: Upon walking into the cavernous church, one's eyes are drawn down the long length of the church and through the portal in the choir screen, finally resting on a piece of inimitable majesty. There, above the altar is a painting seemingly radiating with its own inner light: this enchanting painting is entitled Assumption of the Virgin, or Assunta for short, and was done by Titian in 1518; it was his arrival on the grand stage of art, taking his unrivalled position as the most important artist in Venice and arguably in the same echelon as Raphael and Michelangelo. Depicted in the painting is the precise moment at which the Madonna, draped in sumptuous red and blue robes, floats towards the heavens on a blanket of clouds. Below her are gathered saints and onlookers staring in wonder; flanking her are hosts of angels, and above the Lord awaits.

Commonly known as I Frari, this 14th-century Gothic basilica is made of brick and is the largest church in the city. Compared to the many limestone and marble façades in the city which appear to float on the water, this hulking and imposing structure seems to be a stalwart reminder to the Venetians to keep their feet on the ground. It is a humble, unadorned work of Franciscan tradition, but inside it houses wonders: Titian's altarpiece Assunta is by far the most stunning, but along the aisles are beautifully decorated chapels and tombs of former doges.

entries.name: Scuola Grande di San Giovanni Evangelista (Confraternity of St. John the Evangelist)
entries: This confraternity was founded in 1261 CE by an order of flagellants; however, the practice of flagellation was soon outlawed. The organization was gifted a piece of the True Cross in 1369 CE by Philippe de Mezières, chancellor of the Kingdom of Jerusalem and the Kingdom of Cyprus. The head of the scuola at the time was Andrea Vendramin, patriarch of one of the wealthiest families in Venice. Legends states that the relic was dropped into a canal during a religious procession, but it did not sink; instead, it floated above the water, thwarting attempts to rescue it until Andrea dove in and retrieved it. This event has been immortalized in famous paintings by Carpaccio and Bellini. Now, the confraternity serves as the social meeting house of the Council of Ten.

The exterior of the building boasts a unique open courtyard with a marble screen designed by one of the great architects of the age, Pietro Lombardo (d. 1515). There are {@dice 1d4} condottieri at the portal entrance at all times.
The Scuola Grande di San Giovanni Evangelista may appear in Act III of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.

entries.name: Campo San Polo (San Polo Square)
entries: Venice only has one piazza, the Piazza San Marco, but it has numerous campi, where, in addition to public gatherings taking place, animals would graze and crops would be grown. As the population of Venice steadily increased, many of these campi were paved, but the name campo (which translates to 'field') remained. The largest of these paved campi is the one in the heart of San Polo. Encircled by the Chiesa di San Polo and the palazzi of several of Venice's most venerable families, Campo San Polo is an important locale in the urban social fabric of the city. In its center is one of the few wells in the city, and it is the location of many events, from masked balls during Carnevale, to bull fights, and mass sermons.
The Campo San Polo is featured in Act II and III in {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.

entries.name: Locanda Sturion (The Sturgeon Inn)
entries: Located just south of the Rialto Bridge and flanked by wine warehouses along the Riva del Vin, the Sturgeon is one of the oldest inns in the city and is a popular place among merchants and sailors disembarking at Rialto. It is run by the blithesome couple, Zaneto Karelo and Paulo Paxe (CG human males, early 30s, {@creature merchant of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance|Merchants of Venice}). Zaneto originally hails from a farming family in Friuli, while Paulo comes from a long line of fishermen in Santa Croce. The two men pose as cousins to avoid persecution.

entries.name: Il Diletto ('The Delight' Tavern)
entries: This little osteria is a hole in the wall gem in the dizzying backalleys of the Rialto area. It specializes in small bite-sized food on bread, and it aims to keep its costs affordable. They serve salted cod (baccala), mantis shrimp (canoce), and other seafood delicacies, which are typically eaten with an ombra of white wine. It is run by the genial Ambroso (CG human male, late 20s, {@creature merchant of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}) and his mother Faustina (CG, human woman, late 40s, {@creature merchant of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}). They cater mostly to merchants who come here to haggle while eating standing up and drinking wine, as there is no room for seating. Late at night, the osteria becomes a meeting place for Fóvos, the Dread Gondoliers.

entries.name: Riva del Vin (The Promenade of Wine)
entries: This waterway is where much of the wine comes into the city, along with the Riva degli Schiavoni. Warehouses line this promenade, and the Wine Customs Office sits in one of the stately buildings.

entries.name: Aldine Press

entries: Above the shop entrance the famous dolphin and anchor symbol greets you, along with the motto: "Festina lente," or make haste slowly. Though you might expect a bookseller's shop to be quiet, this place is no mere bookshop, which is evident as soon as you walk in. The front offices are lined with shelves of books, but the rhythmic shuttering and clanking of the printing press machines in the back workshop are an everpresent soundtrack, as is the smell of ink and paper, a ubiquitous bouquet for the nose.

Nestled in the busy center of San Polo just off Campo Sant'Agostin on Calle de la Chiesa is the famous printing house of Aldus Manutius. Though the press gained fame through its publishing of Greek texts, it also has become quite successful in publishing Latin and Italian texts as well, such as Virgil and Dante. Aldus also introduced italics into typography. Additionally, the Press produces portable books called enchiridion, an innovation in the field. The shop became so famous that visitors would stop in, interrupting and annoying Aldus. Eventually Aldus had a front library and shop constructed to separate the public from the work.

Aldus the Elder died in 1515, but the Press continues under the leadership of his widow Maria Manutius (LG, human female, {@creature artisan of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance} but with a 16 Intelligence score) and her father Andrea Torresano (LG, human male, {@creature artisan of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}), who had been a business partner of Aldus. The name of the business is now technically "In the House of Maria Manutius and Andrea Torresano", but they do not correct people who still call it the Aldine Press. The business still runs exactly how Aldus ran it, and it employs over 30 Greek workers. Aldus exclusively spoke Greek with his family and his workers, a tradition Maria continues, but she and Andrea are happy to speak Venetian, Tuscan, or Latin if those are preferred. Maria still keeps the sign that Aldus made at the entrance to the workshop: "Whoever you are, Aldus asks you again and again what it is you want from him. State your business briefly and then immediately go away." She will insist that her late husband was really soft-hearted if anyone makes a comment about his grouchiness.

A frequent visitor to the press is Marin Sanudo the Younger (LG, human male, early 50s, patrizio, old house, but he has the following changes: INT 16, CHA 8, and he does not add proficiency to sword attacks). More information about Marin Sanudo can be found in the description of Palazzo Sanudo in sestiere Santa Croce.

entries.name: Faction: The New Academy
entries: Since Aldus' death in 1515, this Hellenist society rarely meets, but Maria still keeps the secret meeting place clean and orderly should the need arise. Ostensibly it is a group of Graecophone and Graecophile scholars, but the initiates also share a secret purpose: combing Greek texts for secret arcane knowledge, believed to have been lost in the 4th Crusade (1204) and the Fall of Constantinople (1453). The secret chamber in the back of the shop isn't even known to the Greek workers, for fear that the wrong eyes and hands should find the tomes kept there.
Two bright members of the Academy who may make an appearance at the shop and thus want to meet with Maria about the Academy's goals are:

items: {@b Erasmus of Rotterdam} — the Dutch theologian previously visited the Aldine Press and worked with Aldus, and the two thought very highly of each other's work. Erasmus joined the Academy, but his work usually has him traveling elsewhere.

{@b Pietro Bembo} — the Venetian scholar and poet has worked as a Latin secretary for Pope Leo X and is a Knight Hospitaller. However, has recently been made the official historian of the Republic of Venice and the librarian of the Basilica of St. Mark. Aldus' publications of Pietro's works helped the poet rise to prominence, and the two kept up a strong working relationship and friendship after that. After Aldus' death, Bembo frequently stops in to see Maria and the family. When he stops in, if Maria has a particular book that she needs help deciphering, Pietro will most likely help with it in the secret room.

entries.name: Introduction
entries: Castello sprawls eastward from San Marco and Cannaregio, with much of its area taken up by the massive Arsenale shipyards and the dense housing for arsenalotti surrounding the Arsenale. However, the area is not just industry: it is also home to one of the most important promenades for merchant goods, the Riva degli Schiavoni, as well as important churches like San Pietro in Castello, the episcopal seat of the Patriarch of Venice.

entries.name: Arsenale (The Arsenal, Venice Shipyards)

entries: The marangona bell chimes at the break of day, signalling the churning engine of Venetian industry to once again awaken. You watch as scores of arsenalotti, experts in various aspects of ship-building, file into the massive complex through the Magna Porta. Any latecomers are docked pay, and visitors are expressly forbidden unless authorized by the government. This walled behemoth is like a small city unto itself, and what goes on behind those imposing walls determines the fate of not only Venice but also the Mediterranean.

The Arsenale is the official shipyard of the Venetian government, and as such is the churning brain of Venice's maritime might. The name Arsenale is derived from the Arabic dar al-sina, meaning "house of art" or "house of manufacture." and it was founded in the beginning of the 12th century. The complex is vast and has grown with the needs and ambitions of the city. Thousands of workers occupy the various workshops and warehouses of the different areas, and the whole place runs with a staggering speed and efficiency due to its hierarchical and specialized division of labor. Each of the jobs of ship building have been compartmentalized: different areas of the shipyards focus on different aspects of the process—hull-making, caulking, masts, weapons and rigging, and finally sails—and the ship being constructed moves along from one area to another until a finished galleon leaves through the southern sea gate. Though the arsenalotti make less money than some of the private ship builders, they do earn steady salaries and have lifetime benefits. This helps keep them faithful to the Republic, and throughout Venetian history, arsenalotti repeatedly proved both their loyalty and their brawn during periods of war and rebellion. They serve as additional guards for the Doge's Palace and the treasury, as well as serving in the military when war arises, and even as firefighters. They also have been the hands behind the vast carena di nave (ship's keel) ceilings in many of Venice's churches.

Job requirements for arsenalotti include manual dexterity, strength, and silence. Even in raucous Castello taverns, arsenalotti remain carefully vague about the specifics of their workday; shipbuilding processes are top secret, and industrial espionage is considered an act of high treason, punishable by exile or death. For centuries the crenellated walls of the Arsenale have hidden the feverish activity inside from view. Even outside the walls, the arsenalotti tend to stick to their own kind. They intermarry and even have their own market gardens to reduce contact with the rest of the city. Many artisans and workers in the rest of the city resent or despise the arsenalotti due to the favoritism the government shows towards them.

entries.name: Faction: The Fires of Industry
entries: The Fires of Industry is an informal gathering of arsenal workers from different areas of the complex. They meet in taverns or other quiet places outside of working hours. Originally these meetings were intended to build camaraderie and a sense of unity between the different areas of the Arsenale, so that the workers not only had loyalty to Venice but also loyalty to each other (beyond their specific job). However, out of these meetings it became clear that there were many common complaints about working hours, salaries, and benefits for families. Thus, the Fires of Industry has become a union working towards better conditions for arsenalotti, though most of the time they spend their meeting times drinking and commiserating.

The current de facto leader of the Fires is Orsa Zanetti (human arsenalotto), one of the chief sailmakers. Normally the female sailmakers are kept cloistered away from the rest of the Arsenale, but she balks at such orders. Her forceful personality and powerful physique make her a natural leader. She is cantankerous and looking for massive reforms to the way the Arsenale treats its workers.
The Arsenale is featured in Act II of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.

entries.name: San Zanipolo (The Church of Tombs)

entries: Entering this massive brick church feels like entering an endless cavern. Then the light peeks in through the windows and reveals the majesty of the interior. The columns supporting the tall vaulted ceiling are reinforced with dozens of cross beams. The aisles are decorated with the tombs of former doges in various forms of grandeur and excess in their monumentality. Ahead of you, the red and white tiled floor beckons you in further. In this church you feel incredibly small—as you were meant to.

San Zanipolo is the shortened Venetian name for Basilica dei Santi Giovanni e Paolo. A common misconception is that the church is named after the apostles John and Paul; however, it is actually named after two minor martyrs from the fourth century. The church is an important edifice in Venice, as it has become the principal location for ducal funerals and burials.

It is an immense brick church of the Dominican order, similar in style and size to I Frari in sestiere San Polo. Its vast interior includes five apses and three naves, and the ceiling is held up with massive columns and connecting cross beams—which helps disperse the weight of the building. It is said that the church is so large that it could hold all of the population of sestiere Castello when it was completed in the fifteenth century.

entries.name: Campo Santi Giovanni e Paolo (Saint John and Paul Square)
entries: Outside the church San Zanipolo is one of the largest squares in the city. There is a wellhead and a grand equestrian statue of Bartolomeo Colleoni. Colleoni was Venice's greatest condottiero, and when he died he left a great deal of his wealth to the city and asked for a statue in Piazza San Marco. The government accepted the donation but did not fulfill the veteran's wish, as statues are not permitted in the most important square of Venice. Thus, the statue, once it was completed, was placed here. Though it isn't San Marco, it is still a venerated site, next to the church that is home to doge's tombs.
The campo is also home to Scuola Grande di San Marco, which stands next to Zanipolo. This is one of the six grand confraternities of Venice.

At night, adventurers might run into the {@creature ghost} of Marino Faliero, the 55th Doge of Venice. He was beheaded for attempting a coup d'etat, and his name was stricken from the records. Not allowed to enter the church, the resting place of other doges, the headless ghost lingers outside. It will not attack.

entries.name: Chiesa di San Zaccaria (Church of St. Zachariah)

entries: A graceful and stately Istrian stone façade greets you, and a relatively modest wooden door provides entry into this well-appointed church replete with artistic masterpieces. The piece-de-resistance is Giovanni Bellini's Madonna Enthroned with Child and Saints to the left as you enter, a work of gentleness and attention to detail that shows the aging Bellini's having learned from his proteges Giorgione and Titian. Further inside, the Cappella d'Oro (Golden Chapel) showcases frescoes from the century before, and even deeper in the building the floors around the altar are mesmerizing mosaics dating from the ninth and twelfth centuries. You are struck by the wonder of this place, and as you take it all in, you notice you are being watched: the priest, with hawkish eyes, and two nuns, with more curious glances.

Compared to other churches in the city, San Zaccaria is a treasure trove of works of art, and its façade always looks new. This is because the church and adjoining convent receive very generous donations for the convent's taking in "troublesome" and "wayward" daughters. Thus, the convent of San Zaccaria is occupied by a host of nuns, a good portion of whom would rather not be there, and when chance permits, they will continue to find ways to enjoy the delights of the city, regardless of their vows. This is a point of consternation and embarrassment for the priest in charge of the church, Enrico Balestra (LN human male, {@creature clergyman|EchoesOfRenaissance|priest of Venice, clergyman}) and the abbess in charge of the convent, Pulissena Loredan (LN human female, {@creature clergyman|EchoesOfRenaissance|priest of Venice, clergyman}), who is a relative of the current doge Leonardo Loredan. The campo in front of the church and monastery even has a gate to limit visitors, lest the nuns get any ideas.

{@b Secret:} There is a perpetually flooded crypt under the church which holds the tombs of former doges before San Giovanni e Paolo took the mantle of final ducal resting place. The door to this area has been sealed off, but there is a small window in the altar floor that looks down at the crypt. Noises can sometimes be heard coming from below.

entries.name: Chiesa di San Francesco Della Vigna (Church and Monastery of St. Francis in the Vineyard)
entries: This serene area in northern Castello used to be a vineyard (hence the name) and is also where, legend has it, St. Mark washed ashore and was told by an angel that this (the Venetian Lagoon) would be his resting place. The church is modest and austere, in keeping with Franciscan tradition, but has several enchanting works of art that liven up the relatively bare walls. For instance, in one of the chapels is a beautiful rendering of Madonna and various saints by Giovanni Bellini, and in the San Girolamo chapel, marble reliefs by Pietro and Tullio Lombardo depicting the lives of Christ and various saints seem eerily lifelike.

Cristofolo Miro Collari (LE, elf male, {@creature mage}) is a corrupt abbot who has also asserted his influence over the church. He has the power to use the paintings and sculptures in the church to affect reality. He demands much of the local people, his monks, and his congregation, but he regularly does "miracles" of minor magic to keep his influence up. Every June, he holds a festival in the campo, when wine and rustic fare are served up in the church's stately shadow, but sometimes he calls for festivals at other times of the year if he finds he needs to exert his influence and show his magnanimity. He uses these periods of public generosity to pick and choose "helpers" whom he manipulates into favors.

entries.name: Osteria Seppe (Cuttlefish Tavern)

entries: Cuttlefish from the lagoon and cooked in its ink, scampi in vinegar marinade, homemade bigoli pasta, homemade bread, and everflowing wine and ales—this humble but beautiful establishment of wooden beams and fish carvings has some of the best, if not the best, food in the city, and is welcoming to all who have the coin to pay.

Osteria Seppe is run by the genial giant Giorgos Gemistos Apakas (LG human male, mid 30s, {@creature veteran of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}), a large and hirsute man. Giorgos Gemistos was born on Venetian-controlled Crete (the Kingdom of Candia) and came to Venice for opportunities as a younger man, and he worked on ships and in the military for some time before settling down and pursuing the dream of opening a tavern. He found Chiara (below) somewhat fortuitously while visiting family back in Heraklion. She was working as a cook and painter for a local magistrate who was treating her poorly, and word got out in town about her tiefling heritage. Giorgos, having eaten her food while dining with the magistrate, was stuck with guilt and a desire to help this young woman, so he helped her escape and brought her back to Venice. He protects her and all of his employees from any guests who get too rowdy or curious about the chef, as he doesn't want her to be persecuted for her looks.

Chiara Roccio (CG, tiefling female, early 20s, {@creature disciple|EchoesOfRenaissance|malandante disciple}) is famous in this neighborhood, both for her ingenious concoctions in the kitchen, and also for her reclusive nature. She never shows herself to her customers, so rumors abound about the woman behind the culinary mask. The truth is Chiara is not only incredibly shy but is also a tiefling, worried about how people would treat her if they found out. Giorgos Gemistos assures her that she can leave the backrooms disguised, and her food is so delectable that no one would turn her in to the inquisitors, but she knows that she must keep a low profile, for there are things worse than inquisitors who would be interested in her identity. She was born into a malandante witch order, but, not wanting to live that life, she escaped. She stowed away on a boat and ended up in Crete, where she found mostly misfortune. After surviving by drawing sketches of people with coal, she was discovered by a magistrate who took her in as a servant and house artist. However, he was a severely unkind man.

Though she now feels safe with Giorgos Gemistos and his workers, she knows the malandante are powerful and capable of finding what they seek. Thus, she stays hidden, and pours her heart into her cooking. It delights her that she can bring good into the world with her food. When she isn't making magic in the kitchen, Chiara uses her innate magic to make wondrous creations on canvas.

entries.name: Scuola di San Giorgio degli Schiavoni (The Dalmatian Confraternity)

entries: Once you enter this confraternity, you are greeted by merchants who usher you upstairs to the Sala dell'Albergo, as if they are eager to show off their rooms. You soon discover why: you are met with an arresting series of paintings by Carpaccio depicting the patron saints of Dalmatia in vivid narrative detail: in one, the young St. Tryphon, accompanied by a basilisk he has tamed, exorcises an evil spirit from the daughter of Emperor Gordian; in another St. Jerome, unafraid and full of compassion, leads an injured lion into a monastery, as a group of monks flee in terror at the sight of the beast; in still another St. George charges across a desert of bodies and impales a dragon with his lance. Your host looks at you smiling; he never tires of the looks on visitors' faces as they enter.

In 1451, merchants, artisans, sailors, and fishermen from Dalmatia (labeled schiavoni, or Slavs) were given approval by the Council of Ten to form their own confraternity. They moved into this faded beauty of a building and began renovating its chambers and exterior. In the beginning of the 1500s, they hired the famed painter Vittore Carpaccio, who is also of Dalmatian descent, to create paintings honoring the patron saints of Dalmatia: George, Tryphon, Jerome, and recently added Matthew. The building includes meeting rooms for the confraternity as well as chapels and a sacristy. Guests are usually welcomed by Natalis (LN, human male, early 40s, {@creature merchant of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}), who will only allow them upstairs if they have an appointment, are members of the confraternity, or make a donation of 10 gd. When he is not acting as majordomo for the confraternity or pursuing his own business interests, Natalis is an accomplished poet and is not afraid to share his works with those willing to listen.

entries.name: Faction: Schiavoni
entries: The confraternity is open to any members with heritage in the Dalmatian lands and who wish to enrich Venetian culture while also honoring their homeland.

If one or more members of the party are members in good standing in the Scuola, the adventuring party can use the Scuola as a base of operations. There are modest rooms to sleep and keep equipment, and praying at the chapel will grant a point of Inspiration to any who have made concrete efforts to bolster Dalmatian interests and culture.

entries.name: Riva degli Schiavoni (The Dalmatian Promenade)
entries: Originally named for Slavic traders from Dalmatia who brought cargo to the city, this waterfront stretches from the Ponte della Paglia (the oldest stone bridge in Venice) near the Doge's Palace, to the Ponte della Ca' di Dio near the Arsenale. Along the length of the promenade are docks, market stalls of Greek and Slavic merchants, and several palazzi and minor bridges. Near this area are several unofficial lodging houses catering to travelers, mainly from the east.

{@b Lodgings:} There are many rooms for rent by locals off the official record, especially for travelers from Greek isles or the Ottoman Empire. One of these places is run by a Venetian woman named Paolina Briani (NG, human female, late 30s, {@creature commoner of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}), who makes her living renting rooms to Greek and Ottoman merchants who come to trade in the city but can't afford the tariffs and taxes of 'official' channels. Enemies of Paolina (gossips, inquisitors, etc.) claim that she is a courtesan and allows Muslim customers to corrupt Christians, such as the Armenians working with Paolina, into eating meat on days prohibited by Christians. Though Paolina is not stifled by society's restrictions on sexual conduct, she is not a professional courtesan; the vitriol directed at her is no more than hearsay. However, since she is working outside the law in many ways, she treads a dangerous path. She has run afoul of the state inquisitors and the signore della notte of sestiere Castello, Hieronimo Venier.

Venier (NE, human male, {@creature signore della notte|EchoesOfRenaissance}) is a dour man in his late 40s. He loathes his job because he finds it to be too taxing. He longs for a more prestigious position with less need for constant vigilance and walking. While he has the job, he makes his guards' lives harder by having them do most of his rounds—which they must admit is not too bad, as it means they do not have to be around Venier's sour mood. Venier also hates the non-Italian merchants and sailors of the Riva degli Schiavoni district, thinking that they are all criminals. He often will raid warehouses and homes on a whim and imprison people on trumped up charges, which are usually overturned due to lack of eyewitnesses and evidence. If you get on Venier's bad side, which is not hard to do in sestiere Castello, he will summon all his energy and power into making your life miserable.
The Oltremarino guards run a recruitment office on the Riva.

{@b Port of Call:} There are many buildings in the port district between the Arsenale and the Riva which could serve as places to rest and lay low, hiding amidst the hustle and bustle of the area. One in particular can be rented from a lowlife named Nicholas of Kerkyra (CN, dragonborn male, seafarer, {@creature commoner of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}); the more you pay him, the quieter he'll be if people come around asking for you.

entries.name: All'estero ("Abroad" — Winifred's Place)
entries: This humble establishment near the Arsenale offers small rooms and specializes in rustic fare mainly catering to sailors and arsenalotti, though its proximity to Riva degli Schiavoni means all manner of wanderers, merchants, spies, pilgrims, and thieves drop by often. Even the odd dignitary or noble will occasionally stop by the humble yet famous shop, though they usually stick out to the locals.

The name of the shop translates to "abroad" because Winifred, the proprietor, is a woman of constant wanderlust. Though she loves her work and her shop, a big part of her wants to travel the world and feels constrained by the responsibility of running her family place. She soothes that travel itch by running a curiosity shop out of the back of her tavern.

Winifred la Grassetta (NG, elf female, {@creature merchant of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}) is the widow of a well-loved tavernkeeper Dionosio, who died under mysterious circumstances (he went fishing with friends but didn't return). She is from Germanic lands, but after her husband's death she remained in Venice to run the tavern and inn. She is well-loved and supported by her in-laws, who are local fishermen. She is hearty, strong, and stunning—often the object of her customers' affections, but she remains politely distant. She often has a far-off look, wondering about what lies beyond the Mediterranean. "Poor travelers," she muses, with a sad hint of longing. "Always somewhere else."

Winifred has a variety of basic potions and common magic items in her curiosity shop. Though she doesn't have magical knowledge herself, she has a good eye for interesting things, and has a solid reputation for her bartering skills. She would be happy to give a magic item to the adventurers in exchange for another of similar value, though she also works in coin, too.

During the course of the sidequest {@i In the Murk and Mire}, the adventurers may find the remains of Winifred's late husband, Dionosio. If they return to Winifred with evidence of his demise, she will reward them for bringing her closure, with one uncommon magic item each (GM's discretion).

entries.name: Basilica di San Pietro di Castello (Basilica of St Peter of Castello)

entries: Isolated on its own isola, separated from the rest of Castello save for a wooden bridge, this basilica and the patriarch who presides there feel both physically and symbolically distant from the important currents of Venice. The 'state church' of St. Mark's Basilica overshadows this episcopal seat in every imaginable way, and though it is the local church for those in Castello living near to it, San Pietro feels like a family member shunned and forgotten in family portraits.

The basilica is stately and has been renovated multiple times over the years, and since the mid-1400s it has served as the official episcopal seat of Venice. However, no one, including the patriarch, would argue that this church was the most important in Venice. That superlative goes to St. Mark's. What is more, the patriarch is almost always a local choice: for instance, the current patriarch is Antonio Contarini (LN, human male, {@creature Sanctae Romane Ecclesiae|EchoesOfRenaissance}), from one of the most prominent families in the city. Contarini, to his credit, has seen that the basilica which should be Venice's closest connection to the Vatican has fallen into somewhat of a sorry state; therefore, he is funding renovations, rebuilding chapels, restoring floors and walls, and commissioning new furnishings and paintings.

items: Society of the Scepter and the Serpent

entries.name: Introduction
entries: Together with San Polo, Santa Croce was originally part of the Luprian swamp, where the salt pans were located. It was later reclaimed, and is now a tight warren of canals and streets and offers a calm alternative to some of the busier districts.

entries.name: Al Gallion (The Galleon)
entries: The proprietor of this osteria is a retired naval captain named Diego Fernández de Cáceres (dwarf Sopracomito, Galley Captain). Diego is originally from Spain and served in naval battles against the Barbary pirates. He then later sold his services to the Venetians and hunted Genoese pirates. After that he retired and accepted a generous stipend from the government in Venice. He settled down with an Italian woman, Paulina Capodevin from a respectable family of wine merchants. Diego runs the place with his son and daughter, Hector and Alessia.

Al Gallion offers two guest rooms, one with two beds and the other with four, though there is space for more to sleep on the floor. The walls are whitewashed, the linens are a clean and bright yellow, and the desks and beds are fine walnut. It is also far off the beaten track of places where most visitors stay, in places like San Polo or San Marco.

Diego is often sitting in the common room regaling travelers with his naval stories. His injured leg makes it difficult for him to move around. His wife died of illness five years earlier, and his children dutifully keep the place running, along with their spouses.

Al Gallion is a spacious house and is prime real estate. Envious tradesmen and rapacious merchants are waiting for Diego to die so that they can swoop in and offer a buyout to his children, who may be willing to move on once Diego passes.

entries.name: Palazzo dei Duchi di Ferrara (Palace of the Dukes of Ferrara)
entries: War must never get in the way of commerce; despite Ferrara siding against Venice in the War of the League of Cambrai, the Dukes of Ferrara have many close ties with La Serenissima. This stately building on the Grand Canal used to be a palazzo built in the thirteenth century by an exiled noble from Pesaro. The city later purchased the building in the late fourteenth century and granted it to the Duke of Ferrara. Since then it has served as the residence of the ambassadors from Ferrara, and whenever the Duke and Duchess of Ferrara visit they stay in this palace.

The façade facing the Grand Canal is a curious mix of Gothic styles with Byzantine, Roman, and Islamic touches. The row of keyhole arches and delicate pillars have their roots in Islamic designs, as do the pointed merlons on the roof of the building.

The Duke and Duchess of Ferrara, Alfonso I d'Este and Lucrezia Borgia, make an appearance in Act II of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}. The palazzo is featured in Act III of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.

entries.name: Chiesa di San Giacomo Dell'Orio (Church of St. James of the Gold)
entries: In this Romanesque church, one finds oneself enveloped in a cool air and gloomy calm. Founded in the ninth century, rebuilt in the thirteenth century, and added to in the subsequent years, the church houses several pillars pilfered from Constantinople during the Fourth Crusade, including a 6th-century verde antico column with an Ionic order. The carena di nave (ship's keel) ceiling adds a weight and gravitas to the interior, and the church includes a Madonna with Child and Saints from Lorenzo Lotto, one of the more itinerant, and thus more lesser known, masters of the Venetian Renaissance.
