One of the more intriguing art works in the church is Gaetano Zompini's {@i Miracle of the Virgin}, which depicts a man attacking the Virgin Mary's funeral procession, trying to knock over her coffin, only to have his hands fall off and stick to the coffin. The man lies stupefied on the ground.

The priest of the church, Aurelio Cassellera (LG human male, early 30s, {@creature acolyte|EchoesOfRenaissance|priest of Venice, acolyte}) is young and inexperienced, but he was given this position because the patriarch saw great potential in him. Aurelio comes from a family of cobblers, and as the second son, he joined the priesthood. In addition to parishioners not taking him seriously enough as a young priest, Aurelio also has to contend with a serious problem: the church is incredibly haunted. At night, strange voices can be heard echoing in the church, and Aurelio even claims some of the paintings seem to come alive. He hasn't been attacked, but he fears for his congregation. If the adventurers investigate at night, they hear the voices from the green verde antico column cry out in sobs and exclamations. The voices are in Greek; anyone who is in the church at the time and knows Greek can understand that the column's voices are begging someone (or some group of people) to not defile the church by letting their animals trample and defecate on the sacred ground. On a successful {@dc 13} Intelligence ({@skill History}) check, the adventurers can surmise that the voices in the column are referring to an event that happened during the Fourth Crusade, when Venetian-led crusaders sacked Constantinople and pillaged the city.

Not only is the column haunted, but the painting by Zompini of the Miracle of the Virgin is also cursed. When the adventurers enter the church and there is not a service, have them roll a {@dice d20}. On an odd result, the hands which should be stuck to the Virgin Mary's coffin in the painting are missing. If there are any devout Christians in the party, one of them will be attacked by a pair of invisible hands (use the {@creature living mask|EchoesOfRenaissance} stat block).

Lotto's painting Madonna with Child and Saints includes a depiction of St. Sebastian, riddled with arrows. At night, if there is not an evening mass, anyone who comes within 15 feet of the painting must make a {@dc 14} Dexterity saving throw. On a failure, the character takes {@damage 3d6} piercing damage as bloody arrows shoot out from the painting; on a success, the character takes half damage.

entries.name: College of Medical Physicists and Alvise's Elixirs
entries: Located in the Campo di San Giacomo Dell'Orio, this building serves as a modest school for those wanting to learn medicine, a meeting place and social club for doctors, and an elixir shop catering to adventurers and other interested clients. On the ground floor, there is a small office for registering prospective students; an anatomy theater with three rows of elliptical steps; and a shop run by one of the doctors, Alvise. Upstairs is a grand library and offices for doctors to meet in. Normally the dissection of corpses is held only in church buildings or church-approved buildings, but this college was able to be established with the help (and money) of an influential member of the Council of Ten.

Alvise Molin (LG, human male, early 60s, {@creature dottore|EchoesOfRenaissance}) runs Alvise's Elixirs, which specializes in cutting-edge remedies (and potions). Alvise is one of many physicians at the College who trained at the University of Padua and wanted to bring more illuminated study of the humanoid body to Venice. In particular, Alvise is fascinated by unlocking the potential of the body, and how different talents or strengths can be unlocked with the addition of potions. His shop is too niche and expensive for the average resident of Venice, mainly due to the cost of materials, but he tries to offer his creations for the most affordable price he can muster.

Alvise is always on the lookout for ingredients for his potions and elixirs. He can get exotic ingredients quite easily himself—this is Venice, after all. What he requires adventurers for are the rarest, and strangest, ingredients for his most potent creations. Any adventurer willing to venture out and look for the materials themselves would be rewarded handsomely.

entries.caption: Alvise's Ingredient Bounties
rows: 5 quills from a gold hystrix (old world porcupine; use {@creature barbed devil} stat block but without Hurl Flame, Devil's Sight, Infernal language, and unaligned instead of evil)
5 gd per quill
Ten scales from a {@creature giant shark}
25 gd per scale
The reflection of a {@creature medusa} captured on a mirror
300 gd
The ichor of a fiend, preferably at least a quarter bottle's worth
175 gd per quarter-bottle
The gall bladder of a draconid
150–350 gd (based on size/type)

entries.name: Faction: The Society of the Scepter and the Serpent
entries: The Society of the Scepter and the Serpent has a presence here in the College, and any initiates or members in the society have free room and board in the college's humble chambers.
See the Bestiary for more information. Also, the Society of the Scepter and the Serpent are featured in Act II of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.
Alvise's Elixirs may make an appearance in Act I or II of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.

entries.name: Il Pendolo Verdeggiante (The Verdant Pendulum Bookshop)
entries: This bookstore and curiosity shop occupies a cramped and narrow two story home near Campiello de le Strope off of Rio Marin. There is a small wooden sign outside that has the name of the shop written, as well as etchings of fantastical creatures: a human monopod, a manticore, a lionfish, and a wolf boy. Inside the ground floor rooms are cozy and filled with books, with little by way of organization. The upper floor is the owner's private rooms, many of which are also filled with books. The owner, Jorge Acevedo (CG human male, astronomer), is over 70 years old, as far as he remembers, and he moved to Venice long ago from a small hamlet in Spain near Burgos. It is a mystery why he left Spain, and he never speaks on it. He has lost a great deal of mobility in his old age but not enough that he cannot climb the stairs of his fading, run-down home and look out to the stars from his attic. He has an enchanted lens that allows him to see the stars as if they were nearby buildings, and he also has a host of other more mundane devices—quadrants, a triquetra, and armillary spheres. If asked about his enchanted lens and where he got it, he'll say "a friendly man made it for me in exchange for some books. Leonard Digges, Leonardo da Vinci...I can't remember precisely who." He speaks with a smile and a glint in his eye whenever he talks about people, books, or the stars, and his voice is smooth and comforting.
Jorge has books on all manner of subjects, but his favorites are ones concerning astronomy, legendary creatures, the occult, magic, and philosophy. Some of the books included are:

items: {@i Liber Chronicarum} (Nuremberg Chronicle) by Hartmann Schedel
{@i De vita libri tres} (Tree of Life) and {@i Theologia Platonica de immortalitate animae} (The Platonic Theology) by Marsilio Ficino
{@i De hominis dignitate Oratio} (Oration on the Dignity of Man) by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
{@i De Occulta Philosophia, Libri tres} (Three Books of Occult Philosophy) by Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa
{@i Naturalis Historia} (Natural History) by Pliny the Elder
{@i Nomoi} (Book of Laws) by Georgius Gemistus Plethon
{@i De Radiis Stellarum} (On the Stellar Rays) by Al-Kindi
{@i Ghāyat al-Hakīm} (The Aim of the Sage, also known as Picatrix in Latin)

entries: Jorge will sell any book (he has read them all, he claims) and also has a number of common or uncommon magic items for sale (GM discretion). If the adventurers ask Jorge what the name of his shop (the Verdant Pendulum) means, he will claim he doesn't remember. On a successful {@dc 18} Wisdom ({@skill Insight}) check, the adventurers can tell that he is not telling the truth, but that perhaps the truth is too painful to recall.

entries.name: Osteria Brancaleone (Lion & Branch Tavern)
entries: Located near one of many palazzi built by the wealthy and powerful Mocenigo family, this building of gray stone is warm and welcoming. The food and decor is cozy; the specialty dish is ravioli with radicchio and whitefish, as well as the everpresent fresh bread and wine. The Lion & Branch is owned and managed by Giorgio i Baffi, "George the Mustache" (CG, human male, early 30s, {@creature vendor|EchoesOfRenaissance}), recognizable for his immense mustache and prodigious waist.

The signora della notte of sestiere Santa Croce, Olivia Mocenigo (N undead female, {@creature signore della notte|EchoesOfRenaissance} but does not need to eat or sleep), is a frequent visitor to the Lion & Branch. She is undead, specifically a type of creature caught in a liminal space between life and death in which she must complete a task before moving on. She is searching for the person who killed not only her but also her sister and brother (the one who was supposed to take the signore della notte position). She hears her siblings' voices in her head at all times, and though she is able to quiet them at times, she must find the killer and get justice so that her soul and those of her siblings can move on in peace. Ostensibly, she is at the Lion & Branch to socialize, but she is also there because she knows there is a connection between the killer and this tavern.

Giorgio knows there is something not quite right about the Lord of the Night who is always there in the corner booth; first and foremost, she never eats or drinks anything. However, he is smart enough to know that crossing the Lords—not to mention one from the Mocenigo family, who own many of the buildings around his tavern—would not be wise.

entries.name: Chiesa di San Zan Degolà (Church of St. John Beheaded)

entries: Facing the busy campo on the exterior wall of this church is an Istrian relief of a head on a platter. You take note of the church's name, which saint it is dedicated to, and are prepared to write this relief off as a strange tribute. However, as you walk by, you notice a passerby smear mud on the relief of the head...why would someone vandalize a church so openly?

This diminutive church dates back to the early eleventh century and was built thanks to the Venier family, though some believe the church may even be as old as the eighth century CE. Renovations and additions were completed in the thirteenth century, spearheaded by the Pesaro family. The interior is in a Greek Byzantine style, with a carena di nave (ship's keel) ceiling and intriguing frescoes on the walls. Because of the damp and humid nature of a city built on water, frescoes do not usually stand the test of time; therefore, the inside of this church makes one feel like they have drifted back in time.

On the exterior wall facing the campo is a relief sculpture in Istrian stone depicting St. John's severed head on a platter. However, the image is considered a bad omen, and locals will often smear the face relief sculpture with mud, or worse. The adventurers can speak to locals about this bizarre tradition, or if a character comes from Venice and has spent time in Santa Croce, they could already know what is going on here. Superstitious locals equate the head of St. John decorating the church with the dead butcher Biagio (Biasio in Venetian), who in 1503 was discovered to be killing people, cooking them, and serving them in his stew. He was caught when a customer found a finger in his stew and alerted the authorities. Biagio eventually confessed to his murders, but it is unclear how many were killed, as most of the people he killed were street children. Biagio was executed, drawn and quartered, and his body parts were displayed in four parts of the city as an example to the public.

The church relief is not Biagio's head, nor is it the location of his butcher shop (though the site of the shop is close), but it is close enough in people's minds to remind them of how truly despicable people can be.

entries.name: Luganegher Biasio (Abandoned Butcher Shop)
entries: This building was, until recently, a butcher's shop run by a man named Biagio (or Biasio in Venetian). The shop was extremely popular with the locals, especially the sausages and sguaseto, a stew of marinated meat and sausages. Even Venetian nobles delighted in his food. However, it was discovered that Biagio was murdering and cooking people, especially children. When he was caught, he was publicly tortured, beheaded, and quartered, his body parts displayed in different parts of the city. His shop, and house above it, were razed to the ground in 1503. A new building was built on the site, but all who have taken it over have not succeeded in their efforts, as the place has been deemed cursed.

{@b Port of Call:} If the adventurers are willing to endure the creepy, haunted atmosphere of the empty building, this would be an ideal spot for a base of operations because everybody walks by without glancing at the accursed place.

entries.name: Palazzo Sanudo (The Library and Residence of Sanudo the Younger)

entries: You make your way through the vertiginous streets of Santa Croce and find yourself somewhat lost. When you finally find where you are supposed to be, you look up at the building. As far as palazzi go, this one is somewhat underwhelming, and it blends into all the buildings around it. However, there is a relief of a blue-banded shield on the outside of the building, as well as a relief plaque which lists all of Marin's publications thus far. Across a small canal from a large warehouse for millet, this palazzo is the home of Marin Sanudo.

Marino Sanudo the Younger (LG, human male, early 50s, patrizio, old house, with the following changes: 16 Intelligence, 8 Charisma, and he does not add proficiency to sword attacks) is a prodigious writer, collector of books, and a somewhat failed politician—at least in the eyes of his enemies. A member of the Grand Council, and at one point a senator, he is pushing to become the city's official historian, a position Pietro Bembo now holds.

At a young age Sanudo was orphaned, and his elder brother squandered the family fortune and ran off to Syria. Sanudo then lived with his uncle before beginning to make a name for himself. At fifteen, he wrote a book on ancient gods and goddesses, and throughout the course of his adult life he has been writing diaries chronicling the events of the city. He was elected to the Great Council (Maggiore Consiglio) at a younger age than had been previously allowed, and he never squanders a second in the Doge's Palace: he records every moment of every meeting he is in, as he sees it to be his divine mission to be the Republic's historian. He is well educated, a rapacious reader, and compassionate about the plight of the people of Venice (rich and poor), but he is arrogant, pedantic, and self-righteous. Therefore, the adventurers may find his personality too off-putting and may not want anything to do with him. However, if they do befriend him (or at least listen to him earnestly), they find that under all the bombast is a man who deeply cares for his city and his role in it, and he grows exceedingly kind and generous when he knows he is talking to scholarly folk (he will take a special liking to wizards or any character with interest in history and politics). Moreover, his private library is legendary: it has been said that dignitaries visiting Venice want to see three things: the Basilica treasury, the Arsenale, and the library of Sanudo. He is also a frequent visitor to, and customer of, the Aldine Press.

{@b Port of Call:} If the players befriend Manudo, he will offer to let them stay at his palazzo, as he is lonely and devoid of company outside professional conversations. In exchange for conversation and protection (as he thinks he will be targeted for his outspoken beliefs), he offers unlimited access to his library (it is vast, mainly history and politics related) and is a wealth of information on gossip, political goings-on, and the structure of Venetian society.

entries.name: The Floating Vendor Umberto
entries: Umberto (N, unknown heritage, {@creature merchant of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}) rows his large gondola along the canals of Santa Croce and San Polo, shouting the names of the goods he has. Shelves of fruit lined up behind him make the gondola appear larger than normal, and the white-haired hunchback vendor smaller. Usually selling fruits for people to snack on and occasionally bearing other intriguing items, Umberto is a known and loved figure among the folk. With his all day spent going back and forth inside the Grand Canal, Umberto witnesses and hears things that can later be used as a topic of gossip or perhaps information for the ones who can use it. Anything happened or is happening near the Grand Canal, Umberto knows about it.

Any fruit bought from Umberto bears the effects of the {@spell goodberry} spell, and whenever adventurers want to cross the Grand Canal or to one of the nearby islands, they can use Umberto's help to cross without needing a bridge, if Umberto is close by.

items: The Order of the Scepter and Serpent

entries.name: Introduction
entries: Cannaregio was settled more recently than the other sestieri, with much of its urban planning taking effect just a century before. Thus, much of the district is laid out in a more organized manner, with straighter canals and broader canal banks (fondamente). Between the main thoroughfares, there are some twisting and turning alleys, but nothing like the labyrinthine Rialto area. Grand palazzi like Ca' d'Oro line the Grand Canal as in other sestieri, but once one dives deeper into the neighborhood, one finds mainly workshops and unpretentious homes.

entries.name: Ca' d'Oro (The Palace of Gold)
entries: Ca' de Oro (Ca' is the Venetian truncation of casa, or house. Ca' is used for palaces that are not the Doge's Palace) glistens on the waters of the upper Grand Canal; from the water, its mullioned arches and loggie resemble a smaller Doge's Palace. This, a mixture of Gothic with Byzantine, Roman, and Islamic stylings, is the epitome of Venetian Gothic. The real name of the building is the Palazzo Santa Sofia, but the nickname "house of gold" is more well-known (not that the owners mind) due to the magnificent gold-leaf details and lacy arcaded Gothic façade. The palazzo was completed in 1430—built by Giovanni and Bartolomeo Bon—and belongs to the Contarini family, one of the twelve founding families of Venice and still one of the city's most influential. The family includes Antonio Contarini, Patriarch of Venice, and Bartolomeo Contarini, Venetian ambassador to Sultan Selim I. In addition to the opulent Ca' de Oro, the Contarini have several palazzos dotted around Venice, many of which are in San Marco.
Ca' d'Oro is featured in Act II of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.

entries.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria dei Miracoli (The Church of St. Mary of Miracles)
entries: An icon of the Madonna miraculously began weeping in its outdoor shrine in 1480; the throngs of people crowding in to see it soon became a problem. Thus, with public fundraising efforts and marble scavenged from San Marco slag-heaps, this magnificent church was built to be a home for the miraculous crying painting. Much of the marble used was originally looted from Egypt and Syria. The finely decorated wooden barrel vaulted ceiling leads to a stunning domed apse; all of this is supported by the walls and no buttressing or columns, which brings to mind the genius of the architects of Haghia Sophia in Constantinople, but on a much smaller scale. There are also no paintings on the walls; instead the perfect simplicity and grace of the interior brings serenity to visitors.

entries.name: Jewish Ghetto
entries: Since 1516, Jewish artisans and lenders have tended to Venice's commercial enterprises by day, while at night and on Christian holidays they are restricted to the gated island of the Ghetto. Jewish people have lived in Venice since at least the twelfth century, but just recently, in 1516, the government decreed that they be segregated and subject to a strict curfew. Venice, unlike many other European cities, does allow Jewish communities to hold certain important professions, including medicine, banking, fashion, and publishing; nevertheless, racism abounds, and the community is restricted.

After the Spanish Inquisition expelled the Jews or forced conversions, many Sephardic Jews fled and found their way to Venice. As new inhabitants arrived, the limited space of the ghetto meant building more floors on top of existing homes. Thus, in the ghetto many buildings are taller than the average 3 or 4 stories of the rest of Venice. Even more recently, the Ghetto has been extended into the neighboring site of an old copper foundry. This new area is mostly populated by Sephardic and Levantine Jews.

The various communities of the ghetto are German, Italian, Spanish, and Levantine, and all of them are gathering the funds and materials necessary to build proper, larger synagogues for their communities. Only the German Jewish community are allowed to lend money, so they are closer to funding their Scuola Grande Tedesca, which they hope will be completed soon.

While the Ghetto is an overt act of racism and segregation, it has also become an important font of Jewish culture and ideas. It is the principal site of Hebrew publishing in Europe, and Venetians of all faiths visit the area's literary salons and the Italian sermons of rabbi Leon da Modena (LG human male, 50 years old, {@creature rabbi of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}). Leon is an energetic man with a beard that makes him look much older than he is. In addition to being rabbi, he serves as cantor in his synagogue. He has a rich, mellifluous singing voice, and he takes great pains to teach not only Jews but also Christians, hoping for more interfaith understanding and acceptance in the future. He is critical of newer mystical movements in Judaism, and he speaks openly about his struggles with gambling. He is well-loved by most in the community and beyond, but his openness ruffles many feathers amongst the more conservative circles of the Ghetto.

In the corner of the campo is the shop of Leri Fano (NG, human male, 44 years old, {@creature vendor|EchoesOfRenaissance}), who supplies potions and some common or uncommon magic items (GM discretion). Before settling in the ghetto, Leri was a wide traveler and keen trader of magical items. He has a manual of golems, but it is not up for sale.

In another corner of the campo is Dianora's shop. Dianora (LG, human female, 31 years old; use the {@creature rabbi of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance} stat block), sometimes called Dinah bat Rivka, is in her early 30s and inherited the shop from her mother, the community's midwife. In the front, the shop resembles a typical apothecary and is frequented by all the great doctors of Venice, both Jewish and Christian. But to those who know what to ask for, she has a backroom that offers cures of a more spiritual kind: kame'ot (singular form: kame'a): written amulets. Such kame'ot can only be written by a master scribe on kosher parchment, steeped in Kabbalistic learning. The amulets for sale in Dianora's shop are all written by her husband, the great Talmud master Rabbi Isaac ben Modechai (known to later generations of Kabbalah students by the acronym RIM). Dianora's late father, the RIM's teacher Eleazer of Venice, wrote amulets only for the community in the Ghetto, but Dianora and her husband can be persuaded to sell remedies, both physical and spiritual, to all adventurers if they are honest, polite, and mean well—for a fair price, of course. Dianora, when asked about how her work aligns with her beliefs, will say, "Our sages taught in the Talmud that whatever is effective as a remedy is not witchcraft."

Some items in Dianora's shop are listed below, many of which can be tailor-made for the customer. However, Dianora will warn the customer that "the efficacy of my items depends on the righteousness of the user."

entries.name: Biri Grande (The House of Titian)
entries: Titian has just moved into this grand estate in the Biri Grande area of Cannaregio. The area is green and quiet, but it is also poor, unfashionable, and crime-ridden. These do not bother Titian in the slightest, as it enabled him to find a large property at a decent price; moreover, it has a view of the beloved mountains of his homeland to the north. In addition, it is close to the lagoon and to the timber yards at San Francesco della Vigna, where Titian's hometown community of Pieve di Cadore had rights to keep their timber. On a clear day, Titian can even look out across the lagoon past the island of Murano and see the mountains of his homeland some hundred kilometers to the north. Even though Titian still has the workshop on the Grand Canal provided to him by a government stipend, and he does the majority of his work there, he hopes to one day move all of his painting and business affairs to the house in Biri Grande, not to mention raising a family and entertaining his friends.

Titian is in his early 30s and has boundless energy. He is an artist in high demand — the highest demand, in fact: since the untimely death of his main rival Giorgione, in 1510 of the plague, he is the one whom the rich and powerful of Venice seek out for commissions, and he is also busy doing works for other powerful people in Italy. Currently, he is starting work on Bacchus and Ariadne, whose first sketches were done by Raphael, for the Duke of Ferrara. Titian finds that his dreams are filled with dark visions of a fire in the sky and a darkness beneath the depths, but he wakes with renewed energy and the verve of a man half his age. Titian is sociable and courteous, able to rub shoulders with kings and queens and also peasants and fishermen. He is quick with a joke and a kiss on a lady's hand, but he keeps his personal life to himself. He is fully dedicated to his art, and in the vibrancy of his colors is where he puts his real, raw emotions. His paintings show his anger and love, his reverence for the female form, and his considerations of the divine and how it works in daily life through decisive moments.
Titian's home is featured in Acts I and II of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}. Titian features prominently in the story of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.

entries.name: Chiesa di Santa Lucia (Church of St. Lucia)
entries: This humble church was initially dedicated to the Virgin Mary but was later dedicated to St. Lucia, whose remains had been taken from Constantinople during the Fourth Crusade. However, there is a dispute between this church and the Church of Corpus Domini, which is located just down the road. While this church was being refurbished and expanded, the saint's remains stayed at Corpus Domini for so long that the nuns there decided they should continue to be the saint's stewards. After St. Lucia took the remains back, a stealthy group of nuns broke in and stole the remains back to Corpus Domini. They hid the saint under stairs and refused to reveal where the body was, even when pressed by the Council of Ten. Finally, the Council of Ten threatened to wall up the doors of the church of Corpus Domini. When the construction workers arrived to complete this grim entombment, the nuns surrendered and revealed the saint, after which she returned to her eponymous church.

St. Lucia's remains are now protected behind glass imbued with the {@spell alarm} spell thanks to Sister Matthia de Gradi (LN, human female nun, around 35 years old, {@creature acolyte|EchoesOfRenaissance|priest of Venice, acolyte}), who has begun studying magic and procured some scrolls to help in the defense of the saint's body. St. Lucia's face is covered by a bronze mask. One arm is missing because it was held onto by church authorities in Constantinople. Those who are blind, struggling merchants, or writers in need of inspiration might find that St. Lucia has time to talk to them if they listen very carefully. If visitors enter the church at normal hours, they are watched like a hawk by Matthia, who has made it her personal mission to guard the saint from theft. She assumes any visitors have been sent by Corpus Domini.

entries.name: La Spezieria All'Ercole D'Oro (Pharmacy of the Golden Hercules)
entries: This spezieria (pharmacy) has walnut shelves lined with majolica jars of medicines, poultices, perfumes, and salves. The paneled walls are richly decorated with etchings of wise doctors and saints and gods of medicine, including Asclepius, beneath a gilded wood-beam ceiling. The Spezieria used to be frequented by learned patricians, clergy and scholars, being used as a meetingplace for conversation and intellectual discussion before ownership was passed to the daughters of the apothecary master Piero. The Testa d'Oro (Golden Head) apothecary near the Rialto Bridge has become the more popular hangout amongst medical circles.

It specializes in the preparation of unusual medicines and potions, and it has its own "sala dei veleni" or poisons room. Here, rare herbs, potions, spices and compounds, often from the East, are stored. Twin sisters Diana and Daniella Erizo (LG, female half-elves, 23 years old, Scepter & Serpent Macheon) run this shop after the death of their father Piero. Secretly, this is a headquarters of the Scepter and the Serpent, a society dedicated to Asclepius, enemy of the Cult of Bacchus. They are willing to make their sparse magical item and potion shop hidden behind wood paneling available to discerning, and noble, customers.

entries.name: Faction: The Order of the Scepter & Serpent
entries: Rumored to have been founded in the city of Pergamon in Anatolia, the Order is devoted to Asclepius, god of medicine. The symbol of their organization is the asklepian, a rod with a serpent entwined around it, and members of the order are committed to the curing of diseases, tending to the sick, and researching new methods of healing. It is part clerical and part scientific order, and many of the first pharmacies of Europe are secret meeting places of this beneficent order.

In the generations since its founding, the Order has developed a resentment and rivalry with the Cult of Bacchus, which it sees as a main vector for many of the maladies of the day due to its hedonistic behavior.
The Golden Hercules is featured in Act II in {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.

entries.name: Osteria Agricole (The Tilled Earth Tavern)
entries: "Where did you get this bottle? It's positively exquisite!" The well-dressed customer pours himself and his companions another round of the luscious red wine. The handsome woman with dark brown curls behind the counter sharpening a handaxe says, "Let's just say it was a donation!"

This tavern has an impressive array of local wine, and it has a loyal group of customers who treat the place like an informal confraternity. Specialities include red wine made from local Raboso grapes, heaped platters of cured pork fat, cheese drizzled with honey, and polpette (meatballs). Siblings Marco and Vittoria (dwarf {@creature vendor|EchoesOfRenaissance} and occultista respectively) run this cozy place off of Campo dei Mori. The painter Tintoretto, who lives nearby, is a regular customer. Their very impressive collection of wines comes from a long history of trading with smugglers and also getting thieves to steal bottles from noble houses in the city. Marco and Vittoria are members of the criminal guild Garganega.

entries.name: Faction: Garganega
entries: Founded in the late 1400s by Venetians down on their luck and Greek merchants fleeing Morea (taken by the Ottomans), the Garganega has grown to be a successful guild of thieves, robbers, and cutthroats. They specialize in small jobs—stealing from noble houses and reselling for a profit, robbing merchants traveling on the roads of Veneto, and even robbing small ships at times. They do just enough to be successful while also not drawing too much attention from the authorities. If anyone finds out about their operation, they are swiftly dispatched.

{@b Joining the Guild:} If adventurers learn about the guild and prove themselves to not be working for the government, they could have the chance to do some lucrative smuggling or thieving jobs. They will be given a difficult job that requires silence in order to test their mettle.

entries.name: Squero Zoldo (The Zoldo Boat Workshop)
entries: This gondolier workshop was established in the fourteenth century by immigrants from the Dolomites, who brought special wood-cutting techniques that shortened times of boatmaking jobs and innovated the industry. Now the shop specializes in magical hull enhancements and in the new asymmetrical style of gondola, which only requires one gondolier to pilot.

The shop is run by maestro Massimo (CG human male, {@creature artisan of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}), a half-elf, and his partner, and a squerarolo in his own right, Marcello (NG dragonborn male, {@creature artisan of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}). The duo pose as friends and business partners due to potential discrimination, and Marcello stays hidden or disguised in wrappings to hide his heritage. Practically each neighborhood in Venice has at least one squeri, and most of them maintain healthy, spirited competition. However, recently Massimo and Marcello have had troubles with certain rival shops, namely squero Vecio and the San Trovaso of Dorsoduro, who look down on the speedy production methods and new designs of squero Zoldo.

entries.name: Squero Vecio
entries: This workshop specializes in the other types of small boats that ply the canals of Venice — sandolo, batel buranela, topo, and caolirna. The Guild is the oldest in Cannaregio, and its shop is located on the northwestern most point, behind the Church of Corpus Domini. Its spacious dock overlooks the northern lagoon. Run by the stern and commanding Corona Tirabosco (NG, human female, {@creature artisan of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}), who runs her shop with a proverbial iron fist. She has long dark hair that she keeps in a braid, and she is often wearing comfortable workmen's clothes rather than a dress. Her workers respect and follow her every word, as her business acumen and knowledge of the craft are unparalleled. Corona took over the workshop and the guild with the death of her grandfather. She never had any interest in marrying, joining a convent, or playing the prescribed roles of women in Venetian society: her love is the water.

entries.name: Faction: The Vecio Boatmaking Guild
entries: The guild controls the majority of private boatmaking in sestieri Cannaregio, San Polo, and Castello, while San Trovaso controls Dorsoduro, Santa Croce, and San Marco. However, these guilds are friendly competitors and often work together as their business overlaps. The only time they are fiercely competitive is during the regattas. However, the Vecio puts more stock in the boat races other than the gondola, which they believe gets undeserved attention.
{@b Joining the Guild:} Unlike San Trovaso, the Vecio is not as welcome to newcomers unless they can demonstrate some modicum of talent in their meeting with Corona.

entries.name: Introduction
entries: Dorsoduro has the highest and sturdiest land among the Venetian islands. It is home to the Giudecca Canal, which flows through the district, offering an optimal spot for trading ships to moor and deliver their goods. There are numerous quays (zattere) lining the Giudecca canal where wood from Venice's forests would enter the city.

entries.name: Soccorso Smithy

entries: As you walk leisurely along the fondamente stretching away from the Grand Canal, you start hearing the rhythmic pounding of hammer on anvil—the tell-tale sounds of a blacksmith. Yet it is a curious sound in this neighborhood of stately shops, churches, and palazzi. When you get to the outside of the shop, just across from Soccorso Bridge, you realize that the smithy fits in quite well: its interior is glowing and sublime, more like a church where one would worship the art of craft.

Soccorso Smithy is named after Ponte del Soccorso, the bridge just outside the shop's doors. It is run by husband and wife team Lazaro and Fiordelise Agati (LG dwarves, both {@creature artisan of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance|artisans of Venice}). Lazaro and Fiordelise hail from Florence originally, but they came to Venice during the unrest of the late 1400s, after the Medicis were expelled from the city. The two of them worked for two decades in various workshops until they had enough money and clout to open their own place, which they did last year. Quickly they have garnered a reputation for excellent designs, putting the established cutlers and armorers of San Marco and the Arsenale to shame. Due to this, they are under almost constant legal pressure because of the connections the San Marco and Arsenale smiths have. So far, however, there has not been any actionable reason to close the shop, and the fact that it is doing well and brings in customers from outside of Venice as well only makes it more attractive to the city. There are some senators allied with San Marco guilds and the Arsenale still scheming to frame the Agatis for some crime. Luckily, the signore della notte of Dorsoduro, Bortolo Fornera, suspects an attack is imminent and has been keeping some of his guards watching over the smithy at night.

The Soccorso is immaculately clean and shimmers with the glow of divine light. The dwarven couple have been blessed to pursue crafting and be excellent at it, so they see it as a divine calling. Though they do not advertise it to everyone, the Agatis are skilled at making magical weapons and enchanted armor—provided the buyer helps collect necessary ingredients and has the coin and patience to spare.

entries.name: Da Vinci's Workshop

entries: The morning sun bleeds into the airy workshop, illuminating faint traces of dust and stray hairs, as if a fight just ended before you entered. The floor is covered with sand and sawdust, and in the center of the vast space is a wooden contraption with leathery appendages that twist and turn; shelves on the walls are lined with bottles and jars containing unknown ingredients, skulls and plaster models, and the odd bit of armor or weapon. As you make your way further into the workshop, the master is busy adjusting the straps on a suit of armor standing to one side of a vast desk covered in anatomical sketches and schematics for more war machines. "Hand me that crossbow on the shelf, would you? I need to test something..."

Leonardo da Vinci is visiting Venice after long periods in Florence, Milan, and Rome, mainly making plans for weaponry to fund his own research into the human body and its capabilities. Rumors have circulated that da Vinci had moved to France and passed away, but he is here in Venice to finalize some new inventions that he hopes to test out during the Carnival. In his old age, he has grown tired of painting for nobles and crafting weapons of war; drawing inspiration from Venice's topography, he is busy designing new types of ships and floating islands, while at the same time creating ingenious devices to be used in ceremonies and theatrical performances. He is also hoping to make use of Venetian innovations (including those of the University in Padua) in medicine and healing concoctions. There is so much more he wants to make, but he is running out of time.
Leonardo da Vinci is featured in Acts I, II, and III of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.

entries.name: Ca' Foscari (The Palace of the Foscari Family)

entries: A gondola slowly approaches the boat landing within the grand building as the old steward comes out and helps anchor it. The lady getting off the gondola quickly heads towards the door as if afraid of being seen. One of the most magnificent buildings in Venice, the Foscari Palace, welcomes foreign visitors, strangers to Venice, with only one condition: they must bring their secrets along.

Built for the longest-reigning Doge, Ca' Foscari is a four-story building located at the widest bend of the Grand Canal. Though Foscari has long passed, his descendants still reside in the building and annually host the Doge at the point of the Regatta's finish line. There is a gate facing the canal that opens inside the building, allowing gondolas to moor beneath, and a back courtyard where residents can relax while talking about politics with discretion. If there is a foreign dignitary of note in the city, this is the place they most likely would be accommodated if they do not have previous arrangements.

The steward responsible for treating the guests with the utmost hospitality, Girolamo Querini (LG human male, {@creature veteran of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}), is a calm and clever man. Every visitor arriving by gondola is first greeted with his warm welcome as they are towed into the dock underneath the building. Any inquiries regarding the Foscari Family or the stay inside the palace are usually directed to him first and addressed to the proper referent later on.

Federico Foscari (LE human male, 80s, patrizio, ducal house), the nephew of Francesco Foscari has the privilege of being the oldest Foscari family member alive. He lives on the upper floors of the palace with his wife, Giovanna Venier (LE human female, patrizio, ducal house). Dignified and elegant as they look, and not needing to pry into other people's business, they are usually in possession of a great deal of knowledge about their guests and the politics taking place around the city. What their loyal steward Girolamo learns and reports as he provides nobles with their special needs is the main source of Foscari's blackmail plots.
Ca' Foscari is featured in Act II of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.

entries.name: Squero di San Trovaso (The San Trovaso Boatmakers Workshop and Guild)

entries: Resembling a mountain home, a building unlike most in Venice stands alongside the San Trovaso canal. The famous gondola workshop is filled with all kinds of small boats that are either half-finished or upside down. Many people around them work their craft, hammering and chiseling to bring the vessels to life. Away from the ordered cacophony, a group of three sits in the shadow of the building, chattering about the day while sipping from their drinks. Their heads turn toward you and from their expressions, it's clear they are the ones to talk to.

Like the gondolas they make, built with the wood coming from the Mountains of Cadore, the San Trovaso Boatmaking Workshop serves the city of Venice with its beautiful gondolas sailing along the canals. Whether a noble's request for a custom gondola or an order of big quantity asked by a merchant, boatmakers get it done.

The craftsmanship and the order of boatmaking go a long way back in San Trovaso. The knowledge passed down through generations allows the boats made in this place to be more durable against the wear of time. Gondolas that are bought from here don't get affected by any foul weather conditions such as heavy rain or a storm inside Venice even if it's moored away from the characters, provided that conditions aren't exceptionally extreme or magical.

Owner of the San Trovaso boatmaking house and the guild, Tomasso Pisani (LG human male, 60 years old, {@creature artisan of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}), is a stubborn old man with incredible skill in boatmaking craft which he has proven over the years. Believing his days are coming to an end, he wants to leave the workshop in great condition with every part of the process running smoothly and extending his legacy as much as he can. Because of the fact that he doesn't like to change the way things run around in the workshop, he frequently conflicts with his son and business partner, Niccolo Pisani (LG human male, 35 years old, {@creature artisan of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}) in this matter, who wants to achieve more than his ancestors. Niccolo believes that the workshop could do much more than sturdy boats and aims to add some additional qualities to his deliveries using magic by engraving runes on the boats, without informing his father.

The workshop workers ({@creature artisan of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance} stat block) are torn between two sides; different workers might provide different services depending on who they are supporting. Adventurers can use the services shown in the lists by locating an artisan of Venice with the appropriate services in Dorsoduro and buy equipment from them using the general equipment list regardless of which side they take with the owners.

entries.name: Faction: San Trovaso Boatmaking Guild
entries: Dorsoduro's famous boatmaking guild always welcomes new apprentices and makes them feel at home. Being part of the guild grants access to use equipment from the general equipment list for free and allows members to receive services at half the price. Although the guild currently feels divided between its two leaders, rival boatmaking houses in the city inadvertently unite them by igniting their rage. Believing their craft is superior but affordable, the San Trovaso boatmaking guild doesn't get along with others who boast about their work but fail to provide quality boats, especially from inexperienced workshops that have only begun making boats recently.

entries.name: Campo San Barnaba (Square of Saint Barnabas)
entries: In the heart of Dorsoduro, a square shaded by the Church of Saint Barnabas paints a colorful picture. With many vendors selling fruits, vegetables, and other goods brought in from the gardens of the islands and the Terraferma, people of Dorsoduro pour into this marketplace to further decorate their tables. While a merchant dreams of this place, another one closes its stall and goes to gamble the money he earned.

Campo San Barnaba, named after the church it sits beside, is the largest square and marketplace in Dorsoduro. Mainly used for selling everyday items, this marketplace is open every day from morning until afternoon. In the evenings the square is usually frequented with people sitting on benches and chattering, or procuring drinks from the only vendor left in the campo, Lorenzo (CG human male, 30s, {@creature vendor|EchoesOfRenaissance}). Occasionally the Grimani family, the patrons of the church, host feasts at nights for the people around the parish to eat their fill. The most famous and grandest of the feasts throughout the year takes place on the 11th of June. Because of the Grimani family's interest in theater, most of the time these feasts have a stage to perform and sometimes it is left there for the daytime shows as well. Zonchio (LN human male, late 50s, {@creature veteran of Venice|EchoesOfRenaissance}), an old war veteran who fought in sea battles in the Venetian fleet, and currently serving as a guard for the Grimani family, is usually the person responsible for the safety of the campo. During feast days, with his order the stalls are dismantled and tables are placed. Any potentially dangerous individual that needs to be either dealt with or reported to the Grimanis are handled by him.

entries.name: Casin de Nobili (Casino of the Aristocracy)
entries: This unassuming building leaning to the left side of the Church of San Barnaba is actually a gambling house hidden in plain sight. Built for the richest of the city, protected by many guards, and perhaps the first of its kind in Europe, the casino mainly caters to patricians, though their friends and associates are sometimes allowed inside to play a few hands. Inside the house, guests are usually playing Liar's Dice, Craps, or Raffle using dice, and Trionfi using Tarocchi (Tarot) cards.

Playing Raffle with dice is common due to its convenience. Players of the game roll three six-sided dice each and take turns raising the bet. If all the dice of a player are the same roll, it is considered the highest result (three of a kind); if not, having rolled two dice that result the same and one different is (pair) second highest; and no dice being the same roll is the lowest result. If two or more of the players roll the same amount of matching dice, the one with the higher number wins.

Pietro (N, human male, late 20s, condottiero), the servant responsible for the casino is a quiet and humble man, knowing all the noble guests by name and addressing their requests rapidly while they game at their tables. Though he is not necessarily the first face to welcome the guests, whenever cheating is revealed or a discomfort is caused by a guest, he is the one to lead them to the door. Not occurring frequently, when the cheater is a person of high nobility, their way of cheating is seized rather than kicking them out.

The owner of the casino, Domenico Grimani (NE human male, {@creature clergyman|EchoesOfRenaissance|priest of Venice, clergyman}), is the priest of the San Barnaba parish. Domenico loves to spend his time in the casino gambling but as time passes by, his opponents grow thin, with each finding various excuses not to play against him. Knowing that Domenico usually wins by cheating with his sharpened dice and Pietro being a loyal servant not giving out his secrets or seizing his dice, other nobles start playing with different groups or leave when Grimani turns up. Not being able to find any opponent to play with, he starts to grow increasingly frustrated and is in search of solutions to his trouble.

entries.name: San Nicolò dei Mendicoli (Saint Nicholas of the Beggars)
entries: This small church was built around the twelfth century on an islet that was once used by poor sailors for housing, hence the name 'beggars' and the patron saint, St. Nicholas, who is, among other things, the patron saint of sailors and fishermen. Those who live near the church are still mostly sailors and fishermen, and they are known as Nicolotti. They have become a proud gang of the lower class workers, at odds with the 'Castellani,' who are based in Castello and are mainly Arsenale workers. These two groups are rivals in everything from regatta races to fist and stick fights on contested bridges.

entries.name: Ponte dei Pugni (Bridge of Fists)

entries: A cheer rises from the crowd as groaning and punching noises fill the air. People watching from the street, the gondolas on the water, or their windows above await the result of the frenzied brawl. A punch lays down the tall figure staggering toward the banister before the second hit drops him off the bridge, into the cold water. Though it seems the fight is over for now and the winner is obvious, the never-ending feud will continue the next day.

Nestled near Campo San Barnaba, Ponte dei Pugni is more than just a simple crossing over a canal. With the two sides of the bridge belonging to rival clans, the Nicolotti and Castellani, the debt has always been settled in the middle of the bridge, with four marks left on the corners of the bridge implying where the opponents make their stand-off before initiating the fight. Another bridge in Cannaregio sometimes serves the same purpose, but the preferred fighting ground is this 'neutral area' in Dorsoduro.

For nearly two hundred years, these two rival clans have been enemies of each other due to various reasons, like misplaced landowning and previous acts of antagonism. Due to possession of weapons being restricted inside the city, their way of handling disputes in time became mainly their fists or sticks. Whenever a dispute between the clans grew serious enough, they set a time to meet at the bridge and choose a champion amongst them to step onto the bridge. The champion tossing their opponent into the water is considered victorious and is allowed to leave their clan's mark on the bridge. When the brawl doesn't end in such a civil way, more arms from each side tend to join the battle.

entries.name: Faction: Castellani and Nicolotti
entries: The Castellani members largely consist of workers of the Arsenale, and their territory encompasses Castello, San Marco, and Dorsoduro. They believe that the five small districts of Dorsoduro, which were given to the Nicolotti by the doge 200 years ago, belong to them and should be given back. With Tomasso Pisani (LN human male, 40s, arsenalotte, shipwright) as their leader, the Castellani are not happy with the Doge's behavior towards Nicolotti, not taking any penalizing action against them even when they elect a leader and call it the Doge of Nicolotti.

The Nicolotti territory comprises the western parishes of Dorsoduro (added in the 1300s), San Polo, Santa Croce, and Cannaregio. They consist mostly of fishermen, sailors, and artisans not affiliated with the Arsenale. They vividly remember the day their bishop was wrongly killed by the Castellani for his being in association with the Nicolotti. They believe that the Castellani are the reason this city is starting to become corrupted each day, and since the Arsenale workers are favorites of the government, the Nicolotti see the Castellani as wealthier, more connected thugs who can get out of trouble more easily.

San Trovaso Church is neutral ground, with each group having their own entrance to the church for their marriages, funerals, and special days. Each side tries to curry favor with the San Trovaso Boatmakers, who are supposed to stay neutral, but the father and son owners secretly favor sides (Tomasso the Nicolotti, Niccolo the Castellani).

There is no joining these gangs unless you are born and raised in the neighborhoods where they rule. However, you can allow your players to do jobs for one of the gangs and potentially be given the status of "honorary members" if it fits your story.

entries.name: Ca' Dario (Dario Palace)

entries: There is something about how this building sits on the water that seems to stink and fester. It lists ever so slightly to the right; gondoliers keep a wide berth; and the sound of sundered wood, creaking and groaning, occasionally can be heard in the narrow canal nearby. At night, an even stranger host of sounds seems to issue forth from the depths: screaming, crying, cursing. The owners have assured you that the home is perfectly safe, but something surely seems wrong: as you stare at the palazzo from your boat, the house seems to be staring back...

Marietta Dario (Patrizio, New House), the daughter of the former Venetian ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, is currently the owner of the Palazzo Dario. With her father's relationship with the Ottoman officials standing still even after his death, Mariette seizes the opportunity and hosts Ottoman officials and ambassadors in this palace when they visit Venice. Though Marietta's father was loyal to the State of Venice, her new husband Vincenzo Barbaro (Patrizio, Old House) doesn't think they should always stay that way and convinces her to find new ways that would bring them more fortune.

{@b Port of Call:} Any characters from Ottoman lands would find a welcome place to stay here in Ca' Dario, though they may not find it welcome for very long. The palazzo is haunted by {@dice 2d4} {@creature ghost||ghosts}, determined to drive out any new homeowners.

entries.name: Chiesa di Ognissanti (Church of All Saints)
entries: There is a rumor that you can hear all the saints that have ever lived in the church of All Saints. It is believed that any person with the true desire to be enlightened and guided on their path will hear a saint who will lead and speak to them. An adventurer seeking guidance may roll on the table below to determine what they hear.

entries.caption: Voice of the Saints
rows: Saint Sebastian: "Go forth little one, be bold. Let faith be your guide against the spreading darkness. Your path is the right one; brave the hard time and reach the light."
Saint Denis: "Take no pity in the wound you get, as you walk the path to god, filled with thorny bush, you inspire others to join."
Saint Lawrence: "I tell you, do not resist an evil person. If anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn the other cheek. Violence is not the answer and never has it ever been."

Saint George: "Oh, I fear a lie more than I fear to die. Though I can battle dragons, it is I again who am powerless against those who ignore the truth of God. Don't let them spread their misdirection."

entries: The priest of the church Carlo Conti (CN human male, {@creature clergyman|EchoesOfRenaissance|priest of Venice, clergyman}) is a grumpy man in his late 40s. After losing his way several times and being able to find his path back with the help of the old Saints speaking to him, he realized that he might use this miracle of the church to his benefit. Asking money from the visitors of the church, he doesn't let anyone in who doesn't pay more than 10 gd. Touting this church as the holiest of the churches in Venice, he threatens those who enter without his will to be reported directly to the Lords of the Night as if they are defiling a holy place. Slowly losing the ability to hear from the past Saints and turning his back on religion, Carlo believes there is no return for him, and that's why the Saints have left him. Although he repeats it to every visitor, he seems to have forgotten that past Saints always speak to those who have their desires true in their hearts.

entries.name: Introduction
entries: Surrounding the islands that make up the six sestieri of Venice are numerous islands, some inhabited and some no more than silt and tall grass; some were even more important than Venice early in the history of the lagoon, like Malamocco and Torcello, but they have been left to sink into history. Others are prized, for various reasons, for their isolation.

entries.name: Lido di Venezia (The Barrier Island)
entries: To the south, Venice is sheltered from the Adriatic by the Lido, the bastion of the city and once the location of the lagoon's capital (at Malamocco).

entries.name: Overgrown Jewish Cemetery
entries: This cemetery looks more like an overgrown garden and used to be the main Jewish cemetery. Due to the varied origins of the Jews in the city, the gravestones range from Venetian Gothic to Ottoman. Some bear the image of a lion, but it is not the Venetian Lion of St. Mark, but that of Castile and Leon, due to the fact that many Sephardic Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 brought the symbol with them.

entries.name: Faction: Ottoman Spies
entries: There is a forward contingent of spies and soldiers from the Ottoman Empire who have made the old cemetery their base of operations. Any character with a background in the Ottoman lands or with an adversarial relationship to the city-states of Europe can find work amongst this crew, anything from scouting and hunting for food, to intelligence-gathering missions in the city.
The Ottoman camp is featured in Act I and III of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.

entries.name: Isola San Michele (St. Michele Island)
entries: Technically part of sestiere Cannaregio, this small island between the shore of Cannaregio and the island of Murano holds an impressive Renaissance church made entirely of fine Istrian limestone, Chiesa di San Michele in Isola. This is the first Renaissance church in Venice, and attached to the church is also a sizable monastery. The island is also a popular spot for fishermen to go and get away from the busy city without heading further afield into the lagoon.

The monastery hides a prison for dangerous heretics and enemies of the state; the state inquisitors take prisoners here who are deemed too dangerous to keep alive yet also too dangerous to execute publicly; these include any leaders of popular uprisings, witches, monsters, or occultists caught working against the government. Once the inquisitors get all the information they can out of the prisoners—namely, how best to defend against the likes of them—they execute them quietly. The island is littered with secret graves of those who have been brought here.
Isola San Michele makes an appearance in Act II of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.

entries.name: Isola di Murano (Murano, the Island of Glass)
entries: Murano glows with the fires of forges and the energy of industrial innovation. Venetians have been working in glass since at least the tenth century, but due to the fire hazards of glass-blowing, the industry was moved to the island of Murano in the thirteenth century. Yet restricting the industry to a tightly controlled and more secretive area was perhaps the plan all along, as Venice is always on guard when profits are on the line. The Murano glassmaking families live in great comfort, with more allowances afforded them than the average Venetian; for instance, women from their families are able to marry into noble houses. However, their restriction to Murano means that they're living in virtual captivity—gilded cages, but cages nonetheless. Trade secrets are so jealously guarded that any glass worker who leaves the city without government permission is in danger of expulsion from the guild and having his family imprisoned. If he still does not return, assassins are sent to find him.

Though there is competition between the glassmaking houses, since the end result is filling the coffers of the state, and not individual advancement, there is much exchange of ideas and techniques between workshops. Perhaps for this reason, Venice's glassmaking was able to innovate and produce at a level far superior to their competitors.

Because the glassmaking industry is so closely monitored and controlled by the government, any visitors to the workshops who are not expressly given permission run the risk of raising the ire of the government. This could provide some interesting complications for a band of adventurers.

entries.name: Faction: The Society of Sand
entries: "Nothing is built on stone; all is built on sand, but we must build as if the sand were stone."

Amidst the family workshops collaborating and competing for greatness, some glassmakers have begun meeting in secret for a more complex purpose. The Society of Sand, as the group calls itself, is devoted to pushing the limits of glassmaking into unforeseen, powerful arcane heights. They take inspiration from the fact that Venice grew from nothing, from silt and sea, into something tremendous; they hope to unlock the secrets of glassmaking and transform it into new exciting potentialities, from golems, to augury devices, and more. Hidden within the swirling molten glass, anything is possible, or so they believe. However, they work away from the eyes of the government agents to avoid their projects being co-opted or meddled with unnecessarily. The current head of their cabal is Benevuto Barovier (Maestro Vetraio, Glassblower), who also runs his family's workshop, Vetreria di Barovier.

entries.name: Vetreria di Barovier (Barovier's Wondrous Works)
entries: Made famous by the expert glassmaker and enameler maestro Angelo Barovier in the 1400s, the family-run business has continued and thrived since his passing in 1460. They are experts in enameled glass and Venetian Crystal, or cristallo, which Angelo is credited with creating.

The Barovier workshop is run by Benevuto Barovier (LG human male, maestro vetraio, master glassblower), the grandson of Angelo. Benevuto has extended his family's prestigious position in the industry while also delving into more arcane, secret projects: glasswork golems and weapons.

entries.name: Vetreria Sabbatini (Sabbatini Family Glassworks)
entries: This family specializes in lattimo, also known as milk glass, a special type of glass which resembles porcelain. Run by the irrepressible Vendramina Sabbatini (LG, human female, mid 30s, maestro vetraio, master glassblower, with STR 16 and CHA 16), who in the early evening leaves the work to her children and apprentices and patrols the island almost like a self-appointed Lord of the Night. She is famed for her stern glance and her cinquedea shortsword, garishly decorated with millefiori glass.

Vendramina's second oldest son, Luigi, is the most gifted of her scions and has joined the Society of Sand. In the storyline of A Serenade for the Damned, Luigi will be hired for a very special job: creating a glass crystallophone, a musical instrument made of glass bowls with an eerie and potentially maddening song.

entries.name: Vetreria di Zanetto (Favored One Glassworks)
entries: This workshop specializes in avventura—aventurine glass, also called goldstone glass. They make beads and decorative fixtures mostly, and some of their products have recently, and infamously, made their way to the Americas via Christopher Columbus's journeys.

entries.name: Basilica di Santa Maria e San Donato (Basilica of St. Mary and St. Donatus)
entries: This is one of the oldest basilicas in the Venetian lagoon. The original building dates back to the seventh century and was dedicated to St. Mary. Later, during a 12th-century scouring of valuables from Byzantine Greece, the supposed remains of St. Donatus of Euroea (and a few rib bones of a supposed dragon) were brought back to Venice. Thus, the basilica was renamed to honor both Mary and Donatus, the latter of whom may never have existed outside of legend. The remains of the saint and the dragon are suspect, but the real wonder of this basilica is the wondrous floor, a stunning and massive mosaic of precious stones rippling out in circular forms and animal shapes.

entries.name: Isola di Burano (Burano, the Island of Lace)
entries: In recent years, Burano has begun to grow famous for its handmade lace, which graces the frills and ruffs of aristocracy all over Venice. Though it has taken over the island, it is a recent development, only becoming popular and widespread after Venice's acquisition of Cyprus.

entries.name: The Island of Torcello (Ancient Heart of the Lagoon)
entries: Torcello is the island where many of the people who built Venice first settled. To escape the pillaging Huns in 452 CE, people from the Byzantine exarchate of Ravenna fled here, and over the next two centuries Lombards and Franks supplied the lagoon with a steady supply of settlers looking to capitalize on the relative peace, the trade with Byzantium, and the burgeoning salt prosperity. Torcello's fortunes dried up with its swamp by the fourteenth century, but the island is still an important one for the lagoon's history. The only permanent inhabitants are those dedicated to the basilica, led by the Dark Dapifer, a fiend in disguise.

entries.name: Basilica di Santa Maria Assunta (Church of the Assumption of St. Mary)
entries: Built in 639 CE in the Byzantine style, the Basilica di Santa Maria Assunta is the oldest Byzantine-Romanesque structure in the lagoon: it has the earliest mosaics in Venice, as well as the skull of St. Cecilia, the patron saint of music. The demure brick exterior hides vibrant scenes inside the basilica: the mosaic of the Harrowing of Hell shows a victorious Christ, standing on demons and the broken gates of Hell; he leads Adam out by the wrist, to show that man cannot save himself from original sin but only through the acts of God. The Last Judgement mosaic shows the souls of those who have been lost at sea being led to St. Peter by a sea nymph. At the same time, the Devil is portrayed manipulating the scales of Justice while his followers drag sinners to Hell.

For those who follow the Christian faith, the details of the church leave no middle ground for debate: follow the righteous path or be doomed. Those characters who are good-aligned or evil-aligned can both glean some affirmation for their perspective out of the mosaics, granting them a point of Inspiration once per week. Neutral characters gain nothing, as the walls and floors judge them for not choosing a side.

Any bards or musically-inclined characters can pray to St. Cecilia at the altar or the chapel dedicated to her—or better yet, they can play music in her honor. Upon doing so, they are granted {@dice 1d6} temporary hit points, a point of Inspiration, and one more use of Bardic Inspiration (if they're a bard), or {@dice 1d6} temporary hit points and a point of Inspiration if they are not bards. If the adventurer already gained Inspiration from the Basilica's mosaics upon entering the church, you can grant them another boon that seems appropriate, such as directly giving Advantage on the next attack or saving throw.

Adventurers may be tipped off about the strange community on Torcello by another group: the Canticle Company (La Compagnia del Cantico). The company is a group of itinerant musicians and faithful of St. Cecilia, the patron saint of music. They have come to Venice on a pilgrimage to Torcello, but they were turned away by the Emissaries of Loss, who have fully taken over the Basilica. If you want to inform the adventurers about what is going on in Torcello before they go there, or leave a clue that they could later follow, you could have them run into the Canticle Company while traveling around Venice. They could be performing in any campo with signs and symbols of St. Cecilia (roses, swords, and stringed instruments).

entries.name: Faction: Emissaries of Loss (Emissari della Perdita)
entries: These devoted people follow a person whom they believe is a Byzantine Roman prince named Nestorius Theklathon, and they are dedicated to keeping the Christianity of Venice aligned with the East. They mostly keep to themselves, though every now and then they will quietly bring a new convert to live on the silent isle. What most of them don't know is that their leader is not a Byzantine prince but is instead a {@creature dark dapifer|EchoesOfRenaissance}. It feeds off their longing for a past that may never have existed, at least in the way they formulate it. It feeds off their spite for Venice. It feeds off of them, literally. If the adventurers discover the true identity of the leader, the Dark Dapifer will introduce itself as "Thekla."

{@b Port of Call:} If the adventurers need shelter and a place to lay low away from Venice, the Emissaries will welcome them in with food and places to sleep inside the basilica. The longer the party stays there, however, the more likely it is that they notice something is off about the community. People will suddenly disappear and no one will care about it. Others walk around as if sleepwalking. If the adventurers stay longer than one night, they have to make a {@dc 16} Wisdom saving throw every day; on a failure, they gain 1 level of {@condition exhaustion} and lose {@dice 1d4} points from their Strength score.

entries.name: Lazzaretto Vecchio (The Old Quarantine Island)
entries: First established in 1423, the island has served as a quarantine area and hospital for patients inflicted with leprosy and the bubonic plague. There is a monastery on the island dedicated to St. Mary of Nazareth, which served as a place for pilgrims to rest, but otherwise, the island is secluded and sparsely populated—only a few monks usually. This seclusion is why it was chosen as an optimal site to isolate infected people, or suspected of being infected. The island's dedication to St. Mary led to its name: from Nazareth came "nazaretum," and then lazzaretto, although St. Lazarus, the patron saint of lepers, may have lent his name to the island facility as well.
There is also a nearby island, Isola di San Lazzaro, which has been a leper colony since the ninth century. It is also the home of the Order of St. Lazarus in Venice.

entries.name: Faction: The Castaways (I Naufraghi)
entries: The Castaways are a group of lepers, plague victims, and the monks who administer to them. Their leader is Brother Luca (NE, human male, late 30s, {@creature mortidanti|EchoesOfRenaissance|plague doctor, mortidanti}), who is working with select nobles from the Confraternity of St. Roch to better understand the plague's etiologies and how to defeat it. What the Brotherhood doesn't know, though, is that Brother Luca has been conducting his own grisly experiments: he has been convincing the plague victims to eat parts of those who die from plague, in the mistaken belief that consuming the plague will help defend against it.

The Castaways have a fractured relationship with the Order of St. Lazarus, whom they blame for not doing more to cure the disease in previous centuries in the Holy Land. Many Castaway members believe the Order is a relic of the past, and new remedies need to be sought.

entries.name: Faction: Order of St. Lazarus
entries: {@i Supremus Ordo Sancti Lazari Hierosolymitani Sacri Romani Imperii}

The Order of St. Lazarus has a headquarters on the Isola di San Lazzaro, a leper colony island right next to Lazzaretto Vecchio, but the chapter is dwindling. They are cut off from the rest of the city, and the city only gives marginal donations of food and supplies to help the colony. They administer aid to the lepers on their island as well as the ones on Vecchio, and the plague victims. The Castaways do not like their presence, as they believe the Order is doomed and stuck in the past.

The Order of Saint Lazarus was founded in a leper hospital in Jerusalem in the twelfth century. The order's main goal is to care for the people diagnosed with leprosy and research a cure for it. Their order became militaristic over time as their economy relied on donations, and war was the best income source. Although the Crusades are over, the military wing disbanded, and the Pope recently attempted to merge the Order's holdings with the Knights Hospitaller, the Order knights have stayed true to their mission, though their numbers have significantly dwindled—there are only ten knights left, and they are limited to the Isola di San Lazzaro and the Lazzaretto Vecchio by the orders of the Venetian government.

The signature of this order is their green Maltese cross, and members often wear bandages all over their bodies, or at least the visible portions. Most newcomers and low-ranking members are allowed to show their skin, but those who reach knighthood or enter the order as knights must swear an oath to wear the bandages all the time, both to protect others from catching leprosy and as a symbol of unity, silence, precaution, and dedication.

Their leader in Venice is Emanuele Acritano (LG, human male, crusader knight, no shield), a man in his fifties with a furrowed brow, sad brown eyes, and a disheveled beard. He wears the bandages of Lazarus, but has allowed some of his facial features to show through. Though he is technically a knight, he and his followers do not carry swords and shields. He is not stricken with leprosy despite his prolonged contact with members of the colony, and though he is committed to helping the needy, he inwardly believes it unlikely that the Order will ever find a cure. The world has moved on without them. Despite his name, Emanuele is not from Acre; instead he goes by the name to remind himself of the Fall of Acre in 1291, when the Crusades ended.

items: {@b Bandage of Saint:} While wearing these bandages, a member of the order's Constitution score becomes 15 if it isn't higher already.
{@b Face of Leprosy:} People are afraid of those who are cursed with leprosy. Members of the order gain +2 to their Charisma ({@skill Intimidation}) checks.
{@b Nerve Loss:} Leprosy causes numbing and loss of sensation. Members of the order are resistant to fire damage.

{@b Unyielding Spirit:} The suffering and isolation faced by lepers strengthen their resolve. Members of the order gain Advantage on saving throws against being {@condition frightened} or {@condition charmed}.

{@b Familiarity with Fatigue:} Tiredness doesn't affect those who are used to it. Members of the order can remove 1 level of {@condition exhaustion} on a short rest. This effect can only be used once per day.
{@b Cloaked:} Those who are cursed with leprosy cover themselves in sheets of cloth. Members have +2 bonus of Dexterity ({@skill Stealth}) checks.

entries.name: Lazzaretto Nuovo (The New Quarantine Island)
entries: Venice is particularly vulnerable to bouts of plague due to its dense population and limited land area, so the government has been vigilant about catching diseases before they spread. In addition to the Lazzaretto Vecchio, which is now a hospital and colony for "hopeless cases," in the eyes of many in the government, the Lazzaretto Nuovo is the new stopgap measure. Established in 1468, this island is where ships coming to Venice from known plague locations, or suspected of carrying plague, are required to stop and wait forty days.

entries.name: San Giorgio Maggiore (Island of St. George Major)
entries: This island is home to the St. George Monastery and the St. George Church. The monks of the monastery are currently discussing plans to rebuild the church and are enlisting the help of architects and patricians to do so.

The Monastery has been on the island since 982 CE and is a thriving center for theological, artistic, and cultural studies. Due to its picturesque and advantageous position—near the city center but also separate from it—San Maggiore has served as an ideal spot for visiting dignitaries. Although technically part of the sestiere San Marco, the monastery boasts relative autonomy from the government, so it can offer a certain amount of secrecy to those who stay. In the twelfth century, Pope Alexander III and Frederick Barbarossa met at the island, and if it aligns with your story, you could have emissaries of the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V staying at the monastery.
San Giorgio Maggiore makes an appearance in Acts II and III of {@i A Serenade for the Damned}.

entries.name: Giudecca (Island of Exile turned Wealthy Retreat)
entries: This large island just south of Dorsoduro originally served as a place to banish rebellious aristocratic families, but by the 1500s, many patrician families—Dandolo, Mocenigo, and Vendramin to name a few—have transformed the island into a district of gardens and villas.

entries.name: Sant'Erasmo (The Garden of Venice)
entries: Sant'Erasmo is the orto di Venezia, the garden of Venice. The island is long and thin, and it is populated by farmers ploughing their fields of purple artichokes, squash from the New World, asparagus, and other hardy vegetables able to handle the strange lagoon biome. The food grown here goes directly to the Erberia market at Rialto, or various smaller markets.

Other than the farmers, there is also a collection of followers of Bacchus (Cult of Bacchus) who have recently moved to the island. This group hails from all over Italy and the Mediterranean, called to the Venetian Lagoon for some mysterious purpose they do not understand. Not even the head priestesses of the cult, the gerarae and {@dice 1d4} maenads, know what is coming, but they have had visions of some grand Bacchanal in the near future. Once a month they have a bacchanal, and they keep to themselves, though their presence foretells deeper, darker developments.

entries.name: Le Vignole and Isola di Sant'Andrea
entries: The two islands of Vignole Vecchie and Vignole Nuove produce the doge's wine, and the landscape is covered in fields, groves, and vineyards. At the island's southeastern tip a promontory ends in the Isola di Sant'Andrea, the location of castel nuovo, the new fort guarding the entrance to the lagoon from the sea (castel vecchio is on the opposite side of the mouth, at the tip of the Lido).

entries.name: Forte Sant'Andrea (Castel nuovo)
entries: Built in the beginning of the 1500s to replace previous fortifications, this fort and the nearby Castel vecchio on Lido guard the entrance to the lagoon from the Adriatic Sea.
